\hypertarget{M02-mhealth-recency-and-frequency-at-a-fixed-date}{%
\section{mHealth: Recency and Frequency at a Fixed
Date}\label{M02-mhealth-recency-and-frequency-at-a-fixed-date}}

\noindent A manager considering a reminder campaign needs to distinguish a
customer who logs frequently from one who logged recently. Both
customers may have the same total number of records. Recency measures
elapsed time since the last observed activity, while frequency measures
repeated activity within a specified window. Their interpretation
depends on the date at which the manager must make the decision.

For every user with a recorded day by June 30, define recency as the
number of days from the most recent recorded day to June 30. Define
frequency as distinct recorded days during June 1--30. A customer who
last logged on June 30 has recency zero. A customer with no June logs
has frequency zero and remains eligible because an earlier record
establishes membership. July activity is an outcome and enters neither
feature.

The 358 eligible users are grouped using prespecified recency boundaries
of 7 and 30 days and a frequency boundary of 15 days. These cutoffs
define a descriptive comparison; they have not been optimized for a
campaign. The empty high-frequency, high-recency cell follows from the
definitions: a customer whose last log was more than 30 days ago has
zero June logging days.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.16}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.16}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.22}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.22}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.24}}@{}}
\toprule
Recency on June 30 & June Logging Days & Users & Any July Log & Mean
July Logging Days \\
\midrule

0--7 Days & 0--14 & 68 & 92.6\% & 13.90 \\
0--7 Days & 15--30 & 220 & 96.8\% & 22.88 \\
8--30 Days & 0--14 & 34 & 67.6\% & 7.26 \\
8--30 Days & 15--30 & 6 & 83.3\% & 9.67 \\
31+ Days & 0--14 & 30 & 50.0\% & 5.70 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Recent frequent loggers have a higher July logging rate in this cohort.
The six-user cell warrants particular care because a single outcome
changes its rate substantially. These rates describe future activity
among known users; they do not identify which users would respond most
to a reminder. Selecting recipients requires an incremental-effect
comparison and a cost per contact.

\href{https://github.com/joaolcorreia/RFM-analysis}{Joao Correia's RFM
example} combines recency, frequency, and monetary value in transaction
data. mHealth supports the first two dimensions. Calories, entry counts,
and body weight have units different from spending and cannot supply
monetary value. A commercial RFM table would need an actual monetary
variable, a transaction definition, and a consistent observation window.

A coding assistant should receive the snapshot date and the eligible
population explicitly. Ask it to verify that adding July rows leaves
both June features unchanged, that repeated food entries on one day
count only once toward frequency, and that zero-log members remain in
the outcome denominator. Quantile bins require extra care when many
customers share the same integer count; the fixed boundaries here avoid
assigning tied counts to different groups.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/mHealth/recurring_examples/recency.py}{recency.py}.
From its directory, run \texttt{python\ recency.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Describe later logging using features available at a fixed snapshot."""

import json
import pandas as pd
from common import OUTPUT, load_food, make_daily, save_result


def snapshot(daily, cutoff):
    cutoff = pd.Timestamp(cutoff)
    history = daily.loc[daily.date <= cutoff]
    last = history.groupby("Userid").date.max()
    recent = history.loc[history.date > cutoff - pd.Timedelta(days=30)]
    counts = recent.groupby("Userid").date.nunique().reindex(last.index, fill_value=0)
    return pd.DataFrame(
        {"recency_days": (cutoff - last).dt.days, "frequency_30d": counts}
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    daily = make_daily(load_food())
    customers = snapshot(daily, "2016-06-30")
    customers["recency_group"] = pd.cut(
        customers.recency_days,
        [-1, 7, 30, float("inf")],
        labels=["0-7 days", "8-30 days", "31+ days"],
    )
    customers["frequency_group"] = customers.frequency_30d.ge(15).map(
        {True: "15-30 days", False: "0-14 days"}
    )
    july = daily.loc[daily.date.between("2016-07-01", "2016-07-31")]
    customers["july_days"] = (
        july.groupby("Userid").date.nunique().reindex(customers.index, fill_value=0)
    )
    customers["july_any_log"] = customers.july_days.gt(0)
    assert customers.frequency_30d.between(0, 30).all()
    summary = (
        customers.groupby(["recency_group", "frequency_group"], observed=True)
        .agg(
            users=("july_days", "size"),
            july_users=("july_any_log", "sum"),
            july_logging_probability=("july_any_log", "mean"),
            mean_july_days=("july_days", "mean"),
        )
        .reset_index()
    )
    result = {
        "snapshot": "2016-06-30",
        "users": len(customers),
        "groups": summary.to_dict(orient="records"),
    }
    save_result("recency", result)
    summary.to_csv(OUTPUT / "recency.csv", index=False)
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M02-mhealth-chart-choice-denominators-and-customer-differences}{%
\section{mHealth: Chart Choice, Denominators, and Customer
Differences}\label{M02-mhealth-chart-choice-denominators-and-customer-differences}}

\noindent A manager sees nearly unchanged activity on days when customers record
food and considers reducing attention to retention. That comparison
conditions on having a recorded day. A customer who stops logging
disappears from the conditional average. A useful business review
therefore distinguishes the frequency of recorded days from the amount
of activity on those days, with the eligible population fixed before
either reporting month.

The comparison retains the 340 users with at least one observed day
before May 1, 2016. Each user contributes all 31 May days and all 30
June days to the logging denominator. Repeated food entries on one day
count once toward logging coverage. A calendar day without a food entry
receives zero for the logging indicator. Its food consumption remains
unobserved. Food-entry counts retain the recorded rows and describe
recording intensity.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}
\toprule
Measure & May & June \\
\midrule

Eligible Users & 340 & 340 \\
Users With Logs & 317 & 313 \\
Eligible Calendar User-Days & 10,540 & 10,200 \\
Days With Logs & 7,082 & 6,331 \\
Days With Logs / Eligible Days & 67.19\% & 62.07\% \\
Days With Logs / Logger Calendar Days & 72.07\% & 67.42\% \\
Entries per Recorded Day & 11.80 & 11.69 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The conditional logging rate divides by calendar days for users who
logged at least once in that month. Its denominator changes with the
outcome: May contains 317 such users and June contains 313. Both
conditional rates exceed the corresponding fixed-population rates.
Logging coverage in the fixed population falls by 5.12 percentage
points, while entries per recorded day change little. Stable recording
intensity among observed days can coexist with declining coverage of the
eligible population. These patterns support examining disengagement and
recording behavior; they do not identify a change in dietary intake or
an effect of a reminder.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M02_logging_denominators.tex}
\caption{The same logged days produce different rates when the denominator excludes users with no logs.}\label{fig:M02_logging_denominators}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{M02-match-the-display-to-the-decision}{%
\subsection{Match the Display to the
Decision}\label{M02-match-the-display-to-the-decision}}

\noindent The
\href{https://github.com/Financial-Times/chart-doctor/blob/main/visual-vocabulary/README.md}{Financial
Times Visual Vocabulary} organizes displays by the relationship the
reader needs to assess. The first choice is the comparison. A list of
available plotting functions provides little guidance about whether the
manager needs a ranking, a distribution, a trend, or an estimated
contrast.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.33}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.33}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.34}}@{}}
\toprule
Analytical Question & Useful Display & Essential Check \\
\midrule

Which segment is larger? & Sorted bars or dots & Common units and
base \\
Where is the distribution concentrated? & Histogram or ECDF & Bins,
ties, and weights \\
How does a metric change over time? & Line or paired dots & Calendar and
membership \\
How do two variables move together? & Scatterplot or hexagons & Support
and overlap \\
What share belongs to each category? & Aligned shares or bars & Common
denominator \\
How uncertain is a contrast? & Point and interval & Estimand and
sampling unit \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

A bar encodes its magnitude through length from a baseline, so the
logging-rate bars start at zero. Two percentage axes with different
limits would change the visual comparison even when the data are
identical. A dot-and-interval plot can use a narrower, explicitly
labeled scale because the position represents the estimate and the
interval represents its uncertainty. For dense scatterplots,
transparency, hexagonal bins, or a documented sample can reveal
concentrations that overlapping opaque points hide. Bin boundaries and
color limits should stay fixed when comparing customer groups.

Use Illinois Blue and Illini Orange to distinguish the principal series,
with labels and line styles carrying the same information. A heatmap of
a nonnegative count needs an ordered light-to-dark scale. A signed
deviation needs a meaningful center, usually zero, with comparable
positive and negative distances. Unobserved cells need a separate label
or pattern so that a reader can distinguish them from observed zeros.
Small multiples should retain a common scale when the decision depends
on cross-panel magnitudes.

\hypertarget{M02-an-average-decline-can-coexist-with-no-median-change}{%
\subsection{An Average Decline Can Coexist With No Median
Change}\label{M02-an-average-decline-can-coexist-with-no-median-change}}

\noindent The user-level outcome is the fraction of a month's calendar days with a
log. For a value \(x\) between zero and one, its empirical cumulative
distribution is

\[
\widehat F_m(x)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}\{p_{im}\leq x\},
\]

where \(p_{im}\) is user \(i\)'s logging fraction in month \(m\) and
\(N\) is the fixed eligible-user count. The height at \(x\) is the
fraction of users whose logging frequency is at or below that value.
Each user has equal weight. Ties produce jumps, including the jump at
zero for users without a recorded day. The curve avoids a histogram's
bin-width choice, while its denominator and observation unit still
require an explicit definition.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M02_logging_distribution.tex}
\caption{The logging-frequency distributions retain users at zero and reveal the concentration near daily recording.}\label{fig:M02_logging_distribution}
\end{figure}

The zero-logging share is 6.76\% in May and 7.94\% in June. At the other
endpoint, 105 users log on every May day and 89 log on every June day.
The median user's June-minus-May change is zero, while the mean change
is negative. The middle half of individual changes spans approximately
\(-17.58\) to \(+3.36\) percentage points. A mean decline therefore
describes an aggregate change that is distributed unevenly across
customers. It does not imply that every user reduced logging by five
percentage points.

Histograms remain useful when the shape of a distribution matters.
Compare several defensible bin widths and align bins across groups. A
smooth density estimate requires extra care for bounded fractions with
substantial mass at zero and one; smoothing can suggest observations
outside the feasible range or conceal endpoint masses. The
\href{https://seaborn.pydata.org/tutorial/distributions.html}{seaborn
distribution tutorial} discusses these choices. A distribution's spread
and an estimate's uncertainty answer different questions, as the
\href{https://seaborn.pydata.org/tutorial/error_bars.html}{error-bar
tutorial} makes explicit. M3, Section 3.6, calculates uncertainty for
the average paired change.

\hypertarget{M02-reproduce-the-comparison}{%
\subsection{Reproduce the
Comparison}\label{M02-reproduce-the-comparison}}

\noindent The program selects membership before May, counts distinct logged days,
creates complete user-month pairs, and exports only aggregate tables. It
also calculates the paired-user interval used in M3. Missing-month users
remain in the logging calculation. The 5,000 bootstrap draws resample
users with both monthly outcomes together. The deliberately incorrect
independent-day interval is retained with its assumption stated in its
name.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/mHealth/recurring_examples/visualization.py}{visualization.py}.
From its directory, run \texttt{python\ visualization.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Prepare aggregate chart data and paired uncertainty for May and June."""

import json
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from common import OUTPUT, ROOT, SEED, load_food, save_result

MONTHS = ["2016-05", "2016-06"]


def prepare(food):
    # Membership is fixed before May; an absent log is zero logging only.
    members = sorted(food.loc[food.date < "2016-05-01", "Userid"].unique())
    if not members:
        raise ValueError("No users observed before May")
    rates = pd.DataFrame(index=members)
    rows = []
    for month in MONTHS:
        period = pd.Period(month, freq="M")
        part = food.loc[
            food.Userid.isin(members) & food.date.dt.to_period("M").eq(period)
        ]
        counts = (
            part[["Userid", "date"]].drop_duplicates().groupby("Userid").size()
            .reindex(members, fill_value=0)
        )
        rates[month] = counts / period.days_in_month
        observed = int(counts.sum())
        active = int(counts.gt(0).sum())
        assert counts.between(0, period.days_in_month).all()
        rows.append({
            "period": month, "eligible_users": len(members),
            "users_with_logs": active, "observed_user_days": observed,
            "calendar_user_days": len(members) * period.days_in_month,
            "logger_calendar_days": active * period.days_in_month,
            "food_entries": len(part),
            "logging_percent": 100 * rates[month].mean(),
            "conditional_logging_percent": (
                100 * observed / (active * period.days_in_month) if active else None
            ),
            "entries_per_observed_day": len(part) / observed if observed else None,
        })
    return rates, pd.DataFrame(rows)


def ecdf(values):
    """Exact right-continuous CDF; tied values contribute their full mass."""
    values = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    if len(values) == 0 or not np.isfinite(values).all():
        raise ValueError("A nonempty finite sample is required")
    x, count = np.unique(values, return_counts=True)
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "logging_percent": 100 * x, "users_at_value": count,
        "cumulative_percent": 100 * count.cumsum() / len(values),
        "eligible_users": len(values),
    })


def paired_summary(rates, draws=5000):
    # Each sampled index carries both months for the same user.
    difference = rates[MONTHS[1]].to_numpy() - rates[MONTHS[0]].to_numpy()
    if len(difference) < 2 or not np.isfinite(difference).all():
        raise ValueError("At least two complete user pairs are required")
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    indices = rng.integers(0, len(difference), size=(draws, len(difference)))
    bootstrap = difference[indices].mean(axis=1)
    low, high = np.quantile(bootstrap, [0.025, 0.975])
    return {
        "users": len(difference), "bootstrap_draws": draws, "seed": SEED,
        "change_pp": float(100 * difference.mean()),
        "ci_low_pp": float(100 * low), "ci_high_pp": float(100 * high),
        "paired_se_pp": float(100 * difference.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(difference))),
        "individual_change_q25_pp": float(100 * np.quantile(difference, 0.25)),
        "individual_change_median_pp": float(100 * np.median(difference)),
        "individual_change_q75_pp": float(100 * np.quantile(difference, 0.75)),
    }


def main():
    rates, monthly = prepare(load_food())
    comparison = paired_summary(rates)
    # Deliberately wrong independence assumption, retained as a teaching contrast.
    p = monthly.logging_percent.to_numpy() / 100
    n = monthly.calendar_user_days.to_numpy()
    naive_se = float(100 * np.sqrt(np.sum(p * (1 - p) / n)))
    comparison.update({
        "naive_independent_days_se_pp": naive_se,
        "naive_ci_low_pp": comparison["change_pp"] - 1.96 * naive_se,
        "naive_ci_high_pp": comparison["change_pp"] + 1.96 * naive_se,
    })
    cdf = pd.concat([ecdf(rates[m]).assign(period=m) for m in MONTHS], ignore_index=True)
    assert np.allclose(monthly.logging_percent,
                       100 * monthly.observed_user_days / monthly.calendar_user_days)
    assert cdf.groupby("period").users_at_value.sum().eq(len(rates)).all()
    OUTPUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    monthly.to_csv(OUTPUT / "visualization_monthly.csv", index=False)
    cdf.to_csv(OUTPUT / "visualization_ecdf.csv", index=False)
    manifest = json.loads((ROOT.parent / "manifest.json").read_text())
    result = {
        "source_sha256": manifest["files"]["food_entries.csv.gz"]["sha256"],
        "membership": "At least one observed day before 2016-05-01",
        "observation": "user-month; fraction of calendar days with a food entry",
        "interpretation": "descriptive within the selected cohort",
        "months": monthly.to_dict(orient="records"), "paired_change": comparison,
    }
    save_result("visualization", result)
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M02-interactive-charts-must-preserve-the-comparison}{%
\section{Interactive Charts Must Preserve the
Comparison}\label{M02-interactive-charts-must-preserve-the-comparison}}

\noindent An interactive display can help a manager inspect alternative
denominators and distribution shapes. Each control also changes the
information being presented. A month selector should update the
numerator, denominator, labels, and distribution together. Retaining a
stale count after filtering would make a correct plotted height describe
the wrong population. Holding axes at 0--100\% makes changes across
selections comparable.

The
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/mHealth/recurring_examples/results/visualization_interactive.html}{mHealth
chart} compares the all-user and observed-logger denominators for a
selected month. Its second panel displays the selected month's
distribution across the full eligible cohort. The data table remains
visible below the chart, with the observation counts and denominators
for both months. Hover labels supplement the table. A reader can verify
each rate without inferring a value from a bar's height.

\href{https://github.com/altair-viz/altair-tutorial}{Altair's tutorial}
provides a declarative approach in which the chart specifies data
fields, visual encodings, and interactions. The older tutorial's
selection syntax differs from the version used here. The program uses
Altair 5.5.0, a bound parameter, and explicitly fixed scales.
\href{https://altair-viz.github.io/user_guide/interactions/bindings_widgets.html}{The
widget documentation} and
\href{https://altair-viz.github.io/user_guide/saving_charts.html}{HTML-export
documentation} describe these operations. The exported HTML contains
aggregate data and runs without a Python server. Its JavaScript
libraries load from a public CDN, so chart rendering requires internet
access.

Static figures and interactive views should agree on every plotted
value. Run \texttt{visualization.py} before
\texttt{visualization\_charts.py}. The chart program checks the monthly
table against the saved numerical results and uses the same aggregate
data for both forms of display.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/mHealth/recurring_examples/visualization_charts.py}{visualization\_charts.py}.
From its directory, run \texttt{python\ visualization\_charts.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Build TikZ figures and a browser chart from verified aggregate tables."""

import json
import altair as alt
import pandas as pd
from common import OUTPUT, ROOT
from visualization import MONTHS

FIGURES = ROOT.parents[2] / "06_Lecture_Notes" / "figures"
BLUE, ORANGE = "#13294B", "#FF5F05"


def coordinates(x, y):
    return " ".join(f"({a:.8f},{b:.8f})" for a, b in zip(x, y))


def tikz_figures(monthly, cdf, result):
    FIGURES.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    bars = r"""\begin{tikzpicture}
\begin{axis}[ybar,bar width=22pt,width=12.5cm,height=6.3cm,
 ymin=0,ymax=100,ylabel={Calendar Days With Logs (\%)},
 xtick={0,1},xticklabels={May,June},enlarge x limits=0.6,
 legend style={at={(0.5,-0.17)},anchor=north,legend columns=2,column sep=10pt},
 nodes near coords,point meta=y,
 every node near coord/.append style={font=\footnotesize,/pgf/number format/fixed,/pgf/number format/precision=1}]
\addplot[draw=IlliniBlue,fill=IlliniBlue!18] coordinates {ALL};
\addplot[draw=IlliniOrange,fill=IlliniOrange!18] coordinates {CONDITIONAL};
\legend{All eligible users,Users with logs that month}
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
"""
    bars = bars.replace("ALL", coordinates([0, 1], monthly.logging_percent))
    bars = bars.replace("CONDITIONAL", coordinates([0, 1], monthly.conditional_logging_percent))
    (FIGURES / "M02_logging_denominators.tex").write_text(bars)
    distribution = r"""\begin{tikzpicture}
\begin{axis}[width=12.5cm,height=6.5cm,xmin=0,xmax=100,ymin=0,ymax=100,
 xlabel={User's Calendar Days With Logs (\%)},ylabel={Users at or Below That Value (\%)},
 legend style={at={(0.03,0.97)},anchor=north west},grid=major]
"""
    for month, style in zip(MONTHS, ["IlliniBlue,solid", "IlliniOrange,dashed"]):
        part = cdf.loc[cdf.period.eq(month)]
        points = "(0,0) " + coordinates(part.logging_percent, part.cumulative_percent)
        distribution += rf"\addplot[{style},const plot] coordinates {{{points}}};" + "\n"
    distribution += "\\legend{May,June}\n\\end{axis}\n\\end{tikzpicture}\n"
    (FIGURES / "M02_logging_distribution.tex").write_text(distribution)
    comparison = result["paired_change"]
    intervals = r"""\begin{tikzpicture}
\begin{axis}[width=11cm,height=5.5cm,xmin=-10,xmax=1,ymin=-0.6,ymax=1.6,
 xlabel={June Minus May (Percentage Points)},ytick={0,1},
 yticklabels={{Independent days (incorrect)},{Paired user bootstrap}},
 grid=major]
\addplot[Storm,dashed] coordinates {(0,-0.5) (0,1.5)};
"""
    for y, low, high, color in [
        (1, comparison["ci_low_pp"], comparison["ci_high_pp"], "IlliniBlue"),
        (0, comparison["naive_ci_low_pp"], comparison["naive_ci_high_pp"], "Storm"),
    ]:
        points = coordinates([low, high], [y, y])
        intervals += rf"\addplot[{color},very thick,mark=|,mark size=5pt] coordinates {{{points}}};" + "\n"
        intervals += rf"\addplot[{color},only marks,mark=*] coordinates {{({comparison['change_pp']:.8f},{y})}};" + "\n"
    intervals += "\\end{axis}\n\\end{tikzpicture}\n"
    (FIGURES / "M03_logging_uncertainty.tex").write_text(intervals)


def interactive_chart(monthly, cdf):
    records = []
    for row in monthly.to_dict(orient="records"):
        for population, users, denominator, value in [
            ("All eligible users", row["eligible_users"], row["calendar_user_days"], row["logging_percent"]),
            ("Users with logs", row["users_with_logs"], row["logger_calendar_days"], row["conditional_logging_percent"]),
        ]:
            records.append({"period": row["period"], "population": population,
                            "users": users, "calendar_days": denominator,
                            "observed_days": row["observed_user_days"], "percent": value})
    table = pd.DataFrame(records)
    month = alt.param(name="month", value=MONTHS[0],
                      bind=alt.binding_select(options=MONTHS, name="Month: "))
    bars = alt.Chart(table).transform_filter(alt.datum.period == month).mark_bar().encode(
        x=alt.X("population:N", title=None, axis=alt.Axis(labelAngle=0)),
        y=alt.Y("percent:Q", title="Calendar Days With Logs (%)", scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0, 100])),
        color=alt.Color("population:N", scale=alt.Scale(range=[BLUE, ORANGE]), legend=None),
        tooltip=[alt.Tooltip("population:N"), alt.Tooltip("percent:Q", format=".2f"),
                 "users:Q", "observed_days:Q", "calendar_days:Q"],
    ).properties(width=320, height=300, title="The Denominator Changes the Rate")
    curve = alt.Chart(cdf).transform_filter(alt.datum.period == month).mark_line(
        interpolate="step-after", color=BLUE
    ).encode(
        x=alt.X("logging_percent:Q", title="User's Days With Logs (%)", scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0, 100])),
        y=alt.Y("cumulative_percent:Q", title="Users at or Below (%)", scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0, 100])),
        order="logging_percent:Q",
        tooltip=[alt.Tooltip("logging_percent:Q", format=".2f"),
                 alt.Tooltip("cumulative_percent:Q", format=".2f"), "users_at_value:Q", "eligible_users:Q"],
    ).properties(width=320, height=300, title="Distribution Across All Eligible Users")
    chart = alt.hconcat(bars, curve).add_params(month).configure_axis(
        labelColor=BLUE, titleColor=BLUE, labelFontSize=12, titleFontSize=12
    ).configure_title(color=BLUE, fontSize=15).configure_view(stroke=None)
    chart.save(OUTPUT / "visualization_interactive.vl.json")
    html = chart.to_html(embed_options={"renderer": "svg", "actions": False})
    table_text = table.rename(columns={
        "period": "Month", "population": "Population", "users": "Users",
        "calendar_days": "Calendar User-Days", "observed_days": "Days With Logs",
        "percent": "Days With Logs (%)",
    }).to_html(index=False, float_format=lambda x: f"{x:.2f}", border=0)
    n = int(monthly.eligible_users.iloc[0])
    introduction = (
        "<main><h1>mHealth: Logging Coverage</h1><p>Marketing Analytics · By Nathan Yang</p>"
        f"<p>{n} users observed before May 2016. The left chart compares two denominators. "
        "The right chart retains every eligible user, including users with no recorded days. "
        "Change the month to inspect both views. Both axes retain the same scales.</p>"
    )
    description = (
        "<h2>Chart Data</h2><p>Calendar user-days equal users multiplied by days in the month. "
        "No logged day means no observed food entry, without implying zero consumption. "
        "These descriptive comparisons do not estimate a treatment effect.</p>"
        + table_text
        + "<p>Internet access is required to display the charts. "
        "The data table remains available offline.</p></main>"
    )
    css = """<style>body{font:16px system-ui;color:#13294B;max-width:1000px;margin:32px auto;padding:0 24px}
    h1{border-bottom:3px solid #FF5F05;padding-bottom:12px}p{line-height:1.55;max-width:850px}
    table{border-collapse:collapse;font-size:14px}td,th{padding:10px;border-bottom:1px solid #C6C7C6;text-align:right}
    #vis{max-width:100%;overflow-x:auto}th{background:#EEF1F5}select{font-size:16px;padding:6px}.vega-bindings{margin:15px 0}</style>"""
    html = html.replace("</head>", css + "</head>").replace("<body>", "<body>" + introduction)
    html = html.replace("</body>", description + "</body>")
    (OUTPUT / "visualization_interactive.html").write_text(html)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    monthly = pd.read_csv(OUTPUT / "visualization_monthly.csv")
    cdf = pd.read_csv(OUTPUT / "visualization_ecdf.csv")
    result = json.loads((OUTPUT / "visualization.json").read_text())
    pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(monthly, pd.DataFrame(result["months"]), check_dtype=False)
    assert cdf.groupby("period").users_at_value.sum().eq(result["paired_change"]["users"]).all()
    tikz_figures(monthly, cdf, result)
    interactive_chart(monthly, cdf)
    print("Built three TikZ figures, the Vega-Lite specification, and interactive HTML.")
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M02-mcdonalds-measuring-ice-cream-availability}{%
\section{McDonald's: Measuring Ice-Cream
Availability}\label{M02-mcdonalds-measuring-ice-cream-availability}}

\noindent \noindent A restaurant manager deciding where to investigate service
interruptions needs to know which customers could not obtain the
advertised product. A digital ordering system supplies one observation
of availability. McBroken records an indicator named \texttt{is\_broken}
from the ordering channel. An unavailable item can reflect equipment
failure, cleaning, a closed restaurant, depleted inventory, or a problem
in the ordering system. A verification call can distinguish these
mechanisms before a manager sends a technician or changes a promotion.
The analytical outcome is therefore \textbf{recorded order
unavailability}. A repair log would supply a different outcome.

The supplied
\href{../01_Resources/02_M2_Customer_Data_and_Visualization/mcbroken_api_lab/README.md}{McBroken
collection} contains US records from October 25, 2025, through October
24, 2026, plus a longer weekly country series. Rashiq Zahid's
\href{https://mcbroken.com/}{McBroken} is the underlying source;
\href{https://github.com/MrFlynn/mcbroken-archive}{MrFlynn's archive}
preserves successive snapshots. The archive's inspected workflow selects
records with a reported check age below 61 minutes. Its older README
describes a different freshness window, so the retrieval rule and
version matter. An archive commit time records when a file was saved.
The estimated check time also depends on the reported check age.

\hypertarget{M02-coverage-determines-the-population-behind-a-percentage}{%
\subsection{Coverage Determines the Population Behind a
Percentage}\label{M02-coverage-determines-the-population-behind-a-percentage}}

\noindent \noindent Let \(R_{it}\) indicate that address key \(i\) appears in the
selected snapshot on date \(t\), and let \(U_{it}\) equal one when that
record reports unavailability. The observed daily percentage is

\[
100\widehat p_t=100\frac{\sum_i R_{it}U_{it}}{\sum_i R_{it}}.
\]

The denominator counts records observed in that snapshot. An absent
record has an unknown status. It contributes to neither the numerator
nor the denominator. Counting absence as availability would lower the
reported percentage whenever collection coverage falls. The fraction
also differs from the share of customer visits that encounter an
unavailable item: customer arrivals and purchases supply the weights for
that managerial outcome.

The assessment reconciles the store panel with the supplied national
totals and verifies unique store-date keys. The 365-date calendar
contains US records on 356 dates, including three dates with fewer than
2,000 records. Nine dates have no US observations. The July 24, 2026,
snapshot has only two US records, both reporting availability. Its zero
percentage describes those two records. The missing dates remain missing
in the course table.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M02_mcbroken_coverage.tex}
\caption{US record counts and recorded unavailability follow different series. The dashed count threshold is an imposed sensitivity screen, and gaps remain missing.}\label{fig:M02_mcbroken_coverage}
\end{figure}

An equal-day average gives each observed date the same weight. A pooled
fraction gives greater weight to dates with more records. For these
data, the equal-day average is 13.18\% and the pooled record fraction is
13.37\%. Restricting the calculation to dates with at least 2,000
records gives 13.22\% and 13.37\%, respectively. Requiring 5,000 records
leaves 279 dates and gives 13.48\% and 13.47\%. These comparisons
measure sensitivity to coverage restrictions; a count threshold alone
does not make the retained sample representative. The 2,000-record rule
is an explicit teaching choice.

\FloatBarrier

\hypertarget{M02-address-keys-and-restaurant-identity}{%
\subsection{Address Keys and Restaurant
Identity}\label{M02-address-keys-and-restaurant-identity}}

\noindent \noindent The supplied dimension table contains 29,123 address-based
keys and 13,821 exact coordinate pairs. Changes in street spelling can
create a new key at the same coordinates. The discrepancy is a useful
linkage diagnostic, although a coordinate match by itself does not
establish that two records describe the same restaurant. Nearby outlets,
rounded coordinates, and corrected locations require additional review.
The calculations retain the supplied keys and record the coordinate
count without merging outlets automatically.

The median key appears on 112 dates. Among 3,024,184 successive
within-key record pairs, 929,451 span more than one calendar day. A row
shift would silently describe many irregular intervals as one-day
transitions. An exact join on key and next calendar date preserves the
intended horizon. A key that changes spelling between those dates then
lacks a linked outcome. This linkage choice narrows the forecast
population and makes the missing-label count economically relevant.

\hypertarget{M02-verify-the-parser-before-treating-a-status-as-observed}{%
\subsection{Verify the Parser Before Treating a Status as
Observed}\label{M02-verify-the-parser-before-treating-a-status-as-observed}}

\noindent \noindent JSON booleans, missing fields, and text strings require
separate treatment. In Python, \texttt{bool(None)} returns
\texttt{False}, whereas \texttt{bool("false")} returns \texttt{True}.
Either conversion can produce a plausible but incorrect status if the
input schema changes. An unrecognized check-age string also leaves the
check time unknown; substituting zero minutes makes the observation
appear newly collected. The parser below uses constructed edge cases to
preserve these distinctions. The supplied CSV status column passes a
binary-value check, but that check cannot recover information already
lost during its original conversion.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/McBroken/api_checks.py}{api\_checks.py}. From
its directory, run \texttt{python\ api\_checks.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Preserve unknown API values instead of inventing a working machine or check time."""
import re

import pandas as pd


def status(value):
    if value is True:
        return 1
    if value is False:
        return 0
    if value is None:
        return pd.NA
    raise ValueError(f"Expected a JSON boolean or null, received {value!r}")


def check_time(snapshot_utc, text):
    match = re.fullmatch(r"Checked (\d+) minutes? ago", text or "")
    if match is None:
        return pd.NaT
    return pd.Timestamp(snapshot_utc) - pd.Timedelta(minutes=int(match.group(1)))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Constructed edge cases for an AI-generated parser, not observed store data.
    values = pd.Series([status(v) for v in [True, False, None]], dtype="Int64")
    assert values.iloc[0] == 1 and values.iloc[1] == 0 and pd.isna(values.iloc[2])
    assert pd.isna(check_time("2026-10-24T18:00:00Z", None))
    try:
        status("false")
    except ValueError:
        print("A string status requires schema review; an unknown status remains missing.")
    else:
        raise AssertionError("String status was silently accepted")
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M02-assess-and-reproduce-the-availability-comparisons}{%
\subsection{Assess and Reproduce the Availability
Comparisons}\label{M02-assess-and-reproduce-the-availability-comparisons}}

\noindent \noindent The preparation program checks unique keys, join coverage,
status values, check ages, national totals, and the dimension table's
observed-date counts. It creates a complete calendar before calculating
rates. It also constructs exact next-day matches for Section 7.18,
retaining the number of eligible origins when their next-day outcome is
missing. The source-file hashes and selected archive commit identifiers
keep the calculations traceable. The source bundle is required to
rebuild these aggregates; the released aggregate tables support the
subsequent programs directly.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/McBroken/prepare.py}{prepare.py}. From its
directory, run \texttt{python\ prepare.py}. The default input is the
supplied resource bundle; \texttt{-\/-source\ PATH} selects another copy
of its data directory.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Assess supplied McBroken tables and build aggregate, offline teaching inputs."""
import argparse
import hashlib
import json
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
DEFAULT_SOURCE = (ROOT.parents[1] / "01_Resources" /
                  "02_M2_Customer_Data_and_Visualization/mcbroken_api_lab/data")
PREFIX = "mcbroken_daily_2025-10_2026-10_"


def validate_panel(panel, dimension):
    if panel.duplicated(["date", "store_key"]).any():
        raise ValueError("Duplicate store-date records")
    if dimension.store_key.duplicated().any():
        raise ValueError("Duplicate dimension keys")
    if not panel.is_broken.isin([0, 1]).all():
        raise ValueError("Missing or nonbinary status")
    if not panel.store_key.isin(dimension.store_key).all():
        raise ValueError("Unmatched store key")
    if not panel.last_checked_min.between(0, 60).all():
        raise ValueError("Check age outside the supplied archive's range")


def make_transitions(panel, daily):
    """Match exact next calendar dates; retain the count of unlabeled origins."""
    good = daily.n_checked.ge(2000) & daily.offset_hours.abs().le(3)
    origin = panel[panel.date.isin(daily.loc[good, "date"])].copy()
    origin["date"] += pd.Timedelta(days=1)
    origin = origin[origin.date.le(daily.date.max())]
    origin = origin.rename(columns={"is_broken": "previous_unavailable"})
    target = panel[panel.date.isin(daily.loc[good, "date"])][
        ["date", "store_key", "is_broken"]]
    pairs = origin.merge(target, on=["date", "store_key"], how="left",
                         validate="one_to_one")
    return (pairs.groupby(["date", "previous_unavailable"]).is_broken
            .agg(n_origins="size", n_labeled="count", n_unavailable="sum")
            .reset_index())


def main(source):
    source = Path(source)
    used = []
    def read(name, **kwargs):
        path = source / name
        used.append(path)
        return pd.read_csv(path, **kwargs)

    panel = read(PREFIX + "stores_us_panel.csv.gz", parse_dates=["date"])
    dim = read(PREFIX + "stores_us_dim.csv")
    country = read(PREFIX + "country.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
    snaps = read(PREFIX + "snapshots_used.csv")
    weekly = read("mcbroken_weekly_2020_2026_country.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
    weekly_snaps = read("mcbroken_weekly_2020_2026_snapshots_used.csv")
    validate_panel(panel, dim)
    us = country[country.country.eq("USA")].copy()
    if us.date.duplicated().any():
        raise ValueError("Duplicate US snapshot dates")
    actual = panel.groupby("date").is_broken.agg(n_checked="size", n_broken="sum")
    pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(actual.sort_index(),
        us.set_index("date")[["n_checked", "n_broken"]].sort_index(),
        check_dtype=False, check_freq=False)
    days = panel.groupby("store_key").date.nunique()
    pd.testing.assert_series_equal(days.sort_index(),
        dim.set_index("store_key").n_days.sort_index(), check_names=False)
    snaps["snapshot_utc"] = pd.to_datetime(snaps.ts, utc=True)
    snaps["date"] = snaps.snapshot_utc.dt.tz_localize(None).dt.normalize()
    if snaps.date.duplicated().any():
        raise ValueError("Multiple selected snapshots per calendar date")
    daily = pd.DataFrame({"date": pd.date_range(snaps.date.min(), snaps.date.max())})
    daily = daily.merge(snaps[["date", "snapshot_utc", "sha"]], on="date",
                        how="left", validate="one_to_one")
    daily = daily.merge(us[["date", "n_checked", "n_broken"]], on="date",
                        how="left", validate="one_to_one")
    daily["share_unavailable"] = daily.n_broken / daily.n_checked
    target = daily.date.dt.tz_localize("UTC") + pd.Timedelta(hours=18)
    daily["offset_hours"] = (daily.snapshot_utc - target).dt.total_seconds() / 3600
    transitions = make_transitions(panel, daily)
    for col in ["n_origins", "n_labeled", "n_unavailable"]:
        transitions[col] = transitions[col].astype(int)
    assert (transitions.n_unavailable <= transitions.n_labeled).all()
    assert (transitions.n_labeled <= transitions.n_origins).all()

    ordered = panel.sort_values(["store_key", "date"])
    gaps = ordered.groupby("store_key").date.diff().dt.days
    event = pd.Timestamp("2024-10-28")
    weekly["event_week"] = (weekly.date - event).dt.days // 7
    event_data = weekly[weekly.event_week.between(-12, 12)
                        & weekly.country.isin(["USA", "UK", "CA"])].copy()
    event_data = event_data.merge(weekly_snaps[["period", "sha"]], on="period",
                                  validate="many_to_one")
    assert event_data.commit.eq(event_data.sha.str[:12]).all()
    event_data["share_unavailable"] = event_data.n_broken / event_data.n_checked
    out = ROOT / "data"
    out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    daily.to_csv(out / "daily_us.csv", index=False)
    transitions.to_csv(out / "transitions.csv", index=False)
    event_data.drop(columns="share_broken").to_csv(out / "policy_window.csv", index=False)
    assessment = {
        "source_rows": len(panel), "address_keys": len(dim),
        "exact_coordinate_pairs": len(dim[["lat", "lon"]].drop_duplicates()),
        "calendar_days": len(daily), "us_observed_days": len(us),
        "missing_us_days": int(daily.n_checked.isna().sum()),
        "low_coverage_days": int(daily.n_checked.lt(2000).sum()),
        "successive_key_records": int(gaps.notna().sum()),
        "consecutive_day_pairs": int(gaps.eq(1).sum()),
        "long_gap_pairs": int(gaps.gt(1).sum()),
        "median_days_per_key": float(dim.n_days.median()),
        "snapshot_abs_offset_hours_max": float(daily.offset_hours.abs().max()),
        "duplicate_store_dates": 0, "unmatched_keys": 0,
        "country_counts_reconciled": True, "dimension_days_reconciled": True,
        "matching": "Original address keys define the merge; coordinates provide a consistency check.",
        "transition_screen": "Both dates: >=2000 US records and within 3 hours of 18:00 UTC.",
        "status_scope": "The supplied binary field was validated; raw API missingness cannot be recovered from these CSVs.",
    }
    (out / "assessment.json").write_text(json.dumps(assessment, indent=2) + "\n")
    manifest = {
        "source": "Rashiq Zahid, McBroken; snapshots via MrFlynn/mcbroken-archive",
        "urls": ["https://mcbroken.com", "https://github.com/MrFlynn/mcbroken-archive"],
        "files": {p.name: {"sha256": hashlib.sha256(p.read_bytes()).hexdigest(),
                            "bytes": p.stat().st_size} for p in used},
        "rights": "Upstream archive software uses Unlicense; no separate McBroken data license was established. Public teaching outputs are attributed aggregate calculations.",
    }
    (ROOT / "manifest.json").write_text(json.dumps(manifest, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(json.dumps(assessment, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--source", type=Path, default=DEFAULT_SOURCE)
    main(parser.parse_args().source)
\end{Verbatim}

\noindent The coverage program reads the released calendar table,
reports the sensitivity calculations, and generates the two-panel TikZ
figure. Both panels use the same calendar. The percentage axis starts at
zero and retains its full 0--100 range, so a change in the number
observed remains visually distinct from a change in the observed
fraction.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/McBroken/coverage.py}{coverage.py}. From its
directory, run \texttt{python\ coverage.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Compare availability denominators and draw the observed US time series."""
import json
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
FIGURES = ROOT.parents[1] / "06_Lecture_Notes/figures"


def main():
    daily = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "data/daily_us.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
    results = ROOT / "results"
    results.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    rows = []
    for threshold in [0, 1000, 2000, 5000]:
        sample = daily[daily.n_checked.notna() & daily.n_checked.ge(threshold)]
        rows.append({"minimum_checked": threshold, "days": len(sample),
                     "checked_records": int(sample.n_checked.sum()),
                     "unavailable_records": int(sample.n_broken.sum()),
                     "equal_day_percent": 100 * (sample.n_broken / sample.n_checked).mean(),
                     "pooled_record_percent": 100 * sample.n_broken.sum() / sample.n_checked.sum()})
    pd.DataFrame(rows).to_csv(results / "coverage_sensitivity.csv", index=False)
    (results / "coverage.json").write_text(json.dumps({
        "missing_us_dates": daily.loc[daily.n_checked.isna(), "date"].dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d").tolist(),
        "low_coverage_dates": daily.loc[daily.n_checked.lt(2000), "date"].dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d").tolist(),
        "sensitivity": rows}, indent=2) + "\n")
    daily["day"] = (daily.date - daily.date.min()).dt.days
    def points(column, scale):
        return " ".join(f"({r.day},{getattr(r, column) * scale:.6f})"
                        if pd.notna(getattr(r, column)) else f"({r.day},nan)"
                        for r in daily.itertuples())
    figure = r"""\begin{tikzpicture}
\begin{axis}[name=counts,width=12.5cm,height=4.7cm,xmin=0,xmax=364,
 ymin=0,ymax=15000,ylabel={US Records},xtick=\empty,scaled y ticks=false,
 ytick={0,5000,10000,15000},unbounded coords=jump]
\addplot[IlliniBlue] coordinates {COUNTS};
\addplot[Storm,dashed] coordinates {(0,2000) (364,2000)};
\end{axis}
\begin{axis}[at={(counts.south west)},anchor=north west,yshift=-0.55cm,
 width=12.5cm,height=4.7cm,xmin=0,xmax=364,ymin=0,ymax=100,
 ylabel={Unavailable (\%)},xlabel={Days Since October 25, 2025},
 xtick={0,90,180,270,364},unbounded coords=jump]
\addplot[IlliniOrange] coordinates {RATES};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
"""
    (FIGURES / "M02_mcbroken_coverage.tex").write_text(
        figure.replace("COUNTS", points("n_checked", 1))
              .replace("RATES", points("share_unavailable", 100)))
    print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M02-public-signals-of-demand-for-generative-ai}{%
\section{Public Signals of Demand for Generative
AI}\label{M02-public-signals-of-demand-for-generative-ai}}

\noindent A subscription provider deciding where to invest in acquisition needs to
distinguish public attention, product use, and payment. A high position
in an app chart establishes an ordering within that chart. It supplies
neither the number of downloads nor the fraction of consumers who pay. A
pricing page describes the offers available at a particular date, while
transactions reveal which offers customers purchase. Combining these
sources is useful when each measure retains its observation unit and
population.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.33}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.33}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.34}}@{}}
\toprule
Source & Recorded Object & Relevant Interpretation \\
\midrule

App Store top-free chart & App rank in one storefront and capture &
Ordinal position among listed apps; absence means outside the returned
list or otherwise absent from the feed \\
Wikipedia pageviews & View events for a title, project, access method,
and agent category & Attention to selected pages; repeated views and
unpaid users can contribute \\
OpenRouter model list & Listed model, listing timestamp, and posted
token prices & Available API offers at capture; neither realized token
demand nor verified public launch dates \\
Ramp AI Index & Paid-AI adoption among businesses in its stated
transaction sample & Business spending, with a population different from
consumers and app users \\
Consumer subscription panel & Consumer-provider-month payment status &
Adoption, simultaneous subscriptions, and transitions under the panel's
coverage rules \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The supplied
\href{../01_Resources/08_M8_Current_Topics_in_Marketing/genai_demand_lab/README.md}{generative-AI
resource bundle} contains dated public captures and a separate simulated
subscription panel. The captures are historical snapshots. The simulated
panel's counts describe its imposed population and behavioral rules.

\hypertarget{M02-title-changes-and-apparent-demand-declines}{%
\subsection{Title Changes and Apparent Demand
Declines}\label{M02-title-changes-and-apparent-demand-declines}}

\noindent A measurement system can record a substantial decline when attention
moves between page titles. The supplied English Wikipedia capture
contains two Claude titles, \texttt{Claude\_(language\_model)} and
\texttt{Claude\_(AI)}. The
\href{https://doc.wikimedia.org/generated-data-platform/aqs/analytics-api/concepts/page-views.html}{Wikimedia
definition} distinguishes view events from people and explains that
redirects are not automatically added to the target page's views. A
title-specific series therefore requires a stable definition of the
pages being counted.

Restrict the comparison to June through September 2026 and the two named
titles. Both title counts are present on all 122 calendar days. Within
each month, sum the recorded daily events for each title exactly once.
June and September each contain 30 days, so the endpoint comparison uses
equally long windows.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrr@{}}
\toprule
Month & Older Title & Newer Title & Sum of Selected Titles \\
\midrule

June 2026 & 173,190 & 52,103 & 225,293 \\
July 2026 & 25,873 & 148,027 & 173,900 \\
August 2026 & 19,768 & 132,501 & 152,269 \\
September 2026 & 25,872 & 161,884 & 187,756 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The older title falls 85.1\% between June and September. Summing the two
selected titles yields a 16.7\% decline. The difference changes the
managerial interpretation of the apparent loss of attention. The
combined series remains a count of events on these pages. It supplies no
conversion rate from readers to subscribers, and a person can generate
multiple events across titles.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M02_genai_titles.tex}
\caption{Recorded Wikipedia views indexed to June 2026. The older-title index falls to 14.9 in September, while the sum of the two selected titles falls to 83.3. Monthly totals use the supplied capture; both titles have complete daily records in the selected window.}\label{fig:M02_genai_titles}
\end{figure}

\hypertarget{M02-completeness-identity-and-ai-assisted-extraction}{%
\subsection{Completeness, Identity, and AI-Assisted
Extraction}\label{M02-completeness-identity-and-ai-assisted-extraction}}

\noindent An API response and a successful parser provide separate pieces of
evidence. Repeated requests through different aliases can return the
same title-date observation. Deduplicate by the returned title and date,
verify that repeated values agree, and count the observation once.
Preserve the retrieval status separately from the value: a failed
request or an absent record does not by itself establish zero views. The
code below builds the full calendar and returns an unknown combined
count whenever either required title-day is missing.

For a public-price table, retain the model or plan identifier, currency,
billing period, region, and capture date. Separate a monthly
subscription amount from USD per million input or output tokens. A
missing price remains unknown, and a routing service's variable price
needs a separate status. A listing timestamp identifies inclusion in
that marketplace; an event study of public releases needs independently
checked announcement dates and access conditions.

An AI-generated collector should be tested with three small inputs: a
repeated title-date, conflicting values for that key, and a day on which
one title is absent. The expected behavior follows from the observation
unit. It should deduplicate the first case, reject the conflict, and
preserve the missing value in the third. A plausible-looking chart is
insufficient evidence that these rules were implemented.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/GenAI_Demand/measurement.py}{measurement.py}.
From the script's folder, run \texttt{python3\ measurement.py}. Inputs
are read from the supplied local bundle; output tables are written
beside the course scripts.
