"""Assess the supplied Wikipedia capture without making network requests."""
from pathlib import Path
import json

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
SOURCE = HERE.parents[1] / "01_Resources/08_M8_Current_Topics_in_Marketing/genai_demand_lab/data"
OUTPUT = HERE / "results"
TITLES = ["Claude_(language_model)", "Claude_(AI)"]


def unique_views(frame):
    """Count each title-date once; reject conflicting repeated responses."""
    keys = ["date", "article"]
    if frame[keys + ["provider", "views"]].isna().any().any():
        raise ValueError("Missing title, date, provider, or view count")
    if not np.isfinite(frame.views).all() or (frame.views < 0).any():
        raise ValueError("View counts must be finite and nonnegative")
    if (frame.views % 1 != 0).any():
        raise ValueError("View counts must be integers")
    conflicts = frame.groupby(keys)[["provider", "views"]].nunique()
    if (conflicts > 1).any().any():
        raise ValueError("Conflicting repeated title-date responses")
    return frame.drop_duplicates(keys).copy()


def title_calendar(frame, titles, start, end):
    """A missing title-day remains unknown; zero must be explicitly recorded."""
    frame = unique_views(frame)
    dates = pd.date_range(start, end, freq="D")
    selected = frame.loc[frame.article.isin(titles)]
    wide = selected.pivot(index="date", columns="article", values="views")
    wide = wide.reindex(index=dates, columns=titles)
    wide["observed_titles"] = wide[titles].notna().sum(axis=1)
    wide["selected_title_views"] = wide[titles].sum(axis=1, min_count=len(titles))
    wide.index.name = "date"
    return wide


def main():
    raw = pd.read_csv(SOURCE / "wikipedia_pageviews_daily_2026-10-26.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
    clean = unique_views(raw)
    daily = title_calendar(clean, TITLES, "2026-06-01", "2026-09-30")
    rows = []
    for month, group in daily.groupby(daily.index.to_period("M")):
        row = {"month": str(month), "calendar_days": len(group),
               "complete_days": int(group.selected_title_views.notna().sum())}
        for column in TITLES + ["selected_title_views"]:
            # Full-month totals are missing if even one title-day is unknown.
            row[column] = group[column].sum(min_count=len(group))
        rows.append(row)
    monthly = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    assert monthly.complete_days.eq(monthly.calendar_days).all()
    june, september = monthly.iloc[0], monthly.iloc[-1]
    result = {
        "input_rows": len(raw), "unique_title_days": len(clean),
        "exact_duplicates_removed": len(raw) - len(clean),
        "selected_titles": TITLES, "complete_days": int(daily.selected_title_views.notna().sum()),
        "old_title_change_pct": 100 * (september[TITLES[0]] / june[TITLES[0]] - 1),
        "selected_titles_change_pct": 100 * (september.selected_title_views / june.selected_title_views - 1),
        "measurement": "Recorded pageview events for two selected English Wikipedia titles; not unique people or payments",
        "capture_status": "Supplied dated CSV, not a new retrieval; API responses and rename history were not re-collected",
    }
    # Independent aggregate check using the long input rather than the pivot.
    selected = clean.loc[clean.article.isin(TITLES) & clean.date.between(daily.index.min(), daily.index.max())]
    direct = selected.groupby(selected.date.dt.to_period("M")).views.sum().to_numpy()
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(monthly.selected_title_views, direct)
    OUTPUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    daily.to_csv(OUTPUT / "wikipedia_title_days.csv", float_format="%.8f")
    monthly.to_csv(OUTPUT / "wikipedia_months.csv", index=False, float_format="%.8f")
    (OUTPUT / "measurement.json").write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M02-sample-restrictions-and-customer-representation}{%
\section{Sample Restrictions and Customer
Representation}\label{M02-sample-restrictions-and-customer-representation}}

\noindent \noindent A manager comparing engagement across customer groups needs to
know which customers remain in the analysis. A filter that removes
incomplete records can disproportionately exclude customers who use the
service intermittently or record information in a different way. The
resulting estimate describes the retained population. Its relevance to a
broader campaign depends on the relationship between inclusion and the
outcome of interest.

Keep a flag for each restriction and report the denominator before and
after applying it. In the mHealth example, a calorie-range screen
changes the set of recorded days; it does not classify the excluded
users as unhealthy or unreliable. Compare logging frequency,
missingness, and the available earlier-period characteristics of
retained and excluded records. Keep unavailable physiological
information missing. A more elaborate formula does not compensate for an
unobserved input.

The same principle applies to a chart. A segment with no observed
outcomes should remain visible as a coverage issue when it belongs to
the target population. Treating an unobserved response as zero changes
the estimand. Removing that segment from the denominator can change the
apparent success rate. A useful chart therefore pairs its outcome with a
count or coverage measure and keeps the analysis population explicit.

For an AI-assisted cleaning request, specify which transformations are
mechanical corrections and which are analytical restrictions. Ask for a
row-count reconciliation by reason, inspect several affected records
locally, and compare the substantive result under reasonable alternative
screens. The decision concerns whether the marketing recommendation
remains supported for the intended customers.

\hypertarget{M02-earnings-calls-disclosure-requires-an-observed-document}{%
\section{Earnings Calls: Disclosure Requires an Observed
Document}\label{M02-earnings-calls-disclosure-requires-an-observed-document}}

\noindent \noindent A retail communications manager wants to identify firms whose
public pricing statements merit closer reading. The relevant population
is the set of firms and calls available for review. Starting from a
table of extracted matches selects documents on the outcome and
overstates how frequently the topic appears. A firm roster, a call
table, and a match table answer different questions and must retain
their separate observation units.

The supplied snapshot spans November 2, 2021 through November 2, 2026
and includes current-index constituents plus selected comparison firms.
Its roster contains one firm, Winmark, with no supplied calls. Its
Dollar Tree call dated September 3, 2025 has 53 recorded turns but zero
recorded words. That record establishes an extraction problem requiring
review; its zero dictionary count supplies no observed negative language
outcome. The analysis preserves the record and assigns unknown language
presence. All other supplied calls have positive word counts, although
positive length alone does not establish transcript completeness.

For observed call \(c\), define \(D_c=1\) when at least one core
dictionary term occurs and \(D_c=0\) otherwise. For a set of observed
calls \(\mathcal C\), the descriptive incidence is

\[
\widehat p_{\mathcal C}=\frac{\sum_{c\in\mathcal C}D_c}{|\mathcal C|}.
\]

The numerator counts calls once regardless of repeated occurrences. The
denominator counts observed calls, including calls with no matches. Core
terms occur in 112 of 2,325 observed calls, or 4.82\%. Restricting the
denominator to the 445 calls containing any core or broad term produces
25.17\%. Both calculations use the same numerator. The latter measures a
conditional share among already-retrieved documents and is unsuitable as
the overall disclosure frequency.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M02_calls_denominator.tex}
\caption{The same 112 core-positive calls yield 4.82 percent among 2,325 observed calls and 25.17 percent among 445 calls with any dictionary match. Selecting documents on a match changes the population.}\label{fig:M02_calls_denominator}
\end{figure}

A match-level merge would repeat the call's word count once per
occurrence. Aggregate occurrences to call before joining, verify the
keys, and reconcile every term count against the supplied call totals.
The roster summary distinguishes firms with observed zero-match calls
from a firm with no observed calls. The supplied sectors and
current-index selection also make the results descriptive of this
corpus; a comparison across sectors does not estimate market-wide
adoption.

The
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Earnings_Calls/DATA_DICTIONARY.md}{earnings-call
data dictionary} records units, flags, and provenance. The following
program verifies identifiers, group membership, dictionary counts, word
totals, and roster coverage before computing the denominator comparison.
Its flags preserve the original records.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Earnings_Calls/assessment.py}{assessment.py}.
From \texttt{03\_Data\_and\_Code/Earnings\_Calls}, run
\texttt{python\ assessment.py}. Python, pandas, and NumPy are required;
the committed metadata supply all inputs.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Assess keys, counts, coverage, and missing text before measuring disclosure."""
from pathlib import Path
import json
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent


def load_checked():
    calls = pd.read_csv(HERE / 'data/calls.csv', parse_dates=['call_date'])
    mentions = pd.read_csv(HERE / 'data/mentions.csv', parse_dates=['call_date'])
    firms = pd.read_csv(HERE / 'data/firms.csv')
    dictionary = pd.read_csv(HERE / 'data/dictionary.csv')
    for frame, key in [(calls, 'call_id'), (mentions, 'mention_id'),
                       (firms, 'ticker'), (dictionary, 'term_id')]:
        assert frame[key].notna().all() and frame[key].is_unique, key
    assert set(calls.ticker) <= set(firms.ticker)
    assert set(mentions.call_id) <= set(calls.call_id)
    assert set(mentions.term_id) <= set(dictionary.term_id)
    counts = [x for x in calls if x.startswith(('n_', 'words_'))]
    assert calls[counts].notna().all().all()
    assert (calls[counts] >= 0).all().all()
    assert (calls[counts] % 1 == 0).all().all()
    assert (calls.words_management + calls.words_analyst <= calls.words_total).all()
    merged = mentions.merge(calls[['call_id', 'ticker', 'call_date']],
                            on='call_id', validate='many_to_one', suffixes=('', '_call'))
    assert merged.ticker.eq(merged.ticker_call).all()
    assert merged.call_date.eq(merged.call_date_call).all()
    labels = mentions.merge(dictionary[['term_id', 'tier', 'category']],
                            on='term_id', validate='many_to_one', suffixes=('', '_dict'))
    assert labels.tier.eq(labels.tier_dict).all()
    assert labels.category.eq(labels.category_dict).all()
    actual = mentions.groupby(['call_id', 'term_id']).size().unstack(fill_value=0)
    actual = actual.reindex(index=calls.call_id, columns=dictionary.term_id, fill_value=0)
    expected = calls.set_index('call_id')[['n_' + x for x in dictionary.term_id]]
    assert np.array_equal(actual.to_numpy(), expected.to_numpy())
    for tier in ['core', 'broad']:
        terms = dictionary.loc[dictionary.tier.eq(tier), 'term_id']
        assert np.array_equal(actual[terms].sum(axis=1), calls['n_' + tier])
    roster_count = calls.groupby('ticker').size().reindex(firms.ticker, fill_value=0)
    assert np.array_equal(roster_count, firms.n_calls_in_window)
    calls['text_observed'] = calls.words_total.gt(0)
    calls['qa_detected'] = calls.qa_start_turn.ge(0)
    calls['has_core'] = calls.n_core.gt(0).astype(float).where(calls.text_observed)
    calls['has_any'] = (calls.n_core + calls.n_broad).gt(0)
    assert calls.loc[~calls.text_observed, ['n_core', 'n_broad']].eq(0).all().all()
    return calls, mentions, firms, dictionary


def firm_coverage(calls, firms):
    summary = calls.groupby('ticker').agg(
        calls_supplied=('call_id', 'size'), calls_observed=('text_observed', 'sum'),
        core_positive_calls=('has_core', 'sum'))
    output = firms[['ticker', 'company', 'group']].merge(
        summary, on='ticker', how='left', validate='one_to_one')
    cols = ['calls_supplied', 'calls_observed', 'core_positive_calls']
    output[cols] = output[cols].fillna(0).astype(int)
    output['core_call_rate'] = output.core_positive_calls.div(
        output.calls_observed.replace(0, np.nan))
    return output


def main():
    calls, mentions, firms, dictionary = load_checked()
    out = HERE / 'results'; out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    calls[['call_id', 'text_observed', 'qa_detected', 'has_core']].to_csv(
        out / 'call_status.csv', index=False)
    firm_coverage(calls, firms).to_csv(out / 'firm_coverage.csv', index=False)
    report = {
        'supplied_calls': len(calls), 'observed_calls': int(calls.text_observed.sum()),
        'missing_text_ids': calls.loc[~calls.text_observed, 'call_id'].tolist(),
        'undetected_qa_calls': int((~calls.qa_detected).sum()),
        'core_positive_calls': int(calls.has_core.sum()), 'matches': len(mentions),
        'core_matches': int(mentions.tier.eq('core').sum()),
        'firms_in_roster': len(firms), 'firms_with_calls': calls.ticker.nunique(),
        'positive_only_denominator': int(calls.has_any.sum()),
        'wrong_positive_only_rate': float(calls.loc[calls.has_any, 'has_core'].mean()),
        'observed_call_rate': float(calls.has_core.mean()),
        'dictionary_terms': len(dictionary),
    }
    (out / 'assessment.json').write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2) + '\n')
    print(json.dumps(report, indent=2))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M02-access-to-evidence-changes-the-review-sample}{%
\section{Access to Evidence Changes the Review
Sample}\label{M02-access-to-evidence-changes-the-review-sample}}

\noindent \noindent A marketing team evaluating subscription practices may ask
which consumer-agency mechanisms appear most often in recent research.
The observation unit is a paper identified by its DOI. The target
collection includes Journal of Marketing, Journal of Marketing Research,
and Marketing Science records with an online or issue-publication date
from January 2023 through November 5, 2026. A paper published online
before 2023 can enter through its later issue date. Deduplication
prevents counting it twice.

The Crossref census contains 886 DOI records. Excluding 62 notices and
related front matter leaves 824 eligible records, including substantive
commentaries. Retrieval produced 103 full texts or related earlier
versions. The review covers those 103 records and 41 additional papers
selected for their relevance from available abstracts. Access and
purposeful selection determine which mechanisms can be examined in
depth. A metadata census does not establish a complete full-text review.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule
Journal & Eligible & Retrieved & Reviewed \\
\midrule

Journal of Marketing & 273 & 48 & 63 \\
Journal of Marketing Research & 262 & 25 & 43 \\
Marketing Science & 289 & 30 & 38 \\
Total & 824 & 103 & 144 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M02_literature_selection.tex}
\caption{The DOI census passes through eligibility, retrieval, and mechanism coding. Each restriction changes the denominator.}\label{fig:M02_literature_selection}
\end{figure}

The retrieval rates differ across journals. Papers without an accessible
copy can differ in topic, publication date, and author deposit
practices. Coding an inaccessible paper as having no agency mechanism
would convert missing evidence into a substantive conclusion. The
catalog instead preserves an unreviewed status and missing indicators.

A simple bound makes the resulting uncertainty concrete. Across the 824
eligible records, 29 reviewed papers receive the social-cue code and 680
remain unreviewed. If every unknown record eventually receives zero for
that code, its share is 29/824, or 3.5\%. If every unknown record
receives one, its share is 709/824, or 86.0\%. These are bounds on an
eventual literature code, holding reviewed labels fixed. They do not
measure the prevalence of harmful conduct. Their width shows how little
a selected review alone determines a population-wide ranking.

Reconciliation starts with the public catalog, DOI uniqueness, coverage,
and journal totals. The calculation preserves existing review labels and
leaves missing labels unresolved. The
\href{../01_Resources/13_Consumer_Agency_and_Recent_Research/README.md}{collection
protocol} records dates, versions, retrieval attempts, and access gaps.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Consumer_Agency_Literature/assess_coverage.py}{assess\_coverage.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Reconcile the journal census, full-text availability, and review denominators."""
from pathlib import Path
import json
import pandas as pd

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
LIBRARY = HERE.parents[1] / "01_Resources/13_Consumer_Agency_and_Recent_Research"


def main():
    data = pd.DataFrame(json.loads((LIBRARY / "catalog.json").read_text())["resources"])
    assert data.doi.is_unique and data.id.is_unique
    eligible = data.research_screen_eligible.eq(True)
    downloaded = data.download_status.eq("downloaded")
    reviewed = data.review_status.ne("not_reviewed")
    assert not (downloaded & ~eligible).any()
    assert not (downloaded & ~reviewed).any()
    table = data.assign(eligible=eligible.astype(int), downloaded=downloaded.astype(int),
                        reviewed=reviewed.astype(int)).groupby("journal").agg(
        doi_records=("doi", "size"), eligible=("eligible", "sum"),
        downloaded=("downloaded", "sum"), reviewed=("reviewed", "sum"))
    table["access_gaps"] = table.eligible - table.downloaded
    table["download_share_of_eligible"] = table.downloaded / table.eligible
    assert table.doi_records.sum() == len(data)
    assert table.access_gaps.sum() == sum(eligible & ~downloaded)
    # Worst-case bounds use the same eligible-record denominator at both ends.
    # They concern the eventual coding label, not the prevalence of actual harm.
    feature = "social_cues"
    known_positive = int(pd.to_numeric(data.loc[eligible & reviewed, feature]).sum())
    unknown = int(sum(eligible & ~reviewed))
    denominator = int(eligible.sum())
    bounds = {"feature": feature, "eligible": denominator, "reviewed_positive": known_positive,
              "unreviewed": unknown, "lower_bound": known_positive / denominator,
              "upper_bound": (known_positive + unknown) / denominator}
    output = HERE / "results"
    output.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    table.to_csv(output / "coverage_by_journal.csv")
    (output / "missing_evidence_bounds.json").write_text(json.dumps(bounds, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(table.to_string())
    print(json.dumps(bounds, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M02-follow-up-time-and-the-shelf-life-of-ai-findings}{%
\section{Follow-up Time and the Shelf Life of AI
Findings}\label{M02-follow-up-time-and-the-shelf-life-of-ai-findings}}

\noindent \noindent A manager deciding whether to rely on an earlier AI result
needs to distinguish the age of the evidence from evidence that its
effect has changed.
\href{https://zou-group.github.io/llm-claims-shelf-life/}{Queen and Zou
(2026)} provide a selected panel of fifty claims and twenty models. The
released classifications contain 22 expired, seventeen weakened, eight
persistent, and three strengthened findings. Eight of the 1,000
model-claim comparisons are flagged as unreliable. The selection of
claims, tested configurations, and classification rule define the
population behind these counts.

The study puts different outcomes on a relative-effect scale. For an
outcome \(v\) with reference value \(a\) and claim-absent value \(v_0\),
the transformation is \(e=(v-v_0)/(a-v_0)\). An effect of one matches
the reference magnitude; zero matches the specified null. The reference
and null must be distinct and measured in the same units. Relative
effects preserve change within a defined metric. They do not put the
commercial costs of different failures on a common scale.

The mean time from publication to estimated expiration is 15.75 months
among the 22 expired claims. This conditions on having reached the
event. The other 28 observations provide information about how long a
finding remained unexpired before observation ended. Removing them
selects findings that expired soon enough to be observed. Treating their
follow-up times as expiration dates would instead invent events.

\hypertarget{M02-censoring-and-comparable-follow-up}{%
\subsection{Censoring and Comparable
Follow-up}\label{M02-censoring-and-comparable-follow-up}}

\noindent \noindent Let \(t_j\) be a distinct estimated expiration time measured
in months after publication. Let \(n_j\) count claims still observed and
unexpired immediately before \(t_j\), and let \(d_j\) count expirations
at that time. The Kaplan-Meier estimate of the share that remains
unexpired through month \(t\) is

\[
\widehat S(t)=\prod_{t_j\leq t}\left(1-\frac{d_j}{n_j}\right).
\]

An unexpired claim leaves the risk set at its last follow-up date
without contributing an expiration. Events are counted before censoring
at tied times. Comparing \(1-\widehat S(t)\) at a common horizon
separates elapsed follow-up from the snapshot's mixture of older and
newer papers. A population survival interpretation requires censoring
that is independent of event time under the chosen conditioning
variables. Publication cohorts and purposeful selection can challenge
that condition.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M02_claim_followup.tex}
\caption{Estimated expiration shares are 4.0\% at six months, 16.0\% at twelve months, and 38.9\% at twenty-four months. The step calculation retains all fifty selected claims, with 28 right-censored observations. Published estimated dates are treated as fixed.}\label{fig:M02_claim_followup}
\end{figure}

The displayed curve reuses the released point estimates. Several
expiration dates are estimated within intervals, and two follow a count
of recent models. The calculation does not propagate date uncertainty or
fit an interval-censoring model. A smooth model-release trend also
compares different configurations, with differing default reasoning
budgets, rather than identifying a causal effect of calendar time. The
\href{../01_Resources/14_LLM_Evidence_and_Revalidation/README.md}{source
record} retains these distinctions.

\hypertarget{M02-reproduce-the-published-summary}{%
\subsection{Reproduce the Published
Summary}\label{M02-reproduce-the-published-summary}}

\noindent \noindent A valid summary requires unique claim-model identifiers,
preserved unreliable comparisons, and classifications that agree across
the released files. Follow-up calculations use the pinned public
snapshot and the published estimated dates. Model-level threshold counts
concern individual point estimates; the source's fitted classifications
use additional rules and uncertainty.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/LLM_Revalidation/summarize_snapshot.py}{summarize\_snapshot.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Summarize published LLM claim results; no model calls or trend refitting."""
from pathlib import Path
from datetime import date
from collections import Counter
import csv
import json
import statistics

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
SOURCE = HERE.parents[1] / "01_Resources/14_LLM_Evidence_and_Revalidation/source_tables"
END = date(2026, 9, 30)
MONTH = 365.25 / 12


def survival(times, events, horizon):
    """Kaplan-Meier survival, with events before censoring at tied times."""
    if len(times) != len(events) or not times:
        raise ValueError("Equal nonempty time and event lists are required")
    if any(t < 0 for t in times) or any(e not in (0, 1) for e in events):
        raise ValueError("Invalid follow-up time or event indicator")
    result = 1.0
    for time in sorted(set(t for t in times if t <= horizon)):
        at_risk = sum(t >= time for t in times)
        events_now = sum(e for t, e in zip(times, events) if t == time)
        result *= 1 - events_now / at_risk
    return result


def write_csv(path, rows):
    with path.open("w", newline="") as stream:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(stream, fieldnames=list(rows[0]), lineterminator="\n")
        writer.writeheader()
        writer.writerows(rows)


def main():
    claims = list(csv.DictReader((SOURCE / "claims.csv").open()))
    panel = list(csv.DictReader((SOURCE / "panel_values.csv").open()))
    fitted = json.loads((SOURCE / "post_results.json").read_text())["claims"]
    assert len({c["blog_id"] for c in claims}) == len(claims) == 50
    assert len({(r["blog_id"], r["model"]) for r in panel}) == len(panel) == 1000
    assert len({r["model"] for r in panel}) == 20
    assert {r["reliable"] for r in panel} <= {"True", "False"}
    assert all(sum(r["blog_id"] == c["blog_id"] for r in panel) == 20 for c in claims)
    aliases = {"dead": "expired", "attenuated": "weakened"}
    labels = {c["blog_id"]: aliases.get(c["verdict"], c["verdict"]) for c in claims}
    assert set(labels) == {c["id"] for c in fitted}
    assert all(labels[c["id"]] == aliases.get(c["category"], c["category"]) for c in fitted)
    counts = Counter(labels.values())
    lifetimes = []
    for claim in sorted(fitted, key=lambda c: int(c["id"][1:])):
        start = date.fromisoformat(claim["paper_date"])
        event = int(labels[claim["id"]] == "expired")
        stop = date.fromisoformat(claim["death"]) if event else END
        assert start <= stop <= END
        lifetimes.append(dict(claim_id=claim["id"], paper_date=str(start),
            endpoint=str(stop), months=(stop - start).days / MONTH, event=event,
            endpoint_kind=claim["death_kind"] if event else "right_censored"))
    times = [r["months"] for r in lifetimes]
    events = [r["event"] for r in lifetimes]
    expired = [t for t, e in zip(times, events) if e]
    horizons = [dict(months=h, estimated_expired_share=1-survival(times, events, h))
                for h in (6, 12, 24)]
    curve = [dict(months=h, estimated_expired_share=1-survival(times, events, h))
             for h in sorted({0.0, 24.0} | {t for t in times if t <= 24})]
    verdict_rows = [dict(verdict=k, claims=counts[k], share=counts[k]/len(claims))
                    for k in ("expired", "weakened", "persists", "strengthened")]
    model_rows = []
    for model in sorted({r["model"] for r in panel}):
        selected = [r for r in panel if r["model"] == model]
        reliable = [r for r in selected if r["reliable"] == "True"]
        model_rows.append(dict(model=model, name=selected[0]["model_name"],
            reliable_pairs=len(reliable), unscorable_pairs=len(selected)-len(reliable),
            effects_at_or_below_point_two=sum(float(r["e"]) <= .2 for r in reliable)))
    citation_rows = [dict(model=r["model_name"], release=r["release"],
        fabricated_fraction=float(r["value"]), relative_effect=float(r["e"]),
        reliable=r["reliable"]) for r in panel if r["blog_id"] == "C11"]
    summary = dict(claims=len(claims), models=len(model_rows), pairs=len(panel),
        unreliable_pairs=sum(r["reliable"] == "False" for r in panel), verdicts=counts,
        expired_only_mean_months=statistics.mean(expired),
        expired_only_median_months=statistics.median(expired), horizons=horizons,
        observation_end=str(END),
        scope="Published fitted dates treated as fixed; no model runs, refits, or date-uncertainty propagation")
    output = HERE / "results"
    output.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    for name, rows in [("verdicts", verdict_rows), ("lifetimes", lifetimes),
                       ("horizons", horizons), ("followup_curve", curve), ("model_counts", model_rows),
                       ("citation_fabrication", citation_rows)]:
        write_csv(output / (name + ".csv"), rows)
    (output / "snapshot_summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(json.dumps(summary, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M02-customer-differences-and-changes-within-customers}{%
\section{Customer Differences and Changes Within
Customers}\label{M02-customer-differences-and-changes-within-customers}}

\noindent \noindent A retailer deciding whether to revise its retention program
needs to know how spending changes for the same customers. A
distribution of spending levels answers a different question about the
customer base. High-spending customers can remain far above low-spending
customers while both groups change by nearly the same amount. Linking
repeated observations preserves this distinction. Warin's
\href{https://warint.github.io/pystatlas/group-comparisons/}{PyStatlas
paired-comparison and estimation graphics} combine individual
observations with the comparison of interest.

Consider eight synthetic customers observed in two complete one-month
windows. Their initial spending is \$20, \$35, \$50, \$65, \$80, \$95,
\$110, and \$125. The corresponding changes are \$4, \$6, \$5, \$5, \$4,
\$6, \$5, and \$5. Every customer remains in the comparison, with equal
weight. Mean spending rises from \$72.50 to \$77.50 per customer per
month. The \$5 increase is descriptive; these observations contain no
untreated comparison from which to identify the program's causal effect.

For customer \(i\), define the change as
\(d_i=y_{i,\mathrm{after}}-y_{i,\mathrm{before}}\). The average change
and its estimated standard error under independent sampling of customer
pairs are

\[
\bar d=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_i,
\qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\bar d)=\frac{s_d}{\sqrt n},
\qquad
s_d^2=s_{\mathrm{after}}^2+s_{\mathrm{before}}^2-2s_{\mathrm{before,after}}.
\]

Here \(n\) counts customers, each variance uses denominator \(n-1\), and
\(s_{\mathrm{before,after}}\) is the sample covariance of spending
across the two windows. The covariance is positive because customers
largely preserve their relative spending levels. Omitting it discards
the information in the pairing. In these imposed observations,
\(s_d^2=4/7\) dollars squared and the paired standard error is \$0.267.
Treating the two windows as independent samples produces \$18.402. That
independence calculation is inapplicable to this paired design.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M02_paired_spending.tex}
\caption{Eight synthetic customers have spending levels between 20 and 130 dollars, with individual changes of 4, 5, or 6 dollars. Thin lines join each customer’s two observations. The right panel plots all eight changes and their mean of 5 dollars, with a conditional 95\% t interval from 4.368 to 5.632 dollars. The panels label their distinct quantities.}\label{fig:M02_paired_spending}
\end{figure}

A 95\% t interval is \(\bar d\pm t_{0.975,n-1}s_d/\sqrt n\). Its exact
sampling interpretation assumes independent normally distributed
customer differences. Under that hypothetical model, the interval is
{[}\$4.368, \$5.632{]}. The imposed observations themselves have no
sampling uncertainty; the interval demonstrates what the stated sampling
model would imply. With observed customer data, repeated households,
store-level assignment, missing second-window records, and a small
number of independent units require separate attention. A bootstrap
should resample whole customer pairs when customers are the independent
sampling unit.

\hypertarget{M02-reproduce-the-paired-comparison}{%
\subsection{Reproduce the Paired
Comparison}\label{M02-reproduce-the-paired-comparison}}

\noindent \noindent The input contains one unique customer identifier and two
dollar amounts per row. Empty values, nonfinite amounts, negative
spending, and duplicate identifiers fail validation. The calculation
preserves the complete pairs and exports the individual changes used in
the right panel. Reordering complete rows preserves the result;
rearranging only the second-period amounts changes the pairing and its
uncertainty.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Statistical_Graphics/paired_changes.py}{paired\_changes.py}.
From its directory, run \texttt{python\ paired\_changes.py}. Input:
\texttt{inputs/paired\_spending.csv}; dependency: SciPy for the t
critical value.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Synthetic customer spending: preserve pairs when estimating mean change."""
from pathlib import Path
import csv
import json
import math
import statistics as st
from scipy.stats import t

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent


def evaluate(rows):
    if len(rows) < 2:
        raise ValueError("At least two complete customer pairs are required")
    ids = [row["customer_id"] for row in rows]
    if any(not value for value in ids) or len(set(ids)) != len(ids):
        raise ValueError("Customer IDs must be nonempty and unique")
    before = [float(row["before_dollars"]) for row in rows]
    after = [float(row["after_dollars"]) for row in rows]
    if any(not math.isfinite(x) or x < 0 for x in before + after):
        raise ValueError("Spending must be finite and nonnegative")
    change = [b - a for a, b in zip(before, after)]
    n = len(rows)
    mean = st.mean(change)
    se = st.stdev(change) / math.sqrt(n)
    covariance = sum((a - st.mean(before)) * (b - st.mean(after))
                     for a, b in zip(before, after)) / (n - 1)
    independent_se = math.sqrt((st.variance(before) + st.variance(after)) / n)
    margin = float(t.ppf(0.975, df=n - 1)) * se
    return dict(customers=n, mean_before=st.mean(before),
                mean_after=st.mean(after), mean_change=mean,
                paired_standard_error=se, covariance=covariance,
                independent_standard_error=independent_se,
                ci_lower=mean - margin, ci_upper=mean + margin,
                ci_scope="Hypothetical iid normal customer differences; 95% t interval",
                data_scope="Eight imposed pairs; descriptive change, no causal effect")


def main():
    with (HERE / "inputs/paired_spending.csv").open(newline="") as stream:
        rows = list(csv.DictReader(stream))
    result = evaluate(rows)
    output = HERE / "results"
    output.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    (output / "paired_changes.json").write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2) + "\n")
    with (output / "customer_changes.csv").open("w", newline="") as stream:
        writer = csv.writer(stream, lineterminator="\n")
        writer.writerow(["customer_id", "change_dollars"])
        writer.writerows((r["customer_id"], float(r["after_dollars"])
                         - float(r["before_dollars"])) for r in rows)
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M03-m3.-regression-interpretation-and-marketing-decisions}{%
\chapter{Regression, Interpretation, and Marketing
Decisions}\label{M03-m3.-regression-interpretation-and-marketing-decisions}}

\noindent A retailer observes that stores with larger advertising budgets sell
more. The manager wants to know whether another dollar of advertising
would be profitable. The observed relationship combines the response to
advertising with differences in store size, local demand, seasonality,
and the firm's reasons for choosing the budget. Regression provides a
way to summarize conditional relationships. Its value depends on which
variation identifies the comparison and whether that comparison answers
the manager's question.

\hypertarget{M03-a-conditional-mean-and-a-regression-line}{%
\section{A Conditional Mean and a Regression
Line}\label{M03-a-conditional-mean-and-a-regression-line}}

\noindent Let \(Y_i\) be weekly store sales measured in thousands of dollars and
\(X_i\) be weekly advertising expenditure in thousands of dollars. A
simple linear model writes

\[
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\varepsilon_i.
\]

The intercept \(\beta_0\) is the fitted sales level at zero advertising;
its practical interpretation is weak when zero lies far outside the
observed range. The slope \(\beta_1\) is the change in fitted sales, in
thousands of dollars, associated with an additional thousand dollars of
advertising. The residual captures the difference between observed sales
and the fitted line. Linearity is an approximation to the relationship
over the relevant range, not a claim that every customer's behavior is
linear.

Ordinary least squares chooses coefficients to minimize the sum of
squared residuals. In a simple regression with an intercept, its slope
is

\[
\hat\beta_1=\frac{\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)(Y_i-\bar Y)}{\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2}.
\]

The numerator measures whether high-advertising observations tend to
have high sales. The denominator measures how much advertising varies.
When advertising hardly varies, the data provide little information
about a slope, even if the sample contains many rows. A large sample of
nearly identical budgets does not substitute for informative variation.

For three observations \((X,Y)=(1,3),(2,5),(3,7)\), the fitted line is
\(\hat Y=1+2X\). At \(X=2.5\), it predicts sales of \$6,000. If the
sales contribution margin is 30\%, an additional \$1,000 of advertising
is associated with \$600 of contribution from \$2,000 of extra sales.
Treating that association as a return to intervention requires an
identification argument. Even under a causal interpretation, the
incremental contribution is less than the additional advertising expense
in this numerical example.

\hypertarget{M03-multiple-regression-and-the-comparison-it-uses}{%
\section{Multiple Regression and the Comparison It
Uses}\label{M03-multiple-regression-and-the-comparison-it-uses}}

\noindent A multiple regression can include observed store characteristics:

\[
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\gamma Z_i+\varepsilon_i,
\]

where \(Z_i\) might be floor area measured in thousands of square feet.
The advertising coefficient summarizes variation in sales associated
with advertising after removing the linear association with floor area.
A useful way to understand this is to regress advertising on the other
controls, regress sales on the same controls, and regress the resulting
sales residuals on the advertising residuals. The Frisch-Waugh-Lovell
result gives the same advertising coefficient as the full regression
when the residualization includes the same intercept and controls.

``Controlling for'' a variable therefore changes the comparison. It does
not automatically remove all confounding. If managers observe local
demand information that the analyst lacks, their advertising choices may
remain related to unobserved sales determinants. Controls measured after
the intervention can also remove part of the effect or introduce bias.
Select variables using the decision timing and a substantive account of
how the data were generated.

When an omitted variable affects both the predictor and the outcome, the
simple slope can be misleading. In the linear population model above,
suppose the regression disturbance is mean-independent of \(X\) and
\(Z\). Omitting \(Z\) yields a simple-regression slope equal to

\[
\beta_1+\gamma\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.
\]

The extra term has a substantive interpretation. If larger stores sell
more, so \(\gamma>0\), and larger stores spend more on advertising, so
the covariance is positive, the simple advertising slope exceeds the
conditional slope. The equation is a model-based decomposition; its
interpretation depends on the stated linear specification and exogeneity
condition.

\hypertarget{M03-case-study-attractive-markets-and-apparent-competitive-benefits}{%
\section{Case Study: Attractive Markets and Apparent Competitive
Benefits}\label{M03-case-study-attractive-markets-and-apparent-competitive-benefits}}

\noindent \href{https://doi.org/10.3982/QE478}{Igami and Yang (2016)} study entry
and competition among hamburger chains in Canada. Their setting
motivates a general identification problem: attractive markets can
support both more competitors and better outcomes for a focal firm. A
positive relationship between rival presence and performance can
therefore coexist with a negative competitive effect.

Within low-demand markets, suppose stores facing one, two, and three
rivals have sales of 9, 8, and 7 units. Within high-demand markets,
stores facing four, five, and six rivals have sales of 16, 15, and 14
units. Within each demand group, one additional rival is associated with
one unit less sales. Across the six observations, the pooled slope is
approximately \(+1.57\): high-demand markets have more rivals and higher
sales.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M03_omitted_demand.tex}
\caption{A positive pooled relationship can conceal a negative within-market-type relationship.}\label{fig:M03_omitted_demand}
\end{figure}

The within-group slope is \(-1\), while baseline demand differs between
groups. The positive pooled slope reflects that demand composition. In
an actual retail application, market demand may be unobserved, entry may
be forward-looking, and firms may respond strategically.

A manager considering entry should ask which outcomes would change if an
additional competitor entered the same market. Comparing different
markets does not automatically provide that counterfactual. Market fixed
effects, measured demand controls, an instrument, or a credible event
design may improve the comparison, but each uses different variation and
requires its own conditions. A highly predictive regression can remain
unsuitable for interpreting the coefficient as competition's causal
effect.

\hypertarget{M03-transformations-and-economically-meaningful-units}{%
\section{Transformations and Economically Meaningful
Units}\label{M03-transformations-and-economically-meaningful-units}}

\noindent A level-level specification gives an additive interpretation: one more
unit of \(X\) changes fitted \(Y\) by \(\beta_1\). A log-level
specification, \(\log Y=\beta_0+\beta_1X+\varepsilon\), describes
proportional differences in a positive outcome. A one-unit change in
\(X\) changes the fitted log outcome by \(\beta_1\); the corresponding
multiplicative change in the log-scale prediction is \(e^{\beta_1}\), or
\(100(e^{\beta_1}-1)\) percent. The approximation \(100\beta_1\) percent
is useful when the coefficient is small.

A log-log demand model, \(\log Q=\alpha+\beta\log P+\varepsilon\), gives
\(\beta\) an elasticity interpretation over the range where the
specification applies. If \(\beta=-1.5\), a 1\% higher price is
associated with approximately 1.5\% lower quantity. Sales revenue is
\(PQ\), so its local price elasticity is \(1+\beta=-0.5\). Profit also
depends on unit cost. A price that raises revenue can still lower
profit, and observed prices can be endogenous because firms set them in
response to demand.

Zero and negative outcomes need deliberate treatment. Taking a logarithm
of zero is undefined. Adding one changes the scale and interpretation,
especially when values are small or the unit of measurement changes. A
two-part model can separate purchase incidence from positive
expenditure. A suitable generalized linear model may model the
conditional mean directly. The choice should reflect the outcome and
intended estimand, with diagnostics for the selected specification.

Back-transforming a predicted log outcome also needs care.
Exponentiating the predicted conditional mean of \(\log Y\) generally
does not produce the conditional mean of \(Y\), because exponentiation
is nonlinear. Retransformation methods or a model for the mean on the
original scale may be needed when total sales is the target. Evaluate
predictions in the units used for the managerial decision.

\hypertarget{M03-interactions-describe-how-a-relationship-changes}{%
\section{Interactions Describe How a Relationship
Changes}\label{M03-interactions-describe-how-a-relationship-changes}}

\noindent Suppose an analyst expects a promotional message to work differently for
customers with long tenure. A linear interaction specification is

\[
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1D_i+\beta_2T_i+\beta_3D_iT_i+\varepsilon_i,
\]

where \(D_i\) is a message indicator and \(T_i\) is tenure in years. The
fitted message difference at tenure \(t\) is \(\beta_1+\beta_3t\). The
coefficient \(\beta_1\) is the difference at zero tenure, so centering
tenure at a meaningful value can make that coefficient easier to
interpret. The interaction coefficient tells how the fitted difference
changes per year of tenure.

With \(\beta_1=4\) dollars and \(\beta_3=-1\) dollar per year, the
fitted difference is \$4 at tenure zero, \$2 at two years, and zero at
four years. An average coefficient can conceal that variation.
Predictions beyond the observed tenure range should be treated as
extrapolation. In a nonlinear probability model, an interaction
coefficient on the model's index does not directly equal the interaction
in probability; compute and plot the predicted probabilities or marginal
contrasts.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M03_interaction.tex}
\caption{An interaction changes the relevant comparison across customer tenure.}\label{fig:M03_interaction}
\end{figure}

For tenure between zero and five years, the assumed contrast \(4-t\)
crosses zero at four years. In an estimated application, uncertainty
around the contrast and support at each tenure would determine whether
such a crossing is informative.

\hypertarget{M03-uncertainty-dependence-and-practical-importance}{%
\section{Uncertainty, Dependence, and Practical
Importance}\label{M03-uncertainty-dependence-and-practical-importance}}

\noindent A standard error describes sampling uncertainty under an estimator and
its assumptions. A confidence interval provides a range generated by a
procedure with a stated repeated-sampling coverage property. A p-value
assesses compatibility with a particular null under its reference model.
None of these quantities measures the managerial value of an effect by
itself. A precisely estimated increase of one cent may be unimportant; a
wide interval around a large potential benefit may justify another
experiment.

For an approximately normal coefficient estimate, a rough 95\% interval
is the estimate plus or minus 1.96 standard errors, with appropriate
adjustments when a finite-sample reference distribution is needed. If a
sales slope is 2.0 with a standard error of 0.5, that interval is
approximately {[}1.02, 2.98{]} in the slope's units. Report the units
and the comparison alongside the interval.

Heteroskedasticity means that residual variance differs across
observations. Heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors can address that
feature for inference under suitable sampling conditions; they do not
repair omitted-variable bias. Repeated store-week observations may share
persistent store shocks. Clustered standard errors allow dependence
within a specified cluster under their asymptotic conditions. The
relevant number of independent clusters can be much smaller than the
number of rows. With few clusters, conventional approximations may be
unreliable and design-specific methods are needed.

\hypertarget{M03-a-paired-change-requires-paired-uncertainty}{%
\subsection{A Paired Change Requires Paired
Uncertainty}\label{M03-a-paired-change-requires-paired-uncertainty}}

\noindent A manager comparing May and June logging has two observations for each
eligible mHealth user. The target is the average within-user change in
the fraction of calendar days with a recorded entry. Let \(p_{iM}\) and
\(p_{iJ}\) denote the May and June fractions and define
\(d_i=p_{iJ}-p_{iM}\). With users treated as independent sampling units,
an estimated standard error for the average change is

\[
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\bar d)=\frac{s_d}{\sqrt N},\qquad
s_d^2=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_i(d_i-\bar d)^2.
\]

This calculation preserves the dependence between a user's two outcomes.
The variance identity
\(\operatorname{Var}(p_{iJ}-p_{iM})=\operatorname{Var}(p_{iJ})+\operatorname{Var}(p_{iM})-2\operatorname{Cov}(p_{iJ},p_{iM})\)
explains why separately resampling the two months changes the
uncertainty calculation. Persistent user differences can cancel in a
paired contrast. Dependence among days within a user also means that the
number of calendar rows overstates the number of independent sampling
units.

For the fixed population defined in M2, Section 2.14, the average change
is \(-5.12\) percentage points. Resampling complete users with both
months together gives a 95\% percentile-bootstrap interval of
\([-7.93,-2.43]\) percentage points. The standard error calculated from
the dispersion of user-level changes is 1.38 percentage points. An
independent-Bernoulli-day calculation gives 0.66 percentage points and
the narrower interval \([-6.42,-3.82]\). That calculation discards the
observed dependence structure. A plotting library's default error bar
can conceal this difference if the analyst supplies calendar rows
without specifying the resampling unit.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M03_logging_uncertainty.tex}
\caption{The same descriptive mean change has different intervals when the sampling unit is incorrectly changed from users to independent days.}\label{fig:M03_logging_uncertainty}
\end{figure}

The bootstrap treats observed user histories as draws from a common user
distribution, with independence across users and both months fixed. It
does not incorporate shocks shared across the entire platform or
establish representativeness beyond this selected cohort. Both intervals
concern a descriptive temporal difference. A causal claim about a
product change would require an assignment design and uncertainty
appropriate to that design. The full \texttt{visualization.py} program
in M2, Section 2.14.3, calculates the monthly table, paired bootstrap,
and independent-day comparison; \texttt{visualization\_charts.py}
generates the interval figure from those results.

\hypertarget{M03-diagnostics-and-panel-data}{%
\section{Diagnostics and Panel
Data}\label{M03-diagnostics-and-panel-data}}

\noindent Inspect residuals against fitted values and important predictors for
nonlinear patterns and changing variance. Investigate influential
observations, errors in units, and unusual leverage. Multicollinearity
can make individual coefficients unstable even when predictions are
reasonably stable, because several predictors explain nearly the same
variation. Removing a variable solely to obtain a smaller p-value
changes the question and can introduce omitted-variable bias.

Store fixed effects absorb time-invariant differences between stores.
Calendar fixed effects absorb common period-specific shocks. In a
store-week panel, a model with both uses changes within stores relative
to common time movements. It still requires a valid account of
time-varying confounders. If a store raises advertising precisely when
an unobserved local event increases demand, the advertising coefficient
can remain biased.

A fitted model should be evaluated on the task for which it is used. For
prediction, compare held-out errors with a useful baseline. For a
descriptive coefficient, inspect support and sensitivity to
substantively justified specifications. For a causal effect, assess the
design and identifying conditions. A large \(R^2\) indicates in-sample
fit relative to an intercept-only benchmark; it does not establish a
credible intervention comparison.

For repeated food logs, a customer fixed effect can absorb persistent
differences in eating habits while relating changes in variety to
changes in recorded consumption. It leaves time-varying motivation,
activity, and reporting behavior as possible influences. The variety
analysis in \href{https://doi.org/10.1086/720453}{Nielsen and coauthors
(2022)} provides a concrete application. Percentage-change outcomes also
require attention to zero denominators: excluding days with zero prior
vegetable or snack consumption changes the sample relative to an
analysis of total calories. Interpret each coefficient for its own
observed population and outcome definition.

\hypertarget{M03-ai-assisted-implementation-and-practice}{%
\section{AI-Assisted Implementation and
Practice}\label{M03-ai-assisted-implementation-and-practice}}

\noindent Ask an assistant to fit the pooled and demand-group-adjusted regressions
in the six-observation example. Require a table with variable
definitions, units, coefficients, and the exact sample. Verify that the
adjusted rival coefficient is \(-1\) and the pooled coefficient is
\(11/7\approx1.57\). Ask it to explain why adding demand-group
indicators changes the comparison. A numerical match without that
explanation is an incomplete interpretation.

For a larger dataset, specify the formula and desired covariance
estimator before requesting code. Ask the assistant to list dropped rows
and explain how categorical variables were encoded. Have it calculate a
predicted contrast at two values of a moderator and compare the result
with the interaction formula. Treat diagnostic recommendations as
hypotheses to inspect, rather than automatic permission to remove
observations or alter the model.

For practice, consider an advertising coefficient measured per \$1,000
of spending. Re-express the predictor in dollars and explain how the
numerical coefficient changes while fitted sales remain the same. Next
explain why a robust standard error cannot eliminate the bias in the
market-demand example. Finally, distinguish a confidence interval for
the conditional mean from a prediction interval for a new store's
realized sales: the latter also reflects individual outcome variation.

\hypertarget{M03-readings}{%
\section{Readings}\label{M03-readings}}

\noindent \href{https://www.statlearning.com/}{An Introduction to Statistical
Learning} provides a foundation for regression, model assessment, and
nonlinear extensions. The
\href{https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/regression.html}{statsmodels
regression documentation} supports implementation.

\hypertarget{M03-mhealth-breadth-and-next-day-recorded-calories}{%
\section{mHealth: Breadth and Next-Day Recorded
Calories}\label{M03-mhealth-breadth-and-next-day-recorded-calories}}

\noindent The manager observes that users with broader daily food logs often
report more calories and considers using breadth to identify customers
who may want different suggestions. The relevant first comparison
concerns timing: does today's recorded breadth predict the next calendar
day's reported total? Taking the next available row would turn a one-day
comparison into an interval of variable length when customers skip days.

Let \(K_{it}\) be today's recorded category count and \(E_{i,t+1}\) the
next calendar day's reported calories. Among positive consecutive-day
pairs, estimate

\[
\log E_{i,t+1}=\alpha_i+\beta K_{it}+\gamma_{m(t)}+\delta_{w(t)}+u_{it}.
\]

The customer effect \(\alpha_i\) absorbs time-invariant differences in
typical logging and intake. Month and weekday effects describe calendar
variation. The coefficient compares days with different recorded breadth
for the same user, after these additive controls. It remains an
association: changing appetite, omitted meals, or recording effort can
affect both breadth and later totals. The
\href{https://epi.grants.cancer.gov/dietary-assessment-primer/learn/day.html}{NCI
discussion of weekday effects} motivates attention to calendar
composition.

The sample requires positive reported totals on both dates and at least
two eligible pairs per user. It contains 69,648 pairs from 370 users.
Standard errors are clustered by user to allow dependence among
overlapping pairs. The pooled model uses the same month and weekday
controls but omits customer effects. No prior-outcome control or calorie
winsorization is included in either baseline specification.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrr@{}}
\toprule
Specification & Pairs & Breadth Coefficient & Clustered 95\% Interval \\
\midrule

Pooled & 69,648 & 0.02771 & {[}0.01934, 0.03609{]} \\
Customer Fixed Effects & 69,648 & 0.01284 & {[}0.00997, 0.01572{]} \\
Fixed Effects, 100--5,000 on Both Days & 69,216 & 0.01136 & {[}0.00893,
0.01380{]} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

In the fixed-effects model, one additional category corresponds to a
1.29\% higher conditional geometric mean of next-day reported calories,
calculated as \(100(e^{\beta}-1)\). This percentage does not
automatically describe the arithmetic mean. The pooled estimate is
larger, consistent with persistent differences across users contributing
to the pooled association. Its reduction after adding fixed effects does
not identify a causal mechanism.

The third row applies the explicitly imposed review range from M1 to
both dates. It removes 432 pairs and produces a 1.14\% geometric-mean
association. This is a sensitivity comparison on a changed sample, not a
validated nutrition screen. The baseline outcome ranges from 0.64 to
9,190, so the restriction directly addresses observations influential on
the log scale. The adult and percentile screens in M2 answer different
sample questions and should be named separately when used.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M03_mhealth_association.tex}
\caption{Customer controls and a calorie-range sensitivity restriction change the descriptive coefficient.}\label{fig:M03_mhealth_association}
\end{figure}

The intervals quantify sampling uncertainty under the regression and
clustering specification. They do not account for all reporting error or
make breadth an assigned treatment. A recommendation to induce greater
breadth needs evidence about how a particular intervention changes
behavior and outcomes.

The date shift below moves future outcomes back exactly one day before
the merge. The program then applies each sample rule explicitly and
reports pair and user counts. An AI-generated
\texttt{groupby(...).shift(-1)} without a date-gap check would answer a
different question.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/mHealth/recurring_examples/m03.py}{m03.py}.
From its directory, run \texttt{python\ m03.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Estimate descriptive next-calendar-day associations with clustered uncertainty."""

import json
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from common import load_inputs, save_result

food, daily, baskets = load_inputs()
future = daily[["Userid", "date", "food_calories"]].copy()
future["date"] -= pd.Timedelta(days=1)
future = future.rename(columns={"food_calories": "next_calories"})
panel = daily.merge(future, on=["Userid", "date"], validate="one_to_one")
panel = panel.loc[panel.food_calories.gt(0) & panel.next_calories.gt(0)].copy()
counts = panel.groupby("Userid").size()
panel = panel.loc[panel.Userid.isin(counts[counts >= 2].index)].copy()
panel["log_next"] = np.log(panel.next_calories)
panel["month"] = panel.date.dt.month
panel["weekday"] = panel.date.dt.dayofweek
assert (panel.next_calories > 0).all()
restricted = panel.loc[
    panel.food_calories.between(100, 5000) & panel.next_calories.between(100, 5000)
].copy()
counts = restricted.groupby("Userid").size()
restricted = restricted.loc[restricted.Userid.isin(counts[counts >= 2].index)]
fits = {}
base = "log_next ~ category_count + C(month) + C(weekday)"
specifications = [
    ("pooled", base, panel),
    ("user_fixed_effects", base + " + C(Userid)", panel),
    ("restricted_fixed_effects", base + " + C(Userid)", restricted),
]
for name, formula, sample in specifications:
    fit = smf.ols(formula, data=sample).fit(
        cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": sample.Userid}, use_t=True
    )
    coefficient = float(fit.params["category_count"])
    low, high = map(float, fit.conf_int().loc["category_count"])
    fits[name] = {
        "pairs": len(sample),
        "users": int(sample.Userid.nunique()),
        "coefficient": coefficient,
        "se": float(fit.bse["category_count"]),
        "ci_low": low,
        "ci_high": high,
        "geometric_mean_percent": 100 * float(np.expm1(coefficient)),
    }
result = {
    "pairs": len(panel),
    "users": int(panel.Userid.nunique()),
    "min_next_calories": float(panel.next_calories.min()),
    "max_next_calories": float(panel.next_calories.max()),
    "models": fits,
}
save_result("M03", result)
print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
\end{Verbatim}
