\hypertarget{M04-endpoint-retention-continuous-retention-and-acquisition}{%
\subsection{Endpoint Retention, Continuous Retention, and
Acquisition}\label{M04-endpoint-retention-continuous-retention-and-acquisition}}

\noindent Endpoint retention permits cancellation followed by reentry. Continuous
retention requires the same provider to be held in every intervening
month. Of the 430 starting OpenAI subscribers, 129 remain continuously
subscribed through January 2026, a 30.0\% continuous-retention rate. The
162 endpoint subscribers include 33 who returned after at least one
observed gap. A cohort of existing subscribers also differs from a
cohort of newly acquired customers because subscription tenure and prior
survival affect its composition. Applying an acquisition-cohort CLV
formula to this twelve-month endpoint rate would obscure both
distinctions.

Likewise, the supplied \texttt{new} flag records a provider absent from
the previous month's holdings. It can describe first paid entry, reentry
to the category, a complete replacement of previous providers, or an
additional provider while retaining at least one incumbent. In April
2026, the 401 new-provider events comprise 197 first paid entries, 157
category returns, 32 complete provider switches, and 15 provider
additions. There are 400 distinct consumers behind these events because
one consumer starts two providers. The event denominator is therefore
explicit.

A release-month increase in new-provider events can reflect several of
these mechanisms. A causal claim about a release also requires a
credible comparison for what would have happened without it. Timing,
publicity, contemporaneous prices, overlapping releases, and previous
subscription states affect that comparison. The descriptive partition
supports the acquisition decision without treating every new-provider
event as switching.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/GenAI_Demand/retention.py}{retention.py}. From
the script's folder, run \texttt{python3\ retention.py}. Inputs are read
from the supplied local bundle; output tables are written beside the
course scripts.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Measure synthetic subscription stocks, cohorts, and acquisition events."""
from pathlib import Path
import json

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
SOURCE = HERE.parents[1] / "01_Resources/08_M8_Current_Topics_in_Marketing/genai_demand_lab/data"
OUTPUT = HERE / "results"


def acquisition_type(previous, current, ever_paid):
    """Classify a newly held provider using adjacent monthly subscription sets."""
    if not previous:
        return "category_return" if ever_paid else "first_paid_entry"
    if previous.isdisjoint(current):
        return "complete_provider_switch"
    return "provider_addition"


def cohort_outcomes(subs, provider, start, horizon, observed_months):
    """Endpoint and continuous retention for one fixed provider cohort."""
    required = {str(pd.Period(start, freq="M") + k) for k in range(horizon + 1)}
    if not required.issubset(set(observed_months)):
        raise ValueError("Cohort horizon extends beyond the observed calendar")
    cohort = set(subs.loc[subs.month.eq(start) & subs.provider.eq(provider), "consumer_id"])
    if not cohort:
        raise ValueError("Empty starting cohort")
    continuous = cohort.copy()
    rows = []
    for k in range(horizon + 1):
        month = str(pd.Period(start, freq="M") + k)
        active = subs.loc[subs.month.eq(month)]
        own = set(active.loc[active.provider.eq(provider), "consumer_id"])
        any_provider = set(active.consumer_id)
        continuous &= own
        row = {"provider": provider, "start_month": start, "month": month,
               "horizon_months": k, "cohort_size": len(cohort),
               "same_provider": len(cohort & own),
               "other_provider_only": len((cohort & any_provider) - own),
               "no_paid_provider": len(cohort - any_provider),
               "continuous_same_provider": len(continuous)}
        assert row["same_provider"] + row["other_provider_only"] + row["no_paid_provider"] == len(cohort)
        rows.append(row)
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def main():
    consumers = pd.read_csv(SOURCE / "synthetic_consumers.csv")
    subs = pd.read_csv(SOURCE / "synthetic_subscriptions.csv.gz")
    dgp = json.loads((SOURCE / "synthetic_dgp.json").read_text())
    months = sorted(dgp["g_trend"])
    n = len(consumers)
    assert n == dgp["n_consumers"] and consumers.consumer_id.is_unique
    assert not subs.duplicated(["consumer_id", "month", "provider"]).any()
    assert subs.consumer_id.isin(consumers.consumer_id).all()
    assert subs.month.isin(months).all() and subs.price.gt(0).all()
    assert subs["new"].isin([True, False]).all()
    assert subs.tier.isin(["basic", "premium"]).all()
    states = {m: {int(i): set(g.provider) for i, g in s.groupby("consumer_id")}
              for m, s in subs.groupby("month")}
    events, monthly, history = [], [], set()
    previous = {}
    for month in months:
        current = states.get(month, {})
        for consumer, providers in current.items():
            old = previous.get(consumer, set())
            for provider in sorted(providers - old):
                events.append({"month": month, "consumer_id": consumer, "provider": provider,
                               "event": acquisition_type(old, providers, consumer in history)})
        group = subs.loc[subs.month.eq(month)]
        monthly.append({"month": month, "population": n, "payers": len(current),
                        "subscriptions": len(group), "adoption": len(current) / n,
                        "multihomers": sum(len(s) > 1 for s in current.values()),
                        "basic_subscriptions": int(group.tier.eq("basic").sum())})
        history.update(current)
        previous = current
    events = pd.DataFrame(events)
    keys = ["month", "consumer_id", "provider"]
    recorded = set(subs.loc[subs["new"], keys].itertuples(index=False, name=None))
    calculated = set(events[keys].itertuples(index=False, name=None))
    assert recorded == calculated
    monthly = pd.DataFrame(monthly)
    monthly["multihoming_given_payment"] = monthly.multihomers / monthly.payers.replace(0, np.nan)
    monthly["basic_subscription_share"] = monthly.basic_subscriptions / monthly.subscriptions.replace(0, np.nan)
    cohort_start, horizon = "2025-01", 12
    assert str(pd.Period(cohort_start, freq="M") + horizon) <= months[-1]
    providers = sorted(subs.loc[subs.month.eq(cohort_start), "provider"].unique())
    cohorts = pd.concat([cohort_outcomes(subs, p, cohort_start, horizon, months)
                         for p in providers], ignore_index=True)
    last_events = events.loc[events.month.eq(months[-1])]
    counts = last_events.event.value_counts().sort_index()
    last = monthly.iloc[-1]
    result = {"data_type": "synthetic", "population": n, "subscription_rows": len(subs),
              "calendar_months": len(months), "last_month": months[-1],
              "last_payers": int(last.payers), "last_subscriptions": int(last.subscriptions),
              "last_adoption": float(last.adoption),
              "last_multihomers": int(last.multihomers),
              "last_multihoming_given_payment": float(last.multihoming_given_payment),
              "last_acquisition_events": int(len(last_events)),
              "last_acquisition_consumers": int(last_events.consumer_id.nunique()),
              "last_acquisition_types": {k: int(v) for k, v in counts.items()},
              "new_flag_verified": True}
    OUTPUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    monthly.to_csv(OUTPUT / "adoption.csv", index=False, float_format="%.8f")
    cohorts.to_csv(OUTPUT / "cohorts.csv", index=False)
    counts.rename_axis("event").rename("events").to_csv(OUTPUT / "acquisition_types.csv")
    (OUTPUT / "retention.json").write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M04-retention-customer-value-and-choice}{%
\section{Retention, Customer Value, and
Choice}\label{M04-retention-customer-value-and-choice}}

\noindent \noindent A subscription manager can increase measured customer lifetime
value by improving service or by making cancellation harder. Both
mechanisms can raise the probability of another payment. They have
different implications for customer welfare, future trust, and the
sustainability of the relationship. A financial retention model should
therefore distinguish the source of the additional renewal.

A useful comparison holds the final offer fixed and varies the preceding
interaction. One group sees a direct cancellation option. Another can
choose whether to view a retention offer before deciding. Record
cancellation completion, time spent, subsequent charges, refunds, and
informed willingness to continue. Continued payment and a completed
choice are separate outcomes. The model in Section 8.14 provides a
numerical example in which higher renewal raises firm profit while
reducing customer value under explicitly opposed stakes.

The segmentation decision also has distributional consequences. A
cluster defined by earlier spending and visits describes behavioral
similarity. It does not establish an intrinsic customer type or a
justification for restricting access to an essential service. Compare
the proposed treatment with customers' needs and the consequences of
errors. When a segment receives an offer, record who can obtain it, who
is excluded, and whether the exclusion follows the firm's stated
objective.

In a conjoint task, price components and cancellation conditions are
product attributes when they affect the customer's actual choice.
Omitting a mandatory payment from the described price changes the offer
respondents evaluate. The FTC fee rule's current coverage includes
live-event tickets and short-term lodging; applying it requires the
covered transaction and required components. Its scope should be checked
in the
\href{https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/rule-unfair-or-deceptive-fees-frequently-asked-questions}{FTC's
rule guidance}.

\hypertarget{M04-ai-services-buyer-burden-and-the-outside-option}{%
\section{AI Services, Buyer Burden, and the Outside
Option}\label{M04-ai-services-buyer-burden-and-the-outside-option}}

\noindent \noindent A firm pricing an analytics service needs to understand the
customer's best alternative. A customer may buy a competing service,
conduct the analysis internally, or leave the decision unchanged. AI
assistance can improve each of those alternatives. A reduction in the
seller's coding cost therefore need not increase the amount a customer
will pay.

Let \(v\) be a customer's monetary-equivalent value of the delivered
analysis over a specified period, \(b\) its setup and verification
burden, and \(u_0\) the net value of its best alternative. Under
quasilinear utility, the customer weakly prefers purchase at price \(p\)
when \(v-p-b\geq u_0\). Its price ceiling is \(v-b-u_0\). All four
objects refer to the same customer and horizon. The burden includes the
customer's required effort after delivery; the outside option already
includes the costs of pursuing that alternative.

Product design can raise this ceiling by making the output more useful
or reducing integration and verification effort. Competitive
improvements raise \(u_0\) and reduce the ceiling, holding the offered
product fixed. A conjoint exercise should represent realistic
alternatives and implementation requirements. Preference estimates
obtained before customers gain access to a substantially improved
alternative may require new validation.

The conditional pricing calculation in M8, Section 8.17, compares this
participation ceiling with the seller's cost recovery requirement. The
interval can disappear even when the seller becomes more productive.
Measuring actual take-up, substitution, and customer effort is necessary
before treating the assumed sales volume as a forecast.

\hypertarget{M04-clustering-mechanisms-that-can-affect-consumer-agency}{%
\section{Clustering Mechanisms That Can Affect Consumer
Agency}\label{M04-clustering-mechanisms-that-can-affect-consumer-agency}}

\noindent \noindent A subscription firm can use research to identify where a
conversion or retention objective may conflict with customers' ability
to understand and revise their choices. The relevant grouping should
distinguish mechanisms that call for different evaluations. Social
endorsement raises questions about credibility and pressure. Defaults
raise questions about informed selection. Exit friction raises questions
about whether a decision to cancel becomes effective. A high response
rate provides little guidance about which of these mechanisms produced
it.

The primary sample contains 48 retrieved papers coded as having a
reported choice concern or potential dual use. Forty-seven are in the
potential-dual-use category; one explicitly discusses constrained
agency. The twelve binary features describe attention, framing, social
cues, emotion and identity, disclosure, personalization, privacy,
defaults and order, exit and search friction, habits and rewards,
financial commitment, and delegated control. The labels are preliminary
AI-assisted annotations, largely based on abstracts, with selected
full-text checks. They have not undergone independent human
adjudication. Potential misuse is an inference about a mechanism and
does not establish author intent.

For papers \(i\) and \(j\), let \(A_i\) and \(A_j\) contain the
mechanisms coded as present. Jaccard distance measures the proportion of
their combined positive features that they do not share:

\[
d_J(i,j)=1-\frac{|A_i\cap A_j|}{|A_i\cup A_j|}.
\]

The numerator counts shared mechanisms and the denominator counts
mechanisms present in either paper. Shared absences do not create
similarity. This matters when most of the twelve codes are zero. Papers
with no positive mechanism are excluded from this comparison, and
unreviewed papers remain outside the analysis. Average linkage merges
groups according to their average pairwise distance. K-means would
impose a different Euclidean representation and objective.

The program evaluates two through eight clusters and selects the
partition with the largest silhouette score. For a paper, the silhouette
compares its mean distance to its own group with the smallest mean
distance to another group, scaled by the larger distance. The selected
four-cluster solution has a mean silhouette of 0.272. Cluster names
describe the profiles after estimation; they are not inputs to the
algorithm.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
Profile & Papers & Share of 48 \\
\midrule

Social Influence & 19 & 39.6\% \\
Emotion and Identity & 15 & 31.3\% \\
Disclosure, Framing, and Defaults & 8 & 16.7\% \\
Attention, Search, and Control & 6 & 12.5\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M04_agency_clusters.tex}
\caption{Four mutually exclusive clusters contain 19, 15, 8, and 6 papers. The denominator is the 48 retrieved papers coded as potentially relevant to agency concerns.}\label{fig:M04_agency_clusters}
\end{figure}

Social influence is the largest cluster in this selected sample. Every
paper in that group receives the social-cue indicator, and six also
receive the emotion/identity indicator. Emotion/identity is the most
common individual feature across all groups, appearing in 21 of 48
papers. Thus the largest cluster and the most common feature answer
different questions. Clusters partition the papers; feature memberships
overlap. Neither statistic estimates the prevalence or severity of
agency erosion in markets.

Stability checks change the strength of the conclusion. Re-estimation on
200 random 80\% subsamples, holding four clusters fixed, produces a
median adjusted Rand index of 0.794 against the full-sample partition.
Switching to Hamming distance lowers agreement to 0.485. An imposed
stress test that changes one feature per paper yields median agreement
of 0.250. Those values compare partitions, with one indicating identical
grouping and zero corresponding to chance-adjusted agreement. The stress
test is a sensitivity calculation; its feature changes do not represent
an estimated error rate.

Including 36 additional abstract-only risk reviews produces 84 papers
and selects eight clusters, the top of the candidate range. Adding
retrieved protective papers with positive mechanism codes produces 60
papers and selects six clusters. These changes warrant further review
before treating the groups as a stable taxonomy. A manager can still use
the profiles to choose customer-outcome measures: comprehension and
credibility for social influence, informed preferences for emotional
appeals, term recall for disclosure, and successful exit for
cancellation flows.

Reproduction starts with \texttt{coded\_papers.csv} and preserves all
three sample definitions, the code checks, distance calculations, K
selection, paper-level assignments, and sensitivity comparisons. All
feature definitions and status rules appear in the
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Consumer_Agency_Literature/CODEBOOK.md}{codebook}.
Run it from the saved script with the dependencies in the example
folder. Counts and profiles are checked against independent row-wise
totals.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Consumer_Agency_Literature/cluster.py}{cluster.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Cluster coded paper mechanisms; all prevalence estimates condition on the review sample."""
from pathlib import Path
import json
import platform
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import scipy
from scipy.spatial.distance import pdist, squareform
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, cut_tree
import sklearn
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score, adjusted_rand_score

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
FEATURES = [
    "attention_salience", "framing_reference", "social_cues", "emotion_identity",
    "opacity_disclosure", "personalization", "privacy_control", "defaults_order",
    "exit_search_friction", "habits_rewards", "financial_commitment", "delegation_control",
]
RISK = ["potential_dual_use", "reported_choice_concern"]


def select_sample(data, sample):
    """Never convert uncoded papers into zero-feature observations."""
    risk = data.review_status.isin(RISK)
    if sample == "downloaded_risk":
        mask = risk & data.download_status.eq("downloaded")
    elif sample == "all_reviewed_risk":
        mask = risk
    elif sample == "downloaded_with_protective":
        mask = (risk | data.review_status.eq("protective")) & data.download_status.eq("downloaded")
        # Broad governance/inclusion papers without these mechanisms remain in
        # the review catalog; a zero vector has no positive mechanism to compare.
        mask &= data[FEATURES].sum(axis=1) > 0
    else:
        raise ValueError(sample)
    result = data.loc[mask].sort_values("id").reset_index(drop=True)
    if result[FEATURES].isna().any().any():
        raise ValueError("Missing codes require review, not zero imputation")
    if not result[FEATURES].isin([0, 1]).all().all():
        raise ValueError("Mechanism indicators must be binary")
    if (result[FEATURES].sum(axis=1) == 0).any():
        raise ValueError("An uncoded mechanism cannot enter the similarity analysis")
    return result


def partition(matrix, k, metric="jaccard"):
    """Average linkage accepts non-Euclidean distances such as Jaccard."""
    distances = pdist(matrix.astype(bool), metric=metric)
    tree = linkage(distances, method="average")
    labels = cut_tree(tree, n_clusters=[k]).ravel()
    return labels, squareform(distances)


def evaluate_sample(data, name, output):
    sample = select_sample(data, name)
    matrix = sample[FEATURES].to_numpy(dtype=int)
    n = len(sample)
    candidates = []
    for k in range(2, min(8, n - 1) + 1):
        labels, distance = partition(matrix, k)
        sizes = np.bincount(labels)
        candidates.append({"k": k, "silhouette": silhouette_score(distance, labels, metric="precomputed"),
                           "smallest_cluster": int(sizes.min()), "largest_cluster": int(sizes.max())})
    candidates = pd.DataFrame(candidates)
    # This is a declared selection rule, not a claim that nature has K types.
    best = candidates.sort_values(["silhouette", "k"], ascending=[False, True]).iloc[0]
    k = int(best.k)
    labels, _ = partition(matrix, k)
    # Stable presentation IDs: descending size, with original ID breaking ties.
    order = sorted(set(labels), key=lambda c: (-sum(labels == c), c))
    label_map = {c: rank + 1 for rank, c in enumerate(order)}
    sample["cluster"] = [label_map[c] for c in labels]
    counts = sample.groupby("cluster").size().rename("papers").to_frame()
    counts["share"] = counts.papers / n
    profiles = sample.groupby("cluster")[FEATURES].mean()
    counts["most_common_features"] = [
        "; ".join(profiles.loc[c].sort_values(ascending=False, kind="stable").head(3).index)
        for c in counts.index
    ]
    frequency = sample[FEATURES].sum().rename("papers").to_frame()
    frequency["denominator"] = n
    frequency["share"] = frequency.papers / n
    frequency = frequency.sort_values(["papers"], ascending=False, kind="stable")
    # Refit on 80% subsamples, comparing shared rows with the full partition.
    # Quantiles measure conditional algorithm stability, not population uncertainty.
    rng = np.random.default_rng(534)
    stability = []
    for iteration in range(200):
        indices = np.sort(rng.choice(n, size=max(k + 1, int(.8 * n)), replace=False))
        new_labels, _ = partition(matrix[indices], k)
        stability.append(adjusted_rand_score(labels[indices], new_labels))
    alternative, _ = partition(matrix, k, metric="hamming")
    # Perturb one coded bit per paper to expose sensitivity to annotation choices.
    # This imposed stress test is not an estimated annotation error distribution.
    perturbation = []
    for iteration in range(200):
        changed = matrix.copy()
        for row in range(n):
            allowed = np.arange(len(FEATURES))
            if changed[row].sum() == 1:
                allowed = allowed[changed[row] == 0]
            column = rng.choice(allowed)
            changed[row, column] = 1 - changed[row, column]
        new_labels, _ = partition(changed, k)
        perturbation.append(adjusted_rand_score(labels, new_labels))
    folder = output / name
    folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True, parents=True)
    sample.to_csv(folder / "assignments.csv", index=False)
    counts.to_csv(folder / "cluster_sizes.csv")
    profiles.to_csv(folder / "cluster_profiles.csv")
    frequency.to_csv(folder / "feature_prevalence.csv", index_label="feature")
    candidates.to_csv(folder / "k_comparison.csv", index=False)
    pd.DataFrame({"adjusted_rand_index": stability}).to_csv(folder / "subsample_stability.csv", index=False)
    assert counts.papers.sum() == n and np.isclose(counts.share.sum(), 1)
    # Independent row-loop count checks the vectorized feature aggregate.
    for feature in FEATURES:
        assert int(frequency.loc[feature, "papers"]) == sum(int(row[feature]) for _, row in sample.iterrows())
    return {"papers": n, "k": k, "silhouette": float(best.silhouette),
            "cluster_counts": {str(c): int(v) for c, v in counts.papers.items()},
            "largest_features": frequency.head(3).reset_index().to_dict("records"),
            "subsample_ari_quantiles": np.quantile(stability, [.1, .5, .9]).tolist(),
            "hamming_ari": float(adjusted_rand_score(labels, alternative)),
            "one_bit_perturbation_ari_quantiles": np.quantile(perturbation, [.1, .5, .9]).tolist(),
            "valid_perturbation_runs": len(perturbation)}


def main():
    data = pd.read_csv(HERE / "coded_papers.csv")
    assert data.id.is_unique and data.doi.is_unique
    output = HERE / "results"
    output.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    summary = {name: evaluate_sample(data, name, output) for name in [
        "downloaded_risk", "all_reviewed_risk", "downloaded_with_protective"]}
    summary["environment"] = {"python": platform.python_version(), "numpy": np.__version__,
                              "pandas": pd.__version__, "scipy": scipy.__version__, "sklearn": sklearn.__version__}
    (output / "summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(json.dumps(summary, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M05-m5.-text-social-media-and-customer-networks}{%
\chapter{Text, Social Media, and Customer
Networks}\label{M05-m5.-text-social-media-and-customer-networks}}

\noindent A retailer receives thousands of reviews and support messages each week.
The service manager needs to distinguish delivery delays, product
defects, and billing problems, then decide which issues deserve
attention. A count of negative words is an incomplete representation:
``the refund was fast, but the replacement failed'' contains different
evaluations of two aspects of the experience. The analytical task is to
turn language into a defensible measurement of a concept relevant to
action.

Text analysis also raises a sampling problem. Customers who post reviews
can differ from those who remain silent, and the platform can affect
what gets posted or displayed. Social-network analysis adds another
layer: observed connections and similar behavior can reflect influence,
common circumstances, or selection into relationships.

\hypertarget{M05-define-the-construct-and-the-document}{%
\section{Define the Construct and the
Document}\label{M05-define-the-construct-and-the-document}}

\noindent A construct is the concept the analysis intends to measure, such as
delivery dissatisfaction, perceived authenticity, or purchase intent. A
label is the operational category assigned to an observation. A document
might be a complete review, one sentence, a support ticket, or a
conversation. Those units should follow the construct. A review-level
sentiment label can obscure a positive service experience and a negative
product experience in the same review.

Write an annotation codebook before producing labels at scale. It should
define each category, inclusion and exclusion rules, treatment of
ambiguity, and examples near category boundaries. If a message can
contain several problems, a multi-label task may be appropriate. If the
decision requires routing each ticket to one team, define a primary
issue or a routing priority separately from the presence of every issue.

Metadata can be informative and potentially misleading. Ratings may help
validate a sentiment measure but can also leak the intended label into a
prediction exercise. Product category, language, channel, and date can
reveal domain differences. Remove or protect personal information before
sending text to an external service, and use approved data access. A
scraped review is not automatically free of personal or contractual
restrictions.

\hypertarget{M05-representing-language-with-counts-and-weights}{%
\section{Representing Language With Counts and
Weights}\label{M05-representing-language-with-counts-and-weights}}

\noindent A bag-of-words representation counts tokens while largely ignoring their
order. An \(n\)-gram representation retains local sequences, so ``not
good'' can differ from ``good.'' Tokenization, case normalization,
punctuation, and stop-word rules change the resulting features. Removing
negation words can destroy information needed for sentiment. Removing
product names may help focus on attributes or may erase the very object
whose complaints the manager needs to identify.

Term frequency-inverse document frequency gives greater weight to terms
that are frequent in a document but less common across the corpus. One
simple convention is

\[
\operatorname{tfidf}_{wd}=\operatorname{tf}_{wd}\log\left(\frac{N}{\operatorname{df}_w}\right),
\]

where \(\operatorname{tf}_{wd}\) is the frequency of word \(w\) in
document \(d\), \(N\) is the number of documents, and
\(\operatorname{df}_w\) is the number of documents containing the word.
Implementations vary in smoothing, normalization, and term-frequency
definitions. Record the convention rather than assuming a library's
output matches this exact expression.

If ``delivery'' appears in two of three documents, its
inverse-document-frequency term under this convention is
\(\log(3/2)\approx0.405\). A word appearing in every document receives
zero weight. That weighting can help discriminate documents, but a
common term may still be substantively important. Statistical
distinctiveness and managerial importance are different criteria.

Fit a learned vocabulary and IDF weights on training text when
evaluating prediction. Learning them from the test corpus exposes
information about the evaluation distribution. The leakage may appear
minor compared with using labels, yet it still changes the task. A
pipeline makes the training-only transformation explicit and
reproducible.

\hypertarget{M05-embeddings-and-semantic-similarity}{%
\section{Embeddings and Semantic
Similarity}\label{M05-embeddings-and-semantic-similarity}}

\noindent An embedding maps a document or token into a vector learned from
language data. Similar vectors can capture related meanings even when
documents use different words. Cosine similarity compares the angle
between vectors:

\[
\operatorname{cos}(u,v)=\frac{u^\top v}{\|u\|\,\|v\|}.
\]

The normalization removes vector length from the comparison. This is
useful when direction represents meaning in the selected model, but it
does not guarantee that the similarity corresponds to the marketing
construct. Two messages about refunds can be semantically close while
expressing opposite evaluations. Retrieval quality should be checked
with examples that matter for the downstream task.

A simple TF-IDF classifier can be a strong baseline for a well-defined
domain. Embeddings may help with paraphrases, sparse labels, and
semantic retrieval, but they introduce dependence on a pretrained model
and its training domain. Compare alternatives on the same held-out data
and operational criteria. Record model versions because an updated
representation can change nearest neighbors and labels even when the
input text is unchanged.

For interpretation, inspect representative successes and failures. A
model may associate a brand name with complaints because one product had
a recall during training. It can then misclassify neutral mentions after
the issue is resolved. Temporal validation and product-level holdouts
help reveal whether performance depends on such shortcuts.

\hypertarget{M05-sentiment-aspect-labels-and-topic-models}{%
\section{Sentiment, Aspect Labels, and Topic
Models}\label{M05-sentiment-aspect-labels-and-topic-models}}

\noindent A sentiment lexicon assigns scores to words and combines them using
rules. It offers a transparent baseline, but sarcasm, domain-specific
meanings, and context can cause errors. A supervised classifier learns a
mapping from labeled examples to outcomes. Its labels and training
sample define what it learns; a generic ``positive/negative'' dataset
may not represent customer-service severity.

Aspect-based analysis separates the object being evaluated from the
evaluation itself. For the sentence ``delivery was late, but the support
agent solved the problem,'' a useful record might contain
delivery-negative and service-positive labels. A single overall score
discards that distinction. If the action is a logistics intervention,
the aspect-specific measure is closer to the decision.

Topic models describe recurring patterns of word co-occurrence or
document similarity. A topic is an estimated pattern, not automatically
a stable consumer need. In probabilistic models, documents can combine
topics; in clustering approaches, assignments may be discrete or
probabilistic. Analysts supply topic names after inspecting high-weight
words and representative documents. Validate those names with actual
text and examine stability across preprocessing and model choices.

A manager should avoid interpreting an increase in a topic's share
without checking its denominator. More delivery complaints can mean more
delivery problems, more deliveries overall, a changed review prompt, or
fewer reviews about other topics. Combining text measures with
transaction or service-volume data helps distinguish these explanations.

\hypertarget{M05-case-study-a-complaint-detector-under-changing-prevalence}{%
\section{Case Study: A Complaint Detector Under Changing
Prevalence}\label{M05-case-study-a-complaint-detector-under-changing-prevalence}}

\noindent Suppose a classifier identifies a rare but costly product defect. In a
synthetic evaluation population of 1,000 tickets, 200 truly mention the
defect. The classifier detects 160 of them and incorrectly flags 80 of
the 800 other tickets. Sensitivity, or recall, is 80\%; specificity is
90\%; precision is 160/240, or 66.7\%.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrr@{}}
\toprule
Population & True Defect Tickets & True Positives & False Positives &
Precision \\
\midrule

Evaluation sample & 200 & 160 & 80 & 66.7\% \\
Deployment sample & 10 & 8 & 99 & 7.5\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The second row holds sensitivity at 80\% and specificity at 90\%, but
reduces true prevalence to 1\%. Among 990 nondefect tickets, 99 are
flagged. Only eight of the 107 flagged tickets are true positives. A
manager using the original precision to plan review staffing would be
badly misled.

Bayes' rule makes the dependence explicit. If prevalence is \(\rho\),
sensitivity is \(s\), and specificity is \(q\), then

\[
\Pr(\text{defect}\mid\text{flag})=\frac{s\rho}{s\rho+(1-q)(1-\rho)}.
\]

The denominator counts both correct and incorrect flags. For a rare
issue, even a modest false-positive rate can dominate that total. This
is why validation should represent the deployment population or
explicitly adjust for a changed sampling design.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M05_prevalence.tex}
\caption{Precision falls as the target issue becomes rarer, even with unchanged sensitivity and specificity.}\label{fig:M05_prevalence}
\end{figure}

Sensitivity and specificity remain at 0.80 and 0.90 in both populations.
The decline in precision comes entirely from the lower prevalence.
Operational evaluation should also consider the cost of missed defects,
the burden of false alarms, and whether uncertain cases can be routed to
human review.

\hypertarget{M05-human-and-llm-annotation}{%
\section{Human and LLM Annotation}\label{M05-human-and-llm-annotation}}

\noindent LLMs can help draft a codebook, suggest candidate labels, or classify
text using explicit instructions. For a defensible measurement exercise,
preserve the original text, the codebook version, model identifier,
prompt, output schema, and date. Require a bounded output format with an
allowed ``uncertain'' category where appropriate. Validate the output
against the schema and inspect cases that violate the instructions.

A prompt should identify the construct, unit, categories, boundary
rules, and examples. For delivery dissatisfaction, it should distinguish
a complaint about an actual delay from a question about the promised
delivery date. Ask for a short supporting span from the supplied text
when that improves traceability. A fluent explanation is not evidence
that the label is correct; compare it with independent human judgments
on a relevant sample.

Human agreement is informative because the construct may itself be
ambiguous. Double-code a sample, examine disagreements, and refine
definitions before scaling. Report category-specific errors, prevalence,
and performance across languages or product groups. An average accuracy
can conceal systematic failure on the minority category that motivates
the analysis.

Treat text being classified as data. A review may contain language
resembling an instruction to the model. It should not change the
annotation task, request external actions, or supply new system rules.
Separate the fixed task instructions from the document content,
constrain outputs, and inspect unexpected behavior. Use synthetic or
approved text for classroom exercises involving external services.

\hypertarget{M05-networks-connections-reach-and-brokerage}{%
\section{Networks: Connections, Reach, and
Brokerage}\label{M05-networks-connections-reach-and-brokerage}}

\noindent A network represents entities as nodes and relationships as edges. Nodes
might be customers, creators, brands, or products. An edge might
indicate following, communication, co-purchase, or a similarity
criterion. Directed and weighted networks preserve different information
from undirected binary networks. The edge definition should follow the
substantive relationship the analyst intends to study.

Degree counts a node's direct connections. Betweenness summarizes how
often a node lies on shortest paths between other nodes. A person with
few direct contacts can have high betweenness if those contacts connect
otherwise separate groups. Eigenvector-based measures give more weight
to connections with well-connected nodes. These metrics describe network
structure under their definitions; they do not by themselves establish
persuasion, credibility, or the effect of paying a creator.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M05_network_bridge.tex}
\caption{A broker with few direct links can connect two otherwise separate customer groups.}\label{fig:M05_network_bridge}
\end{figure}

Broker R has two direct connections, while each within-group connector
has four. Removing R disconnects the two groups. A customer with fewer
direct contacts can therefore be essential for reaching a different
audience. A marketing campaign may value either role, depending on
message transmission, audience overlap, and the intended outcome.

Observed similarity among connected customers can arise from influence,
homophily, or common exposure. Friends may adopt a product because they
affect one another, because they already share tastes, or because they
see the same promotion. Regressing adoption on friends' adoption does
not distinguish those mechanisms without additional design. Randomized
encouragement, timing restrictions, or credible natural variation can
help, with attention to spillovers and the unit of assignment.

\hypertarget{M05-social-media-case-engagement-and-commercial-value}{%
\section{Social-Media Case: Engagement and Commercial
Value}\label{M05-social-media-case-engagement-and-commercial-value}}

\noindent A brand compares two creators. One receives many comments, but those
comments largely come from an audience that already follows the brand.
The other reaches a smaller group with less overlap. A high engagement
count does not establish more incremental sales. The comparison requires
a target population, exposure definition, outcome horizon, and a way to
measure what would have happened without the collaboration.

Text can help describe comment content, and network overlap can describe
audience duplication. Those measurements support campaign design, but
they should be combined with an evaluation strategy. A test might
randomize eligible regions or audience groups when feasible, or compare
outcomes using a credible observational design. If communication crosses
groups, spillovers can complicate the interpretation of an untreated
group.

For classroom practice, construct two small audience sets and calculate
their overlap. Then compare comments per exposed user with total
comments. Explain why neither is a direct estimate of incremental
profit.

\hypertarget{M05-ai-assisted-workflow-practice-and-readings}{%
\section{AI-Assisted Workflow, Practice, and
Readings}\label{M05-ai-assisted-workflow-practice-and-readings}}

\noindent Start a text exercise with a small manually inspected sample and a
codebook. Build a transparent baseline, reserve an evaluation sample,
and compare a more complex method on the same outcomes. Ask an assistant
to produce a confusion matrix and representative errors, then
independently recompute precision and recall from the counts. Keep model
selection and prompt refinement away from the final test sample.

For practice, calculate accuracy in the first complaint-detector sample:
88\%. Explain why a classifier that always predicts ``no defect'' would
achieve 99\% accuracy in the rare-prevalence deployment sample while
detecting no defects. Next identify how removing ``not'' changes the
meaning of ``not reliable.'' Finally, explain why two highly connected
adopters may share preferences even if neither caused the other's
adoption.

The
\href{https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/feature_extraction.html\#text-feature-extraction}{scikit-learn
text-feature documentation} supports count and TF-IDF representations.
\href{https://github.com/cjhutto/vaderSentiment}{VADER's author
repository} provides a rule-based sentiment baseline.
\href{https://doi.org/10.1007/s11002-020-09535-7}{Hagen and colleagues
(2020)} discuss ways machine learning can support behavioral marketing
research.

\hypertarget{M05-mhealth-classifying-new-food-descriptions}{%
\section{mHealth: Classifying New Food
Descriptions}\label{M05-mhealth-classifying-new-food-descriptions}}

\noindent The manager wants to reduce the effort required to categorize a food
entry. A lookup table may work well for familiar descriptions, while a
text classifier may help with a new description. These are distinct
deployment conditions. Repeated descriptions in both training and test
records can make a random entry split look successful even when the
system will struggle with unseen language.

Normalize descriptions by lowercasing, collapsing whitespace, and
trimming the ends. Retain nonempty descriptions and nonmissing source
categories, then sample 200,000 eligible entries with seed 534. The
sample contains 37,570 distinct normalized descriptions; 1,725 appear
with more than one source category. Those inconsistencies create label
ambiguity. The source category is the prediction target, not a validated
nutritional interpretation of the food.

The first split assigns approximately 20\% of entries to testing. The
second uses a fixed SHA-256 rule to hold out entire normalized
descriptions. Its test entries therefore share no exact normalized
description with training. Both evaluations weight food entries equally,
so frequent descriptions receive more weight. A second evaluation
weighting unique descriptions equally would answer a different product
question.

A training-only lookup chooses the most frequent category for each
description, breaking count ties alphabetically and falling back to the
most frequent training category. The text alternative fits a TF-IDF
vocabulary of unigrams and bigrams on distinct training descriptions,
caps the vocabulary at 20,000 features, and requires a term to occur in
at least two training descriptions. Multinomial naive Bayes uses
smoothing of 0.1 and training description-category counts as weights.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 10\tabcolsep) * \real{0.13}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 10\tabcolsep) * \real{0.17}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 10\tabcolsep) * \real{0.17}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 10\tabcolsep) * \real{0.17}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 10\tabcolsep) * \real{0.17}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 10\tabcolsep) * \real{0.19}}@{}}
\toprule
Evaluation & Test Entries & Familiar Descriptions & Lookup Accuracy &
Text Accuracy & Text Macro F1 \\
\midrule

Entry Split & 40,273 & 88.65\% & 84.90\% & 84.94\% & 0.5531 \\
Description Split & 36,987 & 0\% & 3.82\% & 67.42\% & 0.3465 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Macro F1 averages across the 312 labels present in the combined sampled
data, assigning zero to undefined class scores. Rare labels therefore
matter more than in accuracy. The gap between the two evaluations
reflects both familiarity and the changed test composition; it is not a
causal estimate of leakage's effect. For a service processing new
descriptions, the description-level evaluation is the closer test of
that requirement.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M05_mhealth_text.tex}
\caption{Exact-description familiarity changes the task measured by a text-classification test.}\label{fig:M05_mhealth_text}
\end{figure}

The lookup nearly matches the text classifier on the entry split because
most test descriptions already appear in training. Its collapse on
unseen descriptions reveals how much of that performance depends on
memory. A product could use the lookup for verified familiar terms and
route uncertain new terms for review. Nutrition-based food composition
matching would additionally require portion units, preparation details,
and validated food codes. A category prediction alone supplies none of
those quantities.

An AI assistant can help inspect ambiguous examples and propose a
labeling rubric. Use only permitted local processing, preserve the
original category, and evaluate proposed relabeling against
independently reviewed examples. The code below makes no external model
request and learns every lookup and text transformation from training
rows only.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/mHealth/recurring_examples/m05.py}{m05.py}.
From its directory, run \texttt{python\ m05.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Contrast familiar-description and unseen-description classification."""

import json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, f1_score
from common import SEED, description_holdout, load_food, save_result

food = load_food()
usable = food.loc[food.description.ne("") & food.category.ne("Unclassified")]
sample = usable.sample(n=min(200000, len(usable)), random_state=SEED).reset_index(
    drop=True
)
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
masks = {
    "entry_split": rng.random(len(sample)) < 0.2,
    "description_split": sample.description.map(description_holdout).to_numpy(),
}
results = {}
for name, mask in masks.items():
    train, test = sample.loc[~mask], sample.loc[mask]
    counts = train.groupby(["description", "category"]).size().reset_index(name="count")
    # Break tied category counts alphabetically; learn the lookup only on training rows.
    lookup = counts.sort_values(["count", "category"], ascending=[False, True])
    lookup = lookup.drop_duplicates("description").set_index("description").category
    majority = train.category.value_counts().sort_index().idxmax()
    baseline = test.description.map(lookup).fillna(majority)
    vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2), max_features=20000, min_df=2)
    vectorizer.fit(train.description.drop_duplicates())
    classifier = MultinomialNB(alpha=0.1)
    classifier.fit(
        vectorizer.transform(counts.description),
        counts.category,
        sample_weight=counts["count"],
    )
    prediction = classifier.predict(vectorizer.transform(test.description))
    labels = sorted(set(train.category) | set(test.category))
    results[name] = {
        "train_rows": len(train),
        "test_rows": len(test),
        "familiar_description_fraction": float(
            test.description.isin(lookup.index).mean()
        ),
        "lookup_accuracy": float(accuracy_score(test.category, baseline)),
        "nb_accuracy": float(accuracy_score(test.category, prediction)),
        "nb_macro_f1": float(
            f1_score(
                test.category,
                prediction,
                labels=labels,
                average="macro",
                zero_division=0,
            )
        ),
        "test_label_unseen_in_train_fraction": float(
            (~test.category.isin(train.category.unique())).mean()
        ),
        "metric_classes": len(labels),
    }
ambiguity = sample.groupby("description").category.nunique()
result = {
    "sample_rows": len(sample),
    "descriptions": len(ambiguity),
    "descriptions_with_multiple_labels": int(ambiguity.gt(1).sum()),
    "splits": results,
}
save_result("M05", result)
print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
\end{Verbatim}

import itertools

r["M05"] = {}

\hypertarget{M05-mhealth-text-topics-and-their-denominators}{%
\section{mHealth: Text Topics and Their
Denominators}\label{M05-mhealth-text-topics-and-their-denominators}}

\noindent A product manager wants to organize a large food-description vocabulary
into interpretable groups. Repeated entries make a frequently logged
description prominent, while a catalog of distinct descriptions
emphasizes the range of language available. These populations answer
different questions. A topic model fitted to distinct descriptions can
summarize vocabulary, but its topic shares need a separate choice of
observation unit.

Use all 50,860 distinct nonempty normalized descriptions recorded before
July 1. Fit TF-IDF on these descriptions, retaining at most 3,000
unigram and bigram features, removing English stop words, and requiring
a feature in at least three documents. The maximum document-frequency
threshold is 0.95. Fix the number of nonnegative matrix factorization
components at four as an illustrative specification. No July description
is used to learn the vocabulary, inverse-document frequencies, or
component vectors.

Let \(V\) contain nonnegative TF-IDF features, with one row per training
description. NMF approximates \(V\) by \(WH\), where the rows of \(H\)
contain term patterns and each row of \(W\) gives the associated
nonnegative loadings. The chosen specification minimizes squared
reconstruction error subject to nonnegative factors. Multiplying a row
of \(H\) by a constant and dividing its column of \(W\) by the same
constant preserves the approximation. Before comparing loadings, the
code therefore scales them to correspond to component term vectors with
unit Euclidean norm.

July contains 17,042 distinct nonempty descriptions and 79,957 entries,
including 5,208 descriptions absent from training. Apply the frozen
vectorizer and factorization to July descriptions. Assign each
description to its largest scaled loading when positive. A zero-vector
description remains unassigned. The resulting groups have the following
leading terms and shares.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}
\toprule
Leading Terms & Share of Distinct July Descriptions & Share of July
Entries \\
\midrule

Chicken, Breast, Soup & 14.83\% & 10.12\% \\
Cheese, Cheddar, Pizza & 32.52\% & 29.92\% \\
Chocolate, Bar, Dark & 32.22\% & 38.45\% \\
Salad, Dressing, Greek & 17.01\% & 19.15\% \\
Unassigned & 3.42\% & 2.36\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M05_topic_denominators.tex}
\caption{Weighting descriptions by their observed entry frequency changes the apparent prominence of the same fixed topics.}\label{fig:M05_topic_denominators}
\end{figure}

The chocolate-related component receives a larger share when repeated
entries determine the weights. This result concerns the language and
repetition of recorded entries. The component includes other terms and
does not define a validated food group, calorie share, or measure of
nutritional quality. Assigning a dominant component also discards
information about mixtures. The 583 unassigned descriptions expose a
vocabulary-coverage problem that would be hidden by forcing every text
into a topic.

\href{https://github.com/blueprints-for-text-analytics-python/blueprints-text/blob/master/ch08/Topic_Modeling_Clustering.ipynb}{Blueprints
for Text Analytics, Chapter 8} provides an NMF topic-model example.
\href{https://maartengr.github.io/BERTopic/getting_started/representation/representation.html}{BERTopic's
representation documentation} offers separate methods for describing
topics. An LLM-generated topic name should remain attached to the
component's terms and inspected examples. A fluent name supplies no
independent evidence that a component measures preference,
healthfulness, or a commercial segment.

A useful AI-assisted extension changes one choice at a time: the number
of topics, frequency weighting during fitting, or the vocabulary
threshold. Compare representative descriptions and unmatched texts as
well as reconstruction error. Improving the numerical objective alone
does not establish that a proposed topic label answers the manager's
question.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/mHealth/recurring_examples/topics.py}{topics.py}.
From its directory, run \texttt{python\ topics.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Local topic decomposition of food descriptions with a future-text check."""

import json
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import NMF
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from common import SEED, load_food, save_result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    food = load_food()
    prior = food.loc[(food.date < "2016-07-01") & food.description.ne("")]
    training_text = sorted(prior.description.unique())
    july = food.loc[
        food.date.between("2016-07-01", "2016-07-31") & food.description.ne("")
    ]
    counts = july.groupby("description").size().sort_index()
    vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(
        min_df=3,
        max_df=0.95,
        max_features=3000,
        ngram_range=(1, 2),
        stop_words="english",
    )
    train_matrix = vectorizer.fit_transform(training_text)
    model = NMF(
        n_components=4, init="nndsvda", random_state=SEED, max_iter=500, tol=1e-4
    )
    model.fit(train_matrix)
    future_matrix = vectorizer.transform(counts.index)
    # Put topic term vectors on a common L2 scale before comparing loadings.
    weights = model.transform(future_matrix) * np.linalg.norm(model.components_, axis=1)
    assigned = weights.sum(axis=1) > 1e-12
    labels = np.where(assigned, weights.argmax(axis=1), -1)
    terms = vectorizer.get_feature_names_out()
    rows = []
    for topic in range(4):
        selected = labels == topic
        top = np.argsort(-model.components_[topic], kind="stable")[:6]
        rows.append(
            {
                "topic": topic + 1,
                "terms": terms[top].tolist(),
                "distinct_description_share": float(selected.mean()),
                "food_entry_share": float(
                    counts.to_numpy()[selected].sum() / counts.sum()
                ),
            }
        )
    result = {
        "training_distinct_descriptions": len(training_text),
        "training_entries": len(prior),
        "vocabulary_terms": len(terms),
        "july_distinct_descriptions": len(counts),
        "july_entries": int(counts.sum()),
        "july_new_descriptions": int((~counts.index.isin(training_text)).sum()),
        "july_zero_vocabulary_descriptions": int(
            (future_matrix.getnnz(axis=1) == 0).sum()
        ),
        "july_unassigned_descriptions": int((~assigned).sum()),
        "july_unassigned_entries": int(counts.to_numpy()[~assigned].sum()),
        "iterations": int(model.n_iter_),
        "topics": rows,
    }
    assert model.n_iter_ < model.max_iter
    assert np.isclose(
        sum(row["food_entry_share"] for row in rows)
        + result["july_unassigned_entries"] / counts.sum(),
        1,
    )
    save_result("topics", result)
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M05-review-provenance-and-generated-language}{%
\section{Review Provenance and Generated
Language}\label{M05-review-provenance-and-generated-language}}

\noindent \noindent A retailer using reviews to describe a product needs to
preserve the distinction between an actual customer's experience and
generated wording. An LLM can summarize a collection of genuine reviews,
but its output can introduce an experience that no reviewer reported. A
sentiment classifier can also assign a confident label to a false or
irrelevant text. Model accuracy and the authenticity of the underlying
evidence address different questions.

Preserve the review identifier, source, date, any recorded incentive,
and the text actually analyzed. A summary should retain the relevant
review denominator and material disagreement. A generated quotation
attributed to a customer requires that customer's actual words and
appropriate permission. A synthetic example used to test a parser should
remain labeled synthetic and separate from reviews offered to potential
buyers.

The FTC's Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule addresses specified
conduct involving false reviews and testimonials. Its provisions
distinguish creation, purchase, dissemination, and mere hosting, with
different knowledge conditions. AI generation alone does not determine
whether a testimonial misrepresents experience. The relevant questions
concern the speaker, actual experience, claim, and business conduct. See
the
\href{https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/consumer-reviews-testimonials-rule-questions-answers}{FTC's
questions and answers}.

A useful assessment samples the original texts behind a generated theme,
checks whether each factual claim is supported, and records unsupported
statements separately from ordinary classification errors. The
rare-complaint example in Section 5.5 supplies another check: a high
false-positive share can make a generated summary overstate the
prevalence of a problem even when individual labels have respectable
sensitivity and specificity.

\hypertarget{M05-earnings-calls-pricing-language-speaking-exposure-and-meaning}{%
\section{Earnings Calls: Pricing Language, Speaking Exposure, and
Meaning}\label{M05-earnings-calls-pricing-language-speaking-exposure-and-meaning}}

\noindent \noindent A communications team can use public earnings calls to
identify pricing statements that require contextual reading. The
decision is which statements to examine and what additional evidence to
request. The supplied core dictionary includes dynamic, personalized,
algorithmic, and AI pricing as well as electronic shelf labels. These
terms retrieve heterogeneous business objects. A display technology, a
planned test, and an implemented price rule have different implications
for customers.

\hypertarget{M05-a-call-level-comparison}{%
\subsection{A Call-Level Comparison}\label{M05-a-call-level-comparison}}

\noindent \noindent Among calls with observed text, the supplied retail group has
36 core-positive calls out of 1,241, or 2.90\%; restaurants have 9 of
445, or 2.02\%; and the comparison group has 67 of 639, or 10.49\%.
Calls receive equal weight. Firms with more captured calls consequently
receive more weight in a pooled group rate. The categories differ in
their business models, communication practices, and sample coverage. A
higher rate identifies more frequent use of the specified language
within the observed corpus.

Calendar-quarter summaries use the date on which the call occurred.
Fiscal-quarter labels can refer to different calendar periods across
firms. The first and last quarters have incomplete calendar windows, and
the number of firms varies across quarters. Reporting the call and firm
counts beside each share makes those differences visible. Complete
calendar support does not establish complete capture of every firm's
calls.

\hypertarget{M05-who-speaks-more-about-pricing}{%
\subsection{Who Speaks More About
Pricing?}\label{M05-who-speaks-more-about-pricing}}

\noindent \noindent Management supplies 127 of the 150 core occurrences and
analysts supply 23. Management also speaks far more words. To measure
language intensity for role \(r\) on the same set of observed calls,
calculate

\[
I_r=10{,}000\frac{\sum_{c\in\mathcal C}M_{cr}}{\sum_{c\in\mathcal C}W_{cr}},
\]

where \(M_{cr}\) is the core-occurrence count and \(W_{cr}\) is the
number of words attributed to role \(r\) in call \(c\). The multiplier
expresses occurrences per 10,000 words. The ratio pools word exposure,
so long speaking segments receive greater weight than short ones.

Management's 16,685,338 words imply 0.076 occurrences per 10,000 words.
Analysts' 2,761,999 words imply 0.083. The raw-count ranking reverses
after exposure adjustment. This arithmetic does not establish that
analysts are more concerned about pricing: management includes prepared
remarks and answers, analysts principally ask questions, and role
assignments are heuristic. The rates describe the supplied labels and
text exposure without a population significance claim.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M05_calls_exposure.tex}
\caption{Management has 127 core occurrences and analysts have 23. After dividing by the words attributed to each role, the respective rates are 0.076 and 0.083 per 10,000 words. The two panels use different labeled units and preserve a zero baseline.}\label{fig:M05_calls_exposure}
\end{figure}

The Q\&A detector fails to identify a boundary for 86 supplied calls,
including the empty transcript. Restricting both counts and words to the
2,240 observed calls with detected Q\&A yields 115 management
occurrences in 15,985,597 words, or 0.072 per 10,000. The analyst rate
remains 0.083. This sensitivity addresses the flagged boundaries while
retaining the substantive difference between prepared remarks and
questions. A stronger role comparison would require verified turn labels
and comparable speaking contexts.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Earnings_Calls/disclosure.py}{disclosure.py}.

\texttt{python\ disclosure.py}. Python, pandas, and NumPy are required;
the committed metadata supply all inputs.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Compare pricing-language coverage with explicit call and word denominators."""
import pandas as pd
from assessment import HERE, load_checked


def role_rates(calls, mentions, require_qa=False):
    sample = calls.loc[calls.text_observed & (calls.qa_detected | (not require_qa))]
    core = mentions.loc[mentions.tier.eq('core') & mentions.call_id.isin(sample.call_id)]
    rows = []
    for role in ['management', 'analyst']:
        n = int(core.role.eq(role).sum())
        words = int(sample['words_' + role].sum())
        rows.append({'sample': 'detected_qa' if require_qa else 'all_observed',
                     'role': role, 'calls': len(sample), 'core_matches': n,
                     'words': words, 'per_10000_words': 10000 * n / words if words else float('nan')})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


def main():
    calls, mentions, _, _ = load_checked()
    valid = calls.loc[calls.text_observed].copy()
    groups = valid.groupby('group').agg(
        calls=('call_id', 'size'), positive_calls=('has_core', 'sum'),
        core_matches=('n_core', 'sum'))
    groups['share_percent'] = 100 * groups.positive_calls / groups.calls
    groups.to_csv(HERE / 'results/group_rates.csv')
    roles = pd.concat([role_rates(calls, mentions), role_rates(calls, mentions, True)])
    roles.to_csv(HERE / 'results/role_rates.csv', index=False)
    valid['calendar_quarter'] = valid.call_date.dt.to_period('Q')
    quarter = valid.groupby('calendar_quarter').agg(
        calls=('call_id', 'size'), positive_calls=('has_core', 'sum'),
        firms=('ticker', 'nunique'))
    quarter['share_percent'] = 100 * quarter.positive_calls / quarter.calls
    # Calendar coverage does not imply complete capture of all firms' calls.
    start, end = pd.Timestamp('2021-11-02'), pd.Timestamp('2026-11-02')
    quarter['full_calendar_window'] = [
        q.start_time >= start and q.end_time.normalize() <= end for q in quarter.index]
    quarter.to_csv(HERE / 'results/quarter_rates.csv')
    print(groups.round(4).to_string())
    print(roles.round(6).to_string(index=False))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    (HERE / 'results').mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M05-a-match-is-a-retrieval-decision}{%
\subsection{A Match Is a Retrieval
Decision}\label{M05-a-match-is-a-retrieval-decision}}

\noindent \noindent Consider seven purposeful cases from the supplied excerpts.
Amazon's October 2024 statement concerns displaying current prices and
deals. Eventbrite's August 2023 statement concerns advertising cost per
click. Wendy's February 2024 statement concerns future tests. Kroger's
September 2025 statement concerns shelf-label infrastructure, while its
September 2022 statement describes personalized promotional investment.
Delta's July 2025 statement describes AI-enhanced pricing; a January
2025 question about cabin pricing is recorded as management prepared
remarks and warrants speaker review. Each case has an original match ID
and source URL in
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Earnings_Calls/data/interpretation_cases.csv}{the
interpretation table}.

A coding scheme should identify the priced object, current use versus
future intention, assertion versus question or denial, and the scope of
supporting evidence. The seven examples expose distinctions; their
purposeful selection supplies no estimate of corpus precision. The
original notes' reported precision check lacks the underlying
adjudicated labels needed for independent verification. Recall
additionally requires examining relevant passages that were never
retrieved. Re-running a regex on truncated stored excerpts cannot
measure whole-call recall.

The synthetic contrast set below holds a pricing phrase nearly fixed
while changing its meaning. Denial, intention, and a question all
retrieve the same core term. A sentence describing fares that change
hourly with demand supplies a plausible paraphrase that the dictionary
misses. These are specified counterexamples to an interpretation rule,
with no empirical model-performance claim.

\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Earnings_Calls/construct_checks.py}{construct\_checks.py}.
From \texttt{03\_Data\_and\_Code/Earnings\_Calls}, run
