category \(c\), and \(p_c\) is global popularity used for tie
resolution. The bonus is measured in the same score units as frequency.
It is an imposed objective weight, not an estimated willingness to try a
food or a nutritional benefit. Rank all candidates by this score and
count the fraction of the ten recommendations absent from recent
history.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrr@{}}
\toprule
Novelty Bonus & Recall at 10 & NDCG at 10 & Novel Categories in the
List \\
\midrule

0.00 & 0.4759 & 0.5862 & 4.78\% \\
0.05 & 0.4759 & 0.5862 & 4.82\% \\
0.10 & 0.4759 & 0.5863 & 5.28\% \\
0.20 & 0.4661 & 0.5809 & 9.83\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The grid is a specified sensitivity comparison on the same 299 test
users. It is not used to select a winning policy and then claim an
independent test of that winner. At a bonus of 0.20, novelty roughly
doubles while recall falls by about 0.98 percentage points. At smaller
bonuses, changes in the list can occur among categories that are all
absent from the target, leaving recall unchanged. NDCG can move without
a recall change when relevant categories exchange positions.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M08_mhealth_tradeoff.tex}
\caption{A novelty bonus changes list composition before it substantially changes basket recovery.}\label{fig:M08_mhealth_tradeoff}
\end{figure}

The first three points lie close together in recall even though novelty
rises. The fourth trades some recovery of the recorded basket for
greater novelty. This is an offline relationship between a ranking rule
and historical labels. It does not measure whether customers prefer the
new list, accept the suggestions, or change diet.

A nutrition objective would need a validated nutrient database,
appropriate portions, restrictions supplied by the customer, and an
outcome definition. Source categories and calorie-share variety alone do
not establish healthy choices. The data-cleaning distinctions in M2
therefore affect what the manager can optimize. Dropping low-calorie
days might improve an apparent fit by selecting more complete logs,
while also excluding the customers for whom the interface is hardest to
use.

A concrete next decision is whether to run the M6 user-randomized
comparison, using a prespecified novelty setting and separate measures
of logging, acceptance, and any validated nutrition outcome. The
experiment should preserve the assignment population and record
exposure. An AI assistant can implement the frozen ranking rule and
assess category descriptions, while unsupported health claims remain
outside the factual explanation supplied with the recommendation.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/mHealth/recurring_examples/m08.py}{m08.py}.
From its directory, run \texttt{python\ m08.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Measure an imposed novelty-relevance tradeoff on the same September baskets."""

import json
from common import OUTPUT, load_inputs, save_result
from ranking import candidate_categories, evaluate

food, daily, baskets = load_inputs()
selection = json.loads((OUTPUT / "M07.json").read_text())
windows = {"30_days": 30, "90_days": 90, "all_prior_days": None}
window = windows[selection["chosen_window"]]
candidates = candidate_categories(baskets)
# This grid is a specified sensitivity analysis, not a test-set model search.
weights = [0.0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20]
tradeoff = [
    {
        "novelty_weight": weight,
        **evaluate(baskets, "2016-09-01", candidates, window, novelty_weight=weight),
    }
    for weight in weights
]
assert (
    abs(
        tradeoff[0]["recall_at_10"]
        - selection["test"]["personal_frequency"]["recall_at_10"]
    )
    < 1e-12
)
result = {"history_window": selection["chosen_window"], "tradeoff": tradeoff}
save_result("M08", result)
print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M08-python-calculations-for-the-synthetic-cases}{%
\section{Python Calculations for the Synthetic
Cases}\label{M08-python-calculations-for-the-synthetic-cases}}

\noindent The inputs below are imposed teaching values. Running the program
creates the labeled synthetic CSV files and prints the corresponding
calculations. They are separate from the mHealth estimates. Keep the
script beside \texttt{example\_helpers.py} in
\texttt{03\_Data\_and\_Code/Lecture\_Examples}.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Lecture_Examples/m08_synthetic.py}{m08\_synthetic.py}.
From its directory, run \texttt{python\ m08\_synthetic.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Synthetic numerical examples for M8; run from any working directory."""

import itertools
import json
import math
from example_helpers import write_csv, ols_slope, shares

r = {}
items = {
    "A": ("Coffee", 0.90),
    "B": ("Coffee", 0.85),
    "C": ("Tea", 0.75),
    "D": ("Fruit", 0.65),
}
list_values = {}
for weight in [0, 0.2, 0.3]:
    list_values[str(weight)] = {
        "".join(choice): sum(items[j][1] for j in choice)
        + weight * len({items[j][0] for j in choice})
        for choice in itertools.combinations(items, 3)
    }
ra = lambda s: 100 * (-math.expm1(-s / 20))
rb = lambda s: 80 * (-math.expm1(-s / 40))
sa = (40 * math.log(2.5) + 60) / 3
sb = 60 - sa
r["M08"] = {
    "recommendation_objectives": list_values,
    "carryover": [100 * 0.5**t for t in range(4)],
    "average_A": ra(40) / 40,
    "average_B": rb(20) / 20,
    "marginal_A": 5 * math.exp(-40 / 20),
    "marginal_B": 2 * math.exp(-20 / 40),
    "current_total_contribution": ra(40) + rb(20),
    "optimal_spend_A": sa,
    "optimal_spend_B": sb,
    "optimal_total_contribution": ra(sa) + rb(sb),
    "contribution_gain": ra(sa) + rb(sb) - ra(40) - rb(20),
    "one_unit_transfer_gain": ra(39) + rb(21) - ra(40) - rb(20),
    "manual_total_minutes": 110,
    "assisted_total_minutes": 85,
    "time_reduction_fraction": 25 / 110,
}
assert math.isclose(5 * math.exp(-sa / 20), 2 * math.exp(-sb / 40))
# Independent grid check of the constrained optimum, to the grid's precision.
grid_best = max((ra(i / 100) + rb(60 - i / 100), i / 100) for i in range(6001))
assert abs(grid_best[1] - sa) < 0.01
write_csv(
    "M08_recommendation_synthetic.csv",
    ["item", "category", "relevance_score"],
    [(key, *value) for key, value in items.items()],
)
print(json.dumps(r, indent=2))
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M08-evidence-checks-for-generated-marketing-explanations}{%
\section{Evidence Checks for Generated Marketing
Explanations}\label{M08-evidence-checks-for-generated-marketing-explanations}}

\noindent An analytics manager may accept a fluent business review whose numbers
and interpretation describe different populations. Structured output
helps software locate a metric, period, value, unit, and denominator.
Each field also needs evidence. A correctly formatted statement can
contain the wrong number or describe a causal effect that the underlying
analysis never estimated.

Use the fixed-cohort mHealth review from Section 1.10 as the evidence
source. June contains 6,331 observed user-days out of 10,200 eligible
calendar user-days, giving a logging fraction of 0.620686. A structured
claim must identify that month, denominator, unit, and descriptive
interpretation. Four constructed candidates retain the same field
structure: one reproduces the supported result, one adds 0.10 to its
value, one substitutes the number of logging users for the denominator,
and one labels the result a causal health benefit.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
Constructed Candidate & Format & Evidence Check \\
\midrule

Supported Result & Valid Fields & Accepted \\
Changed Number & Valid Fields & Value Mismatch \\
Changed Denominator & Valid Fields & Denominator Mismatch \\
Causal Health Claim & Valid Fields & Unsupported Interpretation \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

All four candidates pass the same basic structural requirement. Only the
supported claim passes the evidence checks. They are deliberate teaching
inputs, not observed outputs from a particular LLM. The code makes no
external model request and sends no customer data to an AI service. Its
checks concern the declared fields. Free-form prose, omitted
qualifications, and advice require a separate substantive review; an
``interpretation'' field cannot validate an unrestricted paragraph.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M08_evidence_checks.tex}
\caption{A generated statement passes through separate checks for structure, numerical evidence, and substantive interpretation before informing a decision.}\label{fig:M08_evidence_checks}
\end{figure}

\href{https://github.com/google-marketing-solutions/copycat}{Copycat}
demonstrates generation of advertising text from brand examples and
evaluates similarity and memorization. Those diagnostics concern the
generated content. Incremental sales or engagement requires an outcome
comparison under an appropriate exposure design, such as a randomized
test of the generated and existing alternatives. The Gemini and Google
Cloud marketing notebooks in the resource collection supply further
examples of generation and structured extraction; model credentials,
costs, and data permissions are separate requirements for executing
those reference notebooks.

Synthetic consumer panels raise a related distinction. The
\href{https://github.com/pymc-labs/semantic-similarity-rating}{semantic-similarity-rating
package} maps generated text to distributions over response anchors. The
mapping can standardize how generated answers are summarized. Validation
against a target population still requires human outcomes, a sampling
definition, and comparisons held out from prompt or anchor selection.
Generating more answers under the same misspecified prompt reduces
simulation noise around that prompt's distribution while preserving its
systematic difference from consumers. Agreement among generated
respondents is therefore a property to examine alongside external
validity.

A useful AI coding request is: ``Compare every numerical field with its
computed evidence; reject unknown metrics, periods, units, and
denominators; retain the analysis's descriptive interpretation; and test
a correctly formatted false claim.'' The checking rule should be written
before inspecting a favored generated answer. Report the factual error
rate and the time spent checking, alongside any reduction in drafting
time.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/mHealth/recurring_examples/claim_checks.py}{claim\_checks.py}.
From its directory, run \texttt{python\ claim\_checks.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Check constructed structured claims against computed mHealth evidence."""

import json
import math
from copy import deepcopy
from common import load_food, save_result
from reporting import monthly_review


def check_claim(claim, evidence):
    required = {"metric", "period", "value", "unit", "denominator", "interpretation"}
    if not isinstance(claim, dict) or set(claim) != required:
        return ["schema"]
    rows = [row for row in evidence["periods"] if row["period"] == claim["period"]]
    if len(rows) != 1 or claim["metric"] != evidence["metric"]:
        return ["unknown metric or period"]
    row = rows[0]
    errors = []
    if type(claim["value"]) not in (int, float) or not math.isfinite(claim["value"]):
        errors.append("numeric value")
    elif not math.isclose(
        claim["value"], row["logging_fraction"], rel_tol=0, abs_tol=1e-10
    ):
        errors.append("value disagrees with evidence")
    if (
        type(claim["denominator"]) is not int
        or claim["denominator"] != row["calendar_user_days"]
    ):
        errors.append("denominator")
    if claim["unit"] != evidence["unit"]:
        errors.append("unit")
    if claim["interpretation"] != evidence["interpretation"]:
        errors.append("unsupported interpretation")
    return errors


if __name__ == "__main__":
    evidence = monthly_review(load_food())
    june = evidence["periods"][1]
    valid = {
        "metric": "logging_fraction",
        "period": "2016-06",
        "value": june["logging_fraction"],
        "unit": evidence["unit"],
        "denominator": june["calendar_user_days"],
        "interpretation": "descriptive",
    }
    candidates = {"supported": valid}
    changes = {
        "wrong_number": ("value", valid["value"] + 0.1),
        "wrong_denominator": ("denominator", june["users_with_logs"]),
        "causal_claim": ("interpretation", "causal health benefit"),
    }
    for name, (field, value) in changes.items():
        candidates[name] = deepcopy(valid)
        candidates[name][field] = value
    result = {
        "candidate_origin": "constructed teaching examples; no LLM request",
        "checks": {
            name: check_claim(claim, evidence) for name, claim in candidates.items()
        },
    }
    assert result["checks"]["supported"] == []
    assert all(result["checks"][name] for name in changes)
    save_result("claim_checks", result)
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M08-an-executable-chart-can-still-misstate-the-evidence}{%
\section{An Executable Chart Can Still Misstate the
Evidence}\label{M08-an-executable-chart-can-still-misstate-the-evidence}}

\noindent A manager asks an AI assistant to plot monthly customer engagement. The
generated program can run successfully and produce an attractive chart
while changing the population, labeling a fraction as a percentage, or
describing a temporal association as an intervention effect. A chart
therefore needs checks of execution, fidelity to the analytical
question, and readability.
\href{https://github.com/microsoft/VisEval}{VisEval} separates these
dimensions when evaluating generated visualizations.

The mHealth example provides an independent numerical reference. The
requested measure is the percentage of all eligible calendar user-days
with a log. Its two numerators and denominators are computed before
plotting. The following constructed mistakes retain valid numerical
inputs and executable drawing instructions. Each fails a different
substantive requirement.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.33}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.33}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.34}}@{}}
\toprule
Constructed Chart Error & Consequence & Check \\
\midrule

Plot a fraction under a percent label & Values are 100 times too small &
Recompute units \\
Keep only users who logged & Population changes with the outcome &
Reconcile denominators \\
Start rate bars at 60\% & Bar lengths distort magnitudes & Inspect
baseline \\
Declare the time difference causal & Claim exceeds the design & Inspect
interpretation \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The checker below accepts the correct specification and rejects all four
constructed mistakes. Its numerator and denominator checks use the saved
monthly evidence, rather than the plotted value as its own reference.
This is a narrow validator for declared fields. It does not interpret
unrestricted natural-language titles, inspect pixels, or guarantee that
a rendered chart is readable. Review the displayed title, labels,
clipping, color contrast, and all interactive selections separately. A
chart can pass these field checks while still misleading through an
omitted subgroup or an unsupported narrative.

Ask a coding assistant to return the aggregate plotting table, units,
eligibility rule, axis domains, and one hand-calculated plotted value
with its code. A second review should compare those objects with the
original analysis specification. Passing the assistant's own test is
informative only when the expected answer was derived independently. The
\href{https://github.com/Financial-Times/chart-doctor/blob/main/visual-vocabulary/README.md}{Financial
Times vocabulary} supports the choice of display, while
\href{https://github.com/rougier/scientific-visualization-book}{Rougier's
visualization code} provides examples of figure construction and layout.
The managerial claim must remain tied to the evidence and design.

Run \texttt{visualization.py} first to create the evidence table, then
run the assessment. The false charts are constructed teaching cases;
their rejection rates do not measure the reliability of any particular
language model.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/mHealth/recurring_examples/chart_assessment.py}{chart\_assessment.py}.
From its directory, run \texttt{python\ chart\_assessment.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Check a narrow chart specification against the monthly evidence table."""

from copy import deepcopy
import json
import math
from common import OUTPUT, save_result


def check_chart(chart, evidence):
    errors = []
    expected = {row["period"]: row for row in evidence["months"]}
    if chart.get("unit") != "percent of eligible user-days":
        errors.append("axis unit")
    if chart.get("interpretation") != "descriptive":
        errors.append("interpretation")
    if chart.get("mark") == "bar" and chart.get("y_domain", [None])[0] != 0:
        errors.append("bar baseline")
    rows = chart.get("rows", [])
    if sorted(row["period"] for row in rows) != sorted(expected):
        errors.append("period coverage")
    for row in rows:
        ref = expected.get(row["period"])
        if ref is None:
            continue
        value = row["value"]
        target = 100 * ref["observed_user_days"] / ref["calendar_user_days"]
        if not math.isfinite(value) or not math.isclose(value, target, abs_tol=1e-8):
            errors.append("plotted value")
        if row["denominator"] != ref["calendar_user_days"]:
            errors.append("denominator")
    return sorted(set(errors))


def main():
    evidence = json.loads((OUTPUT / "visualization.json").read_text())
    correct = {
        "unit": "percent of eligible user-days", "interpretation": "descriptive",
        "mark": "bar", "y_domain": [0, 100],
        "rows": [{"period": r["period"], "value": r["logging_percent"],
                  "denominator": r["calendar_user_days"]} for r in evidence["months"]],
    }
    cases = {"correct": correct}
    for name in ["fraction_as_percent", "conditional_denominator", "truncated_bar", "causal_title"]:
        cases[name] = deepcopy(correct)
    cases["fraction_as_percent"]["rows"][0]["value"] /= 100
    row = cases["conditional_denominator"]["rows"][0]
    row["denominator"] = evidence["months"][0]["logger_calendar_days"]
    row["value"] = evidence["months"][0]["conditional_logging_percent"]
    cases["truncated_bar"]["y_domain"] = [60, 75]
    cases["causal_title"]["interpretation"] = "causal"
    result = {name: check_chart(chart, evidence) for name, chart in cases.items()}
    assert result["correct"] == []
    assert all(result[name] for name in cases if name != "correct")
    save_result("chart_assessment", {"constructed_cases": result})
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M08-competition-demand-measurement-and-generative-ai}{%
\section{Competition, Demand Measurement, and Generative
AI}\label{M08-competition-demand-measurement-and-generative-ai}}

\noindent A provider deciding whether to cut its subscription price needs to
anticipate where customers come from and how long they remain. New
subscribers can expand the paid category, replace a competing provider,
or add a second service. These responses have different implications for
market size and competitive pressure. Posted prices and public attention
help describe the available offers and interest in them, while demand
analysis requires choices linked to the prices and alternatives
available when those choices occurred.

\href{https://www.nber.org/papers/w35953}{Egan, Russel, Shi, and Yao
(2026)} study paid consumer subscriptions using card transactions. Their
abstract reports 2.9\% paid adoption by April 2026, substantial
turnover, and growing substitutability among providers.
\href{https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15440}{Fradkin (2025)} studies
applications using models through OpenRouter and documents variation in
whether releases expand usage or displace other models. The population
and choice object differ: consumer subscriptions, application-level
model use, and token demand answer different managerial questions. A
descriptive retention gap alone does not identify a structural
substitution parameter.

\hypertarget{M08-a-price-coefficient-with-a-known-interpretation}{%
\subsection{A Price Coefficient With a Known
Interpretation}\label{M08-a-price-coefficient-with-a-known-interpretation}}

\noindent To connect a subscription probability to price, consider an imposed
binary-choice benchmark. A homogeneous consumer chooses whether to hold
one provider in a month. Let \(p_{jt}\) be its price in dollars per
month, \(\delta_j\) its provider intercept, and \(\tau_t\) a common
month effect. A logistic utility difference with price coefficient
\(-\alpha\) implies

\[
s_{jt}=\frac{\exp(\delta_j+\tau_t-\alpha p_{jt})}
{1+\exp(\delta_j+\tau_t-\alpha p_{jt})},
\qquad
\log\!\left(\frac{s_{jt}}{1-s_{jt}}\right)
=\delta_j+\tau_t-\alpha p_{jt}.
\]

The share \(s_{jt}\) is the choice probability for this binary offer.
The coefficient \(\alpha\) measures the reduction in log odds per
additional dollar. Homogeneous tastes, the binary choice structure, and
the absence of lagged subscription states make the inversion exact. With
exact model-implied shares and price variation remaining after provider
and month controls, the regression recovers the imposed coefficient.
With sampled choices, finite-sample uncertainty must also be assessed.

Holding the intercepts fixed, the benchmark's own-price elasticity is
\(-\alpha p_{jt}(1-s_{jt})\). That calculation describes a response
within the specified binary model. Cross-provider substitution requires
an explicit joint choice model and variation that supports its
parameters. Consumers holding several subscriptions need a choice
structure that permits those combinations; a single-choice nested logit
would change that behavior.

\hypertarget{M08-why-subscriber-stocks-and-new-subscriptions-differ}{%
\subsection{Why Subscriber Stocks and New Subscriptions
Differ}\label{M08-why-subscriber-stocks-and-new-subscriptions-differ}}

\noindent The supplied simulator draws heterogeneous consumer affinity and monthly
logistic shocks, adds provider quality and inertia from last month's
holdings, and selects a set of subscriptions subject to a cost of
additional providers. Premium status is assigned after the
provider-holding decision. A common utility shift is recalibrated each
month to approach the target adoption path. These rules produce a useful
dynamic teaching panel, but they differ from the homogeneous binary
benchmark.

Construct one row for every available provider-month using the price
table, including combinations with zero subscribers. Divide the number
of basic-plan holders by the full roster to form a stock share. Divide
new basic-plan holders by that same roster to form a flow share. The
current data contain 179 available provider-months; all have positive
stock and flow shares, so the two regressions use the same observations.
Each regression includes provider and month effects.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.30}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.40}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.30}}@{}}
\toprule
Share Used in the Regression & Price Coefficient per Dollar &
Interpretation \\
\midrule

Basic-plan stock divided by the consumer roster & -0.0300 & Descriptive
log-odds projection of current holdings \\
New basic-plan holders divided by the consumer roster & -0.0499 &
Descriptive log-odds projection of acquisition flow \\
Exact homogeneous binary-model probability & -0.0600 & Recovery of the
imposed coefficient under the benchmark \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The simulator also imposes a utility price coefficient of \(-0.0600\).
The flow slope is numerically closer to it in this realization. That
proximity does not establish recovery: average choices across
heterogeneous consumers generally do not obey the
representative-consumer logit formula, and changing the outcome from
holdings to acquisitions leaves selection, inertia, competing offers,
and premium assignment in the data-generating process. The common
utility recalibration also fixes aggregate adoption near its target as
prices and qualities vary. A promotion counterfactual must specify which
of those objects remains fixed.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M08_genai_price.tex}
\caption{Three price coefficients calculated on the same 179 provider-month price observations. The dynamic simulation gives a stock slope of -0.0300 and a flow slope of -0.0499; exact binary-logit probabilities recover -0.0600. The dots are point calculations without confidence intervals and do not measure real-market price sensitivity.}\label{fig:M08_genai_price}
\end{figure}

An acquisition flow divided by all consumers also differs from an
acquisition probability among eligible nonsubscribers. For a
provider-level holding indicator \(D_{ijt}\), its acquisition hazard
conditions on \(D_{ij,t-1}=0\). A new-holder count divided by \(N\)
combines that hazard with the proportion eligible to acquire the
provider. Changes in the eligible population can therefore change the
flow share even when its conditional response is stable. Plan-level
flows require an additional definition of upgrades, downgrades, and new
provider relationships.

\hypertarget{M08-evaluating-an-ai-generated-demand-analysis}{%
\subsection{Evaluating an AI-Generated Demand
Analysis}\label{M08-evaluating-an-ai-generated-demand-analysis}}

\noindent A useful coding specification states the consumer roster, available
alternatives, monthly price units, subscription-history definition, and
target coefficient before requesting a model. Require the code to retain
zero-count provider-months, check whether prices vary after the fixed
effects, and reject undefined log odds. A pseudocount changes the
transformed outcome and should follow an explicit statistical model
rather than conceal zero shares.

For a simulation, compare the estimator with the generator line by line.
The price appearing in a utility equation, the recorded price of a
chosen premium plan, and the average amount paid are different objects.
Verify whether the program holds category attractiveness fixed or
recalibrates it when prices change. Then test the estimator on exact
probabilities from a model for which its equation is correct. The
benchmark below passes that test; the dynamic-panel regressions retain
their descriptive interpretation.

The regression uses NumPy least squares and checks the price slope
independently by removing provider and month effects from both price and
the transformed share. Agreement verifies the linear calculation.
Identification of a price response additionally requires justified price
variation, a suitable choice model, and uncertainty that respects the
level at which prices and shocks vary. The 60,000 simulated consumers do
not create 60,000 independent price assignments.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/GenAI_Demand/demand.py}{demand.py}. From the
script's folder, run \texttt{python3\ demand.py}. Inputs are read from
the supplied local bundle; output tables are written beside the course
scripts.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Contrast descriptive price regressions with an exact binary-logit benchmark."""
from pathlib import Path
import json

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
SOURCE = HERE.parents[1] / "01_Resources/08_M8_Current_Topics_in_Marketing/genai_demand_lab/data"
OUTPUT = HERE / "results"


def design(frame):
    # All provider intercepts plus all but one month effect; no extra intercept.
    fixed = pd.concat([pd.get_dummies(frame.provider, dtype=float),
                       pd.get_dummies(frame.month, drop_first=True, dtype=float)], axis=1)
    x = np.column_stack([fixed.to_numpy(), frame.basic_price.to_numpy()])
    if np.linalg.matrix_rank(x) != x.shape[1]:
        raise ValueError("Price is not separately identified from the fixed effects")
    return x


def price_projection(frame, shares):
    shares = np.asarray(shares, dtype=float)
    if not np.isfinite(shares).all() or not ((shares > 0) & (shares < 1)).all():
        raise ValueError("Log-odds require shares strictly between zero and one")
    x = design(frame)
    y = np.log(shares) - np.log1p(-shares)
    beta = np.linalg.lstsq(x, y, rcond=None)[0]
    # Independent Frisch-Waugh-Lovell check of the price coefficient.
    controls, price = x[:, :-1], x[:, -1]
    price_residual = price - controls @ np.linalg.lstsq(controls, price, rcond=None)[0]
    y_residual = y - controls @ np.linalg.lstsq(controls, y, rcond=None)[0]
    fwl = float(price_residual @ y_residual / (price_residual @ price_residual))
    np.testing.assert_allclose(beta[-1], fwl, atol=1e-10)
    return {"price_coefficient": float(beta[-1]), "rows": len(frame),
            "residual_price_sum_squares": float(price_residual @ price_residual)}


def main():
    subs = pd.read_csv(SOURCE / "synthetic_subscriptions.csv.gz")
    consumers = pd.read_csv(SOURCE / "synthetic_consumers.csv")
    prices = pd.read_csv(SOURCE / "synthetic_basic_prices.csv")
    dgp = json.loads((SOURCE / "synthetic_dgp.json").read_text())
    keys = ["month", "provider"]
    assert consumers.consumer_id.is_unique and not prices.duplicated(keys).any()
    assert not subs.duplicated(["consumer_id"] + keys).any()
    basic = subs.loc[subs.tier.eq("basic")]
    stocks = basic.groupby(keys).size().rename("basic_holders")
    flows = basic.loc[basic["new"]].groupby(keys).size().rename("new_basic_holders")
    frame = prices.merge(stocks, on=keys, how="left", validate="one_to_one")
    frame = frame.merge(flows, on=keys, how="left", validate="one_to_one")
    frame[["basic_holders", "new_basic_holders"]] = frame[["basic_holders", "new_basic_holders"]].fillna(0)
    # Zero filling is justified by the complete simulated population and price support.
    frame["stock_share"] = frame.basic_holders / len(consumers)
    frame["flow_share"] = frame.new_basic_holders / len(consumers)
    common = frame.loc[frame.stock_share.between(0, 1, inclusive="neither") &
                       frame.flow_share.between(0, 1, inclusive="neither")].copy()
    results = []
    for name in ["stock_share", "flow_share"]:
        results.append({"outcome": name, **price_projection(common, common[name])})
    # Exact model-implied shares: homogeneous binary choice, no inertia or multihoming.
    # Provider/time intercepts vary, but the same price design and alpha are retained.
    x = design(common)
    intercepts = np.linspace(-4.0, -3.0, common.provider.nunique())
    time_effects = np.linspace(0.0, 0.2, common.month.nunique() - 1)
    controls = np.r_[intercepts, time_effects]
    alpha = dgp["alpha_price"]
    utility = x[:, :-1] @ controls - alpha * common.basic_price.to_numpy()
    benchmark_share = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-utility))
    benchmark = price_projection(common, benchmark_share)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(benchmark["price_coefficient"], -alpha, atol=1e-10)
    results.append({"outcome": "exact_binary_logit", **benchmark})
    result = {"data_type": "synthetic", "available_provider_months": len(frame),
              "common_positive_share_rows": len(common), "excluded_zero_share_rows": len(frame) - len(common),
              "imposed_utility_price_coefficient": -alpha, "projections": results,
              "interpretation": "Stock and flow slopes are descriptive projections of a heterogeneous dynamic simulation; only the exact binary benchmark recovers its imposed coefficient by construction"}
    OUTPUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    frame.to_csv(OUTPUT / "provider_months.csv", index=False, float_format="%.10f")
    pd.DataFrame(results).to_csv(OUTPUT / "price_projections.csv", index=False, float_format="%.10f")
    (OUTPUT / "demand.json").write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M08-retention-procedures-profit-and-customer-value}{%
\section{Retention Procedures, Profit, and Customer
Value}\label{M08-retention-procedures-profit-and-customer-value}}

\noindent \noindent A subscription firm wants to increase renewals. It can improve
the underlying service or alter the interaction that precedes the same
renewal decision. Questions, default options, and retention prompts can
change the probability that a customer continues. These procedures leave
the final button press with the customer while changing the conditions
under which that choice is made. Evaluating their consequences requires
a measure of customer value in addition to the renewal rate.

\hypertarget{M08-a-fixed-offer-and-opposed-stakes}{%
\subsection{A Fixed Offer and Opposed
Stakes}\label{M08-a-fixed-offer-and-opposed-stakes}}

\noindent \noindent Consider an eligible customer facing the same final offer
under several procedures. A procedure can include an introductory
question or an optional retention interaction. Let \(s_k\) denote the
probability of renewal under procedure \(k\), and let \(s_0\) denote
renewal under direct choice. The probabilities refer to the same
population and outcome horizon.

\begin{assumption}[Fixed Offer and Opposed Stakes]
\label{ass:retention-stakes}
The available procedures form a finite set $K$. Each procedure has a stable renewal probability $s_k$. Renewal yields firm margin $\nu>0$ dollars and customer value $-\sigma<0$ dollars relative to declining. These stakes are common across procedures and customers in the represented population. The offer, outcome horizon, and population are fixed; procedure costs and additional time costs are zero.
\end{assumption}

\noindent Assumption \ref{ass:retention-stakes} imposes a setting in
which the customer would prefer to decline according to the stated value
measure. It does not infer that preference from the observed renewal
probability. In an application, informed valuations, subsequent regret,
or another justified measure would have to support the welfare
interpretation. Heterogeneous stakes or procedure-specific costs require
a different calculation.

The expected changes relative to direct choice separate the firm's and
customer's consequences:

\[
\Delta\Pi_k=\nu(s_k-s_0),\qquad
\Delta V_k=-\sigma(s_k-s_0).
\]

Here \(\Delta\Pi_k\) is expected profit and \(\Delta V_k\) is expected
customer value, both in dollars per eligible customer over the common
horizon. Increasing renewal raises profit and lowers customer value
under the imposed stakes. Their sum is \((\nu-\sigma)(s_k-s_0)\). A
positive combined change can therefore coexist with a loss borne by the
customer.

\hypertarget{M08-a-numerical-comparison}{%
\subsection{A Numerical Comparison}\label{M08-a-numerical-comparison}}

\noindent \noindent Suppose direct choice produces a renewal probability of 0.20.
An alternative procedure produces 0.10, and another produces 0.60. Set
firm margin to 11 dollars and customer loss from renewal to 10 dollars.
These are synthetic inputs. Relative to direct choice, the high-renewal
procedure raises expected firm profit by 4.40 dollars, reduces customer
value by 4 dollars, and raises combined surplus by 0.40 dollars per
eligible customer. Relative to the low-renewal procedure, it reduces
customer value by 5 dollars.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M08_retention_welfare.tex}
\caption{Synthetic changes in expected profit and customer value relative to direct renewal at probability 0.20. Firm margin is 11 dollars per renewal and customer loss is 10 dollars per renewal. The low-renewal procedure gives changes of -1.10 and +1 dollar; direct choice gives zero changes; the high-renewal procedure gives +4.40 and -4 dollars.}\label{fig:M08_retention_welfare}
\end{figure}

The two benchmarks answer different questions. Direct choice measures
the consequence of adding the preceding interaction. The low-renewal
procedure measures the consequence of selecting the firm's preferred
interaction instead of the customer's preferred one within this
particular set. Neither comparison establishes that every renewal is
harmful in other markets. The welfare result depends on the specified
preference ordering and fixed stakes.

\hypertarget{M08-what-repeated-experimentation-selects}{%
\subsection{What Repeated Experimentation
Selects}\label{M08-what-repeated-experimentation-selects}}

\noindent \noindent A firm can estimate each procedure's renewal probability and
deploy the one with the highest sample rate. More precise estimates
improve selection according to that objective. The implication for
customers depends on how the objective relates to their value.

\begin{assumption}[Stable Experimental Comparisons]
\label{ass:retention-testing}
The procedure set is specified before testing. Each procedure receives an independent sample of $T$ customers from the same population, with independent Bernoulli renewal outcomes of probability $s_k$ and complete observation over the common horizon. The probabilities remain unchanged at deployment. The firm selects a procedure with the largest sample renewal rate. The stakes in Assumption \ref{ass:retention-stakes} apply.
\end{assumption}

\noindent Under Assumption \ref{ass:retention-testing}, each sample rate
converges to its procedure's renewal probability as \(T\) grows. Because
the set is finite, the largest estimation error across the set also
converges to zero. The true renewal rate of the selected procedure
therefore converges to the largest available rate. Ties do not change
the welfare comparison because the common stakes assign the same
expected value to equal renewal probabilities.

The selected procedure consequently approaches the highest firm profit
and the lowest customer value in that set. The result is conditional on
opposed interests, stable response probabilities, and the specified
selection rule. Testing procedures with different products, prices, time
costs, or informed customer values requires those differences to enter
the objective. Accurate experimental measurement supplies evidence about
the measured outcome; it does not choose the appropriate objective for
the firm or regulator.

\hypertarget{M08-customer-control-and-the-evaluation-design}{%
\subsection{Customer Control and the Evaluation
Design}\label{M08-customer-control-and-the-evaluation-design}}

\noindent \noindent A cancellation evaluation should observe whether customers can
refuse optional retention content before exposure. A refusal button
available only after several required screens leaves the earlier
interaction compulsory. Record the entire path, time to completion,
additional charges, and eventual service use. Keep every eligible
assigned customer in the denominator, including people who abandon the
process.

An independent customer-value outcome can distinguish a useful retention
offer from a costly delay. A customer who voluntarily accepts a lower
price may benefit from the additional interaction. A customer who wants
to leave may lose time or incur another charge. Their common renewal
indicator conceals that difference. Report the financial, behavioral,
and customer-value outcomes together, with the population and horizon
that each represents.

\hypertarget{M08-reproduce-the-comparison}{%
\subsection{Reproduce the
Comparison}\label{M08-reproduce-the-comparison}}

\noindent \noindent The following program constructs the three imposed procedures
and compares their expected monetary consequences with direct choice. It
loads no outside records. The CSV has one row per procedure,
probabilities in fractions, and monetary changes in dollars per eligible
customer. The checks independently aggregate the high-renewal comparison
over 100 customers and reconcile it with the per-customer calculation.
Run the program from any directory with Python 3; it uses only the
standard library and writes its CSV and JSON beside the script.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/Lecture_Examples/retention_welfare.py}{retention\_welfare.py}.

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Synthetic retention procedures with fixed, opposed monetary stakes.

Run with Python 3 from any directory. Uses only the standard library.
No customer data are loaded. All probabilities and values are imposed.
Outputs are dollars per eligible customer relative to direct choice.
"""
from pathlib import Path
import csv
import json
from math import isclose


def evaluate(probabilities, direct, firm_margin, customer_loss):
    if not 0 <= direct <= 1:
        raise ValueError("Direct-choice probability must be in [0, 1].")
    if firm_margin < 0 or customer_loss < 0:
        raise ValueError("This example requires opposed nonnegative stakes.")
    rows = []
    for procedure, probability in probabilities.items():
        if not 0 <= probability <= 1:
            raise ValueError("Each renewal probability must be in [0, 1].")
        change = probability - direct
        profit = firm_margin * change
        value = -customer_loss * change
        rows.append({
            "procedure": procedure,
            "renewal_probability": probability,
            "firm_profit_change": round(profit, 10),
            "customer_value_change": round(value, 10),
            "combined_surplus_change": round(profit + value, 10),
        })
    return rows


def main():
    probabilities = {"low_renewal": 0.10, "direct": 0.20,
                     "high_renewal": 0.60}
    margin, loss = 11.0, 10.0
    rows = evaluate(probabilities, 0.20, margin, loss)
    low, direct, high = rows
    assert direct["firm_profit_change"] == 0
    assert direct["customer_value_change"] == 0
    # Independent expected-level calculations use 100 eligible customers.
    n = 100
    baseline_profit = n * 0.20 * margin
    selected_profit = n * 0.60 * margin
    assert isclose(high["firm_profit_change"],
                   (selected_profit - baseline_profit) / n)
    assert isclose(high["customer_value_change"], -40 * loss / n)
    assert high["firm_profit_change"] == 4.4
    assert high["customer_value_change"] == -4.0
    assert high["combined_surplus_change"] == 0.4
    assert isclose(high["customer_value_change"] -
                   low["customer_value_change"], -5.0)
    folder = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
    with (folder / "retention_welfare.csv").open("w", newline="") as f:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=list(rows[0]))
        writer.writeheader()
        writer.writerows(rows)
    report = {"input_type": "synthetic imposed probabilities and stakes",
              "unit": "dollars per eligible customer",
              "benchmark": "direct choice, renewal probability 0.20",
              "firm_margin": margin, "customer_loss_per_renewal": loss,
              "procedures": rows}
    (folder / "retention_welfare_results.json").write_text(
        json.dumps(report, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(json.dumps(report, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M08-regulatory-scope-and-a-marketing-recommendation}{%
\section{Regulatory Scope and a Marketing
Recommendation}\label{M08-regulatory-scope-and-a-marketing-recommendation}}

\noindent \noindent A manager considering a new price display, review summary, or
subscription process needs to identify which conduct a rule covers. The
relevant jurisdiction, product, effective date, and exceptions determine
how the legal source bears on the proposed action. A statute, binding
rule, agency interpretation, settlement, and proposed rule have
different authority. Their differences affect the inference an analyst
can draw from them.

As checked on November 2, 2026, the FTC's March 2026 negative-option
announcement seeks comments on possible amendments and refers to the
vacated 2024 rule. An advance notice does not itself adopt replacement
obligations. A subscription analysis must examine operative federal and
applicable state requirements rather than infer a current universal
cancellation rule from the title of an earlier announcement. The
\href{https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/03/ftc-seeks-public-comment-response-advance-notice-proposed-rulemaking-regarding-negative-option}{FTC
notice} identifies the procedural status.

A practical decision record states the action, customer population,
commercial objective, and expected customer consequences. It then
matches the relevant legal source to the conduct. For example, an
advertising claim requires support for the claim customers understand; a
review summary requires truthful provenance; and a consequential
delivery system requires attention to actual access. The
\href{../ETHICS_AND_REGULATION.md}{primary-source guide} records the
scope and status of the public sources used in these cases.

A firm can preserve a profitable service while reducing unwanted
interaction, improve the information customers receive, or redesign an
experiment to measure consequences outside its conversion objective.
Each proposal should name the affected outcome, an observable benchmark,
and the evidence that would support adoption.

\hypertarget{M08-pricing-communication-customer-outcomes-and-regulatory-evidence}{%
\section{Pricing Communication, Customer Outcomes, and Regulatory
Evidence}\label{M08-pricing-communication-customer-outcomes-and-regulatory-evidence}}

\noindent \noindent A firm considering a new pricing system must evaluate the
price rule, the information it uses, and the consequences for customers.
Public statements can identify questions for that evaluation. The
earnings-call interpretation cases in Section 5.14 separate price
displays, advertising prices, future tests, shelf-label infrastructure,
personalized promotions, and a statement about AI pricing. The
accompanying Python and source-linked case table reproduce the
classification exercise. These disclosures identify different objects
and evidence scopes.

A digital shelf label reduces the cost of updating posted prices. It
does not specify whether updates follow time, inventory, customer
attributes, or a common promotion. A personalized promotion can alter
the effective price without changing the posted shelf price. An
assessment therefore needs the offer, eligibility rule, input data,
realized prices, and available alternatives. Customer value also depends
on product suitability, search costs, information, and the ability to
decline. A commercial revenue result alone does not measure those
outcomes.

The
\href{https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/ftc_gov/pdf/p246202_surveillancepricing6bstudy_researchsummaries_redacted.pdf}{FTC's
January 2025 staff research summaries}, pages 1--3, describe US
intermediary tools involving price targeting, customer segmentation, and
product ranking. The document reports preliminary findings of a Section
6(b) study and explains limitations of its coverage. It is a research
publication with no rule effective date; its publication does not
establish a violation by a company in the earnings-call sample. Evaluate
a concrete practice against the applicable jurisdiction, conduct, and
current legal authority.

For a proposed promotion, specify which customers qualify, which
information determines the offer, and whether a common-price alternative
is available. Compare customer and firm outcomes under a credible
evaluation design. Use the call evidence to request missing operational
facts, and keep a dictionary match, a management assertion, verified
implementation, and measured customer effects distinct in the
recommendation.

\hypertarget{M08-reusable-code-customer-alternatives-and-economic-value}{%
\section{Reusable Code, Customer Alternatives, and Economic
Value}\label{M08-reusable-code-customer-alternatives-and-economic-value}}

\noindent \noindent A marketing team deciding whether to build a reusable analysis
package needs an expected workload and a comparable output. Saving time
on one run may leave the setup cost unrecovered. A service provider
selling the package faces a further question: how much value remains for
customers relative to the alternatives they can now use themselves?

\hypertarget{M08-reuse-requires-enough-comparable-uses}{%
\subsection{Reuse Requires Enough Comparable
Uses}\label{M08-reuse-requires-enough-comparable-uses}}

\noindent \noindent Let \(K\) be the initial hours needed to construct and
validate a reusable procedure. Let \(c_0\) be hours per completed
analysis under the existing process, \(c_1\) hours using the new
procedure, and \(m\) maintenance and adaptation hours per use. For \(n\)
uses within a common planning horizon, the net hours saved are

\[
H(n)=nc_0-\{K+n(c_1+m)\}.
\]

The comparison holds the required output and its quality fixed. All
hours refer to actual work in the two alternatives. If
\(c_0\leq c_1+m\), additional uses cannot recover a positive setup
burden. If \(c_0>c_1+m\), the break-even workload is \(K/(c_0-c_1-m)\).
A fractional threshold must be exceeded by an integer number of uses
before savings become positive.

In a hypothetical quarter, construction and validation take six hours.
Each existing analysis takes two hours, while the reusable procedure
takes 1.25 hours plus 0.25 hours for adaptation and upkeep. Net savings
are one-half hour per use before setup. Twelve uses recover setup
exactly; the thirteenth creates a positive saving. At 24 uses, total
effort falls from 48 to 42 hours. The 37.5\% reduction from two hours to
1.25 hours per execution becomes a 12.5\% reduction in total effort
after setup and upkeep at that workload.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M08_reuse_costs.tex}
\caption{The reusable procedure begins with six setup hours and crosses the existing process at twelve uses. Both produce outputs of the same required quality.}\label{fig:M08_reuse_costs}
\end{figure}

The mHealth aggregation functions are a useful setting for this
decision. They can preserve common keys, cohort rules, and
transformations across subsequent analyses. A new source with different
daily-total semantics still requires adaptation and checks. A smaller
documented function may remain more economical than a large package
whose dependencies and assumptions are costly to maintain. The numerical
workload and hours above are imposed; they do not measure development
time in the course repository.

\hypertarget{M08-shared-ai-improvements-can-narrow-a-feasible-price-interval}{%
\subsection{Shared AI Improvements Can Narrow a Feasible Price
Interval}\label{M08-shared-ai-improvements-can-narrow-a-feasible-price-interval}}

\noindent \noindent Consider a provider selling one analytics package per customer
over a specified period. A customer's delivered value is \(v\) dollars,
its non-price implementation burden is \(b\), and its best alternative
gives net utility \(u_0\), also in monetary-equivalent units. Under the
quasilinear participation condition in M4, Section 4.16, the largest
acceptable price is \(v-b-u_0\). The provider incurs fixed cost \(F\)
and unit cost \(c\). Conditional on \(n>0\) sales, a common price covers
those costs when

\[
c+\frac{F}{n}\leq p\leq v-b-u_0.
\]

The left endpoint is the seller's zero-profit price; the right endpoint
leaves the buyer indifferent to its alternative. Strictly positive gains
on both sides require a price strictly inside the interval. These are
participation and cost-recovery conditions for the stated valuations and
volume. They do not identify an equilibrium price or establish that the
assumed customers will purchase.

Hold delivered value at \$200, buyer burden at \$40, fixed cost at
\$1,000, and conditional volume at 50 customers. The following
hypothetical cases change the seller's unit cost and the customer's
outside option.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.15}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.21}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.21}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.21}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.22}}@{}}
\toprule
Scenario & Unit Cost & Outside-Option Utility & Seller Price Floor &
Buyer Price Ceiling \\
\midrule

Initial & \$20 & \$80 & \$40 & \$80 \\
Seller Automation & \$10 & \$80 & \$30 & \$80 \\
Shared Adoption & \$10 & \$140 & \$30 & \$20 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Seller automation lowers the price floor by ten dollars. If customers
subsequently gain a much better alternative, the ceiling falls below
that floor. At 50 sales, the assumed offer cannot simultaneously cover
the provider's stated costs and satisfy buyer participation. Product
improvements, lower buyer effort, or different costs could change the
comparison. Greater volume is a hypothesis requiring demand and capacity
evidence; it cannot simply be inserted to make the arithmetic favorable.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M08_ai_price_bounds.tex}
\caption{Seller automation lowers the cost-recovery floor, but a stronger customer alternative can lower the buyer ceiling below it. All amounts and the fifty-customer volume are hypothetical.}\label{fig:M08_ai_price_bounds}
\end{figure}

The provider's competitive advantage can therefore depend on reliable
integration, relevant proprietary inputs, or reduced customer effort,
provided those features create demonstrated value. Model access alone
may also improve the customer's alternative. Repeated accepted delivery,
willingness to pay, and costs over the full lifecycle determine whether
the proposed service is economically useful.

\hypertarget{M08-reproduce-the-cost-and-price-comparisons}{%
\subsection{Reproduce the Cost and Price
Comparisons}\label{M08-reproduce-the-cost-and-price-comparisons}}

\noindent \noindent Run
\texttt{python3\ 03\_Data\_and\_Code/AI\_Workflows/investment.py} with
Python 3.10 or later. The program uses only imposed inputs. It writes a
CSV of total hours for zero through 24 uses and another with one row per
pricing scenario. Hours and dollars remain separate units. Direct profit
and utility balances verify the pricing endpoints, and the reuse
calculation checks the zero-saving and first-positive-saving workloads.

\FloatBarrier
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Python source:
\href{../03_Data_and_Code/AI_Workflows/investment.py}{investment.py}

\begin{Verbatim}[breaklines,breakanywhere,fontsize=\small]
"""Conditional reuse costs and buyer/seller price bounds; all inputs are imposed."""
import csv
import json
from pathlib import Path

OUT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "results"


def reuse_hours(uses, setup, old_per_use, new_per_use, upkeep_per_use):
    if uses < 0 or min(setup, old_per_use, new_per_use, upkeep_per_use) < 0:
        raise ValueError("Uses and hours must be nonnegative")
    old = uses * old_per_use
    new = setup + uses * (new_per_use + upkeep_per_use)
    return old, new, old - new


def price_bounds(value, outside_utility, buyer_burden, unit_cost, fixed_cost, volume):
    if volume <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Conditional volume must be positive")
    # Quasilinear buyer utility: value - price - burden >= outside utility.
    ceiling = value - outside_utility - buyer_burden
    # Zero seller profit: volume * (price - unit_cost) >= fixed_cost.
    floor = unit_cost + fixed_cost / volume
    return floor, ceiling


def write_csv(name, rows):
    with (OUT / name).open("w", newline="") as f:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=list(rows[0]))
        writer.writeheader()
        writer.writerows(rows)


def main():
    OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    reuse = []
    for n in range(25):
        old, new, saved = reuse_hours(n, 6, 2, 1.25, 0.25)
        reuse.append({"uses": n, "old_hours": old,
                      "reusable_hours": new, "net_hours_saved": saved})
    assert reuse[12]["net_hours_saved"] == 0
    assert next(r["uses"] for r in reuse if r["net_hours_saved"] > 0) == 13
    assert reuse[24]["net_hours_saved"] == 6
    pricing = []
    for scenario, unit_cost, outside in [
        ("Initial", 20, 80), ("Seller automation", 10, 80), ("Shared adoption", 10, 140)
    ]:
        floor, ceiling = price_bounds(200, outside, 40, unit_cost, 1000, 50)
        # Direct monetary balances verify both boundary calculations.
        assert 50 * (floor - unit_cost) - 1000 == 0
        assert 200 - ceiling - 40 == outside
        pricing.append({"scenario": scenario, "unit_cost_dollars": unit_cost,
                        "fixed_cost_dollars": 1000, "conditional_volume": 50,
                        "value_dollars": 200, "buyer_burden_dollars": 40,
                        "outside_utility_dollars": outside,
                        "price_floor_dollars": floor, "price_ceiling_dollars": ceiling,
                        "feasible": floor <= ceiling})
    assert [r["feasible"] for r in pricing] == [True, True, False]
    write_csv("reuse_costs.csv", reuse)
    write_csv("price_bounds.csv", pricing)
    summary = {"scope": "Hypothetical equal-quality costs and monetary valuations.",
               "reuse_break_even_uses": 12, "first_positive_saving_uses": 13,
               "pricing": "Conditional on 50 sales; no demand or equilibrium is estimated.",
               "price_bounds": pricing}
    (OUT / "investment_results.json").write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=2) + "\n")
    print(json.dumps(summary, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\end{Verbatim}

\hypertarget{M08-model-updates-and-the-decision-to-revisit-an-analysis}{%
\section{Model Updates and the Decision to Revisit an
Analysis}\label{M08-model-updates-and-the-decision-to-revisit-an-analysis}}

\noindent \noindent A marketing team with a working analysis must decide whether a
model update warrants another development effort. The answer depends on
the unresolved task and the cost of changing its implementation. A
useful record connects the managerial objective to the observed failure,
the suspected cause, the comparison needed, and the conditions under
which the current output remains usable.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.33}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.33}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\columnwidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.34}}@{}}
\toprule
Recorded Difficulty & Change Worth Investigating & Appropriate
Comparison \\
\midrule

Pricing statements are retrieved with missing surrounding context &
Better retrieval or a model that handles the required context & New
complete calls with independently assessed labels \\
A generated join multiplies customer rows & A checked join helper or
clearer key specification & Hand-checkable duplicate cases and fresh
schemas \\
Unlogged meals are absent from mHealth records & Additional measurement
or a narrower recorded-behavior target & Evidence about logging coverage
and the chosen outcome \\
Delivery requires too much manual correction & A simpler procedure or
tested reusable components & Accepted output, total effort, and errors
across new tasks \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Record the actual accessible model and tools before evaluating a
proposed update. A capability described elsewhere may be unavailable in
the intended environment. Preserve the current procedure while
developing a challenger, then freeze the challenger and evaluate both on
fresh cases with the same criteria. Expected benefits should include
subsequent uses and downstream constraints; setup, verification, and
maintenance belong in the cost comparison.

A difficulty register is a provisional diagnosis. An update can matter
through a mechanism that the team failed to record, while an apparently
relevant update may offer no practical benefit. Some effort should
therefore examine alternative explanations and unanticipated uses. The
allocation depends on the value and cost of that exploration. Keeping a
previously validated procedure can be the appropriate decision when the
challenger fails to improve the relevant outcome.

Retain the executable code, input definitions, supported population,
checks, costs, and known failure conditions for each accepted procedure.
A model replacement, changed data schema, or shifted customer population
can invalidate parts of the earlier evidence. Revalidation should
address those dependencies explicitly. A larger code archive becomes
useful only when its contents improve subsequent work enough to justify
retrieval, adaptation, and upkeep.

\hypertarget{M08-revalidation-exposure-and-customer-consequences}{%
\subsection{Revalidation, Exposure, and Customer
Consequences}\label{M08-revalidation-exposure-and-customer-consequences}}

\noindent \noindent The cost of relying on an outdated result depends on how often
the workflow is used and what a failure does. If a configuration has
failure probability \(p\) over \(N\) comparable uses and loss \(L\) per
failure, its expected failure loss is \(NpL\). Independence across uses
is unnecessary for this expectation when each has the stated marginal
probability; dependence matters for the distribution of aggregate loss.
Falling error rates can coexist with substantial exposure as use
expands. The relevant acceptance threshold follows from consequences and
feasible alternatives.

The claim panel in Section 2.21 supplies hypotheses to revisit. Its
expiration categories allow residual effects and exceptions among
individual models. They do not establish that a deployment satisfies the
firm's reliability objective. The paired example in Section 7.22 shows
why a higher pooled score can coexist with greater stipulated loss. A
revalidation decision should connect the suspected change to recoveries,
regressions, downstream costs, and the remaining uses over which an
improvement can matter.

A fixed regression set detects recurrence of known problems. Fresh tasks
examine whether the procedure transfers. Changes to a judge or parser
should be evaluated separately using saved outputs, as in Section 5.18.
Record the intended upgrade, evidence used in selecting it, acceptance
criteria set before the final comparison, and a way to return to the
previous procedure. Review after relevant system or data changes, with
additional scrutiny where exposure and consequences are high. The
reported lifetime of selected research claims does not determine a
universal review interval.

For a marketing research bibliography, verify both whether a cited work
exists and whether it supports the assertion. A decline in fabricated
references does not eliminate erroneous details or unsupported uses of
real sources. Correct references also do not identify who authored a
document. For customer recommendations, assess factual support,
suitability, and the customer's ability to revise the choice. A changed
capability finding does not itself change those decision criteria.

\hypertarget{M08-consumer-agency-and-subscription-cancellation}{%
\section{Consumer Agency and Subscription
Cancellation}\label{M08-consumer-agency-and-subscription-cancellation}}

\noindent \noindent A subscription manager can increase retention through valuable
service, an understood price concession, or a difficult exit process.
These changes can generate similar payment records while producing
different customer consequences. Consumer agency concerns whether a
person can understand the offer, choose it, and revise that decision.
The evaluation should connect the interface to those capabilities before
treating retained revenue as evidence of successful relationship
management.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M08_agency_outcomes.tex}
\caption{Useful service and obstructed cancellation can both raise observed retention. Distinguishing them requires evidence about customer intent, comprehension, effective exit, and later charges.}\label{fig:M08_agency_outcomes}
\end{figure}

The cancellation-policy record illustrates why a manager must identify
the governing jurisdiction and legal instrument. The Eighth Circuit
vacated the FTC's 2024 Negative Option Rule on July 8, 2025 because of a
procedural deficiency. Effective February 12, 2026, the FTC restored the
earlier prenotification rule. A March 13, 2026 advance notice sought
comments on possible changes; it did not itself impose a replacement
cancellation obligation. The October 14, 2026 notice concerns
information collection under the restored rule. Sources:
\href{https://ecf.ca8.uscourts.gov/opndir/25/07/243137P.pdf}{court
opinion},
\href{https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-02-12/pdf/2026-02866.pdf}{February
action},
\href{https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-03-13/pdf/2026-04952.pdf}{March
notice}, and
\href{https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-14/pdf/2026-20971.pdf}{October
notice}.

Separate protections remain relevant. For covered online negative-option
transactions, ROSCA requires material-term disclosure, express informed
consent, and simple mechanisms to stop recurring charges. California
strengthened its Automatic Renewal Law effective July 1, 2025; the
Attorney General's guidance emphasizes online cancellation without
obstruction for online enrollment. New York City's rule took effect
October 1, 2026 and requires simple cancellation, with scope and sector
exceptions specified in the adopted text. Sources:
\href{https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-111publ345/pdf/PLAW-111publ345.pdf}{ROSCA
Section 4},
\href{https://oag.ca.gov/news/press-releases/attorney-general-bonta-issues-consumer-alert-california\%E2\%80\%99s-automatic-renewal-law}{California
guidance}, and
\href{https://www.nyc.gov/content/dam/nycgov/nyc-main/pdf/2026/Click-to-Cancel-Rule.pdf}{New
York City rule}. The legal-status check is dated November 5, 2026.

For an evaluation, record the first cancellation attempt, enrollment
channel, successful cancellation, elapsed time, subsequent charges, and
the customer's understanding of any accepted alternative. A voluntary
retention offer and a required obstacle can both precede continued
payment. Their classification depends on the consumer's feasible choices
and the applicable rule. New York City's rule permits retention offers
subject to restrictions against obstruction and unreasonable delay.
Treating every offer as prohibited would misstate that distinction.

\hypertarget{M08-mechanisms-beyond-exit-friction}{%
\subsection{Mechanisms Beyond Exit
Friction}\label{M08-mechanisms-beyond-exit-friction}}

\noindent \noindent Exit friction is one way agency can be weakened. Research on
choice architecture identifies other mechanisms that deserve separate
evaluation. \href{https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2023.0373}{Choice
Architecture, Privacy Valuations, and Selection Bias in Consumer Data}
shows in the retrieved earlier manuscript that defaults and anchors can
change stated privacy valuations and the composition of data supplied.
Increasing data volume can either worsen or reduce selection bias
depending on whose decisions change and how much coverage improves. A
consent-maximizing interface therefore needs an evaluation of
comprehension and representation alongside response rates.

\href{https://doi.org/10.1177/00222437231193343}{Is It as Bad as It
Looks?} compares cumulative and incremental quantitative scores. Its
full-text discussion reports that consumers infer less extreme
performance from a deviating score in cumulative form and can become
less likely to search for alternatives after a negative episode. A
platform deciding how to show ratings should assess whether consumers
understand both the latest performance and the historical record. Hiding
a material deterioration would be a possible misuse of the mechanism;
the experiment does not establish that all cumulative summaries are
deceptive.

\href{https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2022.1402}{Framing Price Increase as
Discount} examines reference-price manipulation in online retail. The
verified publisher abstract describes coordinated increases in selling
and reference prices that can make a higher price appear discounted. A
pricing evaluation should preserve transaction prices and the basis of
the comparison price over time. The paper supports a concrete concern
about the information supplied to consumers; it does not justify
treating every promotion as an agency violation. The full text remains
unavailable in this collection.

Immersive services present a broader control problem. The
residential-care evidence in
\href{https://doi.org/10.1177/00222429251319312}{Immersive Service}
connects agency to service boundaries, assigned roles, routines, and
opportunities for voice. Assessing desired control and feasible
responsibility can improve service design even where consumers need
substantial assistance. This differs from assuming that maximum
independent action is always the consumer's goal.

\hypertarget{M08-interpreting-the-literature-clusters}{%
\subsection{Interpreting the Literature
Clusters}\label{M08-interpreting-the-literature-clusters}}

\noindent \noindent Section 4.17 groups the retrieved, coded papers by their
mechanisms. Social influence is the largest cluster in that sample,
while emotion and identity is the most common overlapping feature.
Cancellation rules focus on a consequential mechanism even if exit
friction appears in fewer retrieved papers. A publication count gives
each paper equal weight and contains no measure of market exposure,
customer loss, or severity. A rare mechanism in the research sample can
affect many consumers.

The managerial implication is to select safeguards and outcome measures
at the mechanism level. Social influence calls for credible endorsement
and freedom from pressure. Disclosure and framing call for comprehension
and accurate comparisons. Personalization calls for evaluation of fit,
surplus, and control over data. Cancellation calls for effective
execution of the consumer's exit decision. The
\href{../01_Resources/13_Consumer_Agency_and_Recent_Research/CATALOG.md}{individual
review cards} preserve source-specific implications, and the
\href{../01_Resources/13_Consumer_Agency_and_Recent_Research/Policy/README.md}{policy
record} preserves legal scope and status.

\hypertarget{M08-ai-experimentation-and-personalized-pricing}{%
\section{AI Experimentation and Personalized
Pricing}\label{M08-ai-experimentation-and-personalized-pricing}}

\noindent A policy that improves a firm's experimental outcome still requires a
reasoned evaluation of the conduct it implements. Misra and his
coauthors' work on AI-assisted messaging and personalized pricing
supplies distinct cases: the first learns from within-campaign
experimental comparisons, while the second estimates demand and examines
the distribution of surplus. Marketing Dialectics, Sections 9.14--9.18,
examines their findings, safeguards, and remaining ethical questions.
Its original pricing example shows how a majority can benefit while
aggregate customer surplus falls, and how a restriction on personalized
offers can change both firm and customer outcomes.

The FTC's August 2026 proposed personalized-pricing statement cites Dubé
and Misra's pricing study. New York's disclosure requirements, proposed
surveillance-pricing restrictions, and price-gouging rules address
different conduct and legal conditions. A marketing recommendation must
specify the data use, offer, jurisdiction, and customer population. The
\href{../01_Resources/16_AI_Experimentation_and_Pricing/02_Policy/README.md}{policy
source record} distinguishes current law, proposals, and inquiries as
checked on November 6, 2026.

\hypertarget{M09-marketing-dialectics}{%
\chapter{Marketing Dialectics}\label{M09-marketing-dialectics}}

\noindent \Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\hypertarget{M09-when-a-commercial-result-becomes-a-claim-about-customers}{%
\section{When a Commercial Result Becomes a Claim About
Customers}\label{M09-when-a-commercial-result-becomes-a-claim-about-customers}}

\noindent \noindent A subscription manager must decide whether to retain a
cancellation sequence that raises paid renewal. One explanation is that
the sequence helps customers discover a service feature they value.
Another is that it makes leaving sufficiently difficult that some
customers continue paying against their wishes. Both mechanisms can
produce the same billing record. The decision therefore depends on the
reasons for renewal, the customer's understanding of the offer, and the
practical ability to refuse it.

The claim that higher renewal demonstrates customer benefit contains a
premise: continued payment expresses an informed wish to continue at the
stated terms. That premise requires evidence. A manager can calculate
renewal accurately and still draw an unjustified conclusion about the
customer. Equally, the existence of a retention offer does not establish
manipulation. A relevant discount, clearly explained and freely refused,
can improve the customer's available options.

Kant's critique of dialectical reasoning asks how reason comes to treat
its own demands for explanation as knowledge about objects. In a
marketing application, the corresponding discipline is to identify what
connects an observed result to a broader claim. This is an adaptation of
Kant's critical approach to an empirical decision. A disputed
interpretation of a customer metric is not, by itself, a transcendental
antinomy. The philosophical connection concerns the examination of
premises and the limits of a conclusion.

Three questions organize the decision. What does the evidence establish
about the practice? Which assumptions connect that finding to customer
interests? Which ethical principles justify the action? A favorable
answer to one question leaves the others substantive. An experiment may
identify an increase in purchases while leaving the quality of consent
unresolved. A transparent offer may respect a customer's choice while
producing too little revenue to remain commercially viable.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\input{figures/M09_claim_scope.tex}
\caption{A commercial outcome, a customer outcome, and an ethical judgment require different supporting premises.}\label{fig:M09_claim_scope}
\end{figure}

The upper path connects an intervention to a measured commercial outcome
through a causal design. A second path requires a valid customer outcome
measure and a defined comparison. The ethical judgment additionally
depends on a stated principle concerning treatment of persons. No arrow
permits sales to stand in for all three conclusions.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}

\hypertarget{M09-kants-dialectic-and-the-limits-of-reason}{%
\section{Kant's Dialectic and the Limits of
Reason}\label{M09-kants-dialectic-and-the-limits-of-reason}}

\noindent \hypertarget{M09-the-search-for-an-unconditioned-explanation}{%
\subsection{The Search for an Unconditioned
Explanation}\label{M09-the-search-for-an-unconditioned-explanation}}

\noindent \noindent In the \emph{Critique of Pure Reason}, the understanding
organizes experience through concepts and judgments. Reason seeks
relations among those judgments and asks for more complete explanations.
Given something conditioned, it looks for the condition on which it
depends. Repeating that question creates a demand for an unconditioned
ground that would complete the explanation. The difficulty arises when
the demand for completeness is treated as establishing an object that
theoretical reason can know independently of possible experience. Kant
develops this account in the introduction to the Transcendental
Dialectic, especially A293/B349 through A308/B365. The A and B
references identify the original first- and second-edition pagination.
\href{https://www.gutenberg.org/files/4280/4280-h/4280-h.htm}{Kant,
\emph{Critique of Pure Reason}}

Kant distinguishes transcendental illusion from a mistake that
disappears once a faulty inference is corrected. The attraction of an
unconditional explanation persists after criticism has exposed its
source. The task of critique is to prevent that attraction from becoming
an unjustified judgment. This distinction gives an important reason to
revisit assumptions. Recognizing a tempting inference once does not
guarantee that an attractive new result will cease to invite it.

The three major divisions of the Dialectic concern the soul, the world
as a whole, and God. The paralogisms examine inferences from the unity
of thinking to claims about the soul as an object. The antinomies
concern opposed arguments about the world considered as a completed
totality. The ideal of pure reason concerns the supposed highest being
and attempts to establish its existence. These are specific arguments
within Kant's critical philosophy. Their marketing relevance comes from
the practice of examining the transition from a valid use of reason to
an unsupported claim, rather than from equating a customer segment,
dataset, or company with one of these metaphysical objects.

\hypertarget{M09-antinomies-and-the-shared-premise}{%
\subsection{Antinomies and the Shared
Premise}\label{M09-antinomies-and-the-shared-premise}}

\noindent \noindent Kant presents four cosmological conflicts: whether the world
has limits in time and space; whether composite substances ultimately
consist of simple parts; whether causality through freedom is necessary
alongside natural causality; and whether an absolutely necessary being
exists. The apparent strength of opposing arguments calls attention to
their common framework. In Kant's diagnosis, treating the world of
appearances as a completed whole of things in themselves generates the
conflict. His resolutions depend on the particular antinomy. The
mathematical and dynamical antinomies do not all receive an identical
verdict. The \emph{Prolegomena}, §§50--54, supplies a shorter treatment.
\href{https://www.gutenberg.org/files/52821/52821-h/52821-h.htm}{Kant,
\emph{Prolegomena}}

The third antinomy is especially relevant to discussions of prediction
and agency. Its thesis argues for a causality through freedom; its
antithesis argues that events occur through natural laws. Kant's
critical solution distinguishes the explanation of events as appearances
from the intelligible standpoint under which freedom can be thought. The
first Critique's resolution does not supply an empirical demonstration
that a particular choice was free. Interpretations of transcendental
idealism and the relationship between these standpoints remain disputed.
\href{https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant-transcendental-idealism/}{Stang,
\emph{Kant's Transcendental Idealism}}

A marketing model that predicts a purchase therefore does not settle a
metaphysical question about freedom. Prediction can reflect stable
preferences, recurring needs, constraints, exposure, or a combination of
these. Conversely, an unpredictable choice can arise from poor
measurement or random error. Neither predictive success nor prediction
